conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What is anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: A severe, life-threatening, generalised (usually IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction with rapid onset and airway, breathing and/or circulation compromise. It is a clinical diagnosis and a time-critical emergency.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What is the single most important treatment in anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Prompt intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh — given immediately, without waiting for IV access, antihistamines or steroids. Delayed adrenaline is associated with fatal outcomes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What clinical combination makes anaphylaxis likely?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Sudden onset of a life-threatening Airway, Breathing and/or Circulation problem, usually (but not always) with skin/mucosal changes, after exposure to a likely allergen. The ABC problem is what defines anaphylaxis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: How does anaphylaxis differ from a mild/moderate allergic reaction?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: A mild/moderate reaction has skin symptoms (urticaria, itch, swelling) WITHOUT airway, breathing or circulation compromise; anaphylaxis has ABC involvement and requires immediate IM adrenaline.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: Can anaphylaxis occur without skin changes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Yes — skin changes are absent or subtle in up to ~20% of cases. Do not withhold adrenaline just because there is no rash if there is an ABC problem after allergen exposure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What are the commonest triggers of anaphylaxis in children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Foods lead in children — cow's milk, egg, peanut, tree nuts, sesame, fish/shellfish, wheat and soya; also insect stings, drugs (e.g. penicillins, NSAIDs) and latex.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What airway features suggest anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
• Tongue/lip/throat swelling
  • throat tightness
  • a hoarse voice
  • and stridor.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What breathing features suggest anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
• Wheeze
  • breathlessness
  • increased work of breathing
  • falling SpO₂
  • cyanosis
  • and exhaustion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What circulatory features suggest anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
• Pallor
  • floppiness
  • tachycardia
  • hypotension (age-specific)
  • dizziness
  • collapse
  • and reduced consciousness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: Which features tend to predominate in children versus adults in anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Respiratory features (wheeze, stridor) often predominate in children, whereas shock/hypotension is relatively more common in adults — but any ABC involvement means anaphylaxis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What is the IM adrenaline dose for a child aged 6 months to 6 years?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: 150 micrograms of 1:1000 adrenaline (0.15 mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What is the IM adrenaline dose for a child aged 6–12 years?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: 300 micrograms of 1:1000 adrenaline (0.3 mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What is the IM adrenaline dose for a child over 12 years (and adults)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: 500 micrograms of 1:1000 adrenaline (0.5 mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What is the IM adrenaline dose for an infant under 6 months?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: 100–150 micrograms of 1:1000 adrenaline (0.1–0.15 mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: By what route and site is adrenaline given in anaphylaxis, and how often can it be repeated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh; repeat the same dose after 5 minutes if there is no improvement.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: How should a child in anaphylaxis be positioned?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
• Lie flat and raise the legs if there is circulatory compromise;
  • sit up if breathing is the main problem;
  • recovery position if unconscious.
Do NOT suddenly sit or stand the child up — a sudden posture change can cause fatal cardiac arrest.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: After giving IM adrenaline, what supportive measures are used?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
• High-flow oxygen (15 L/min via a non-rebreathe mask),
  • an IV crystalloid fluid bolus (10 mL/kg) for circulatory compromise,
  • monitoring,
  • and treating wheeze as for asthma (e.g. salbutamol).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What defines refractory anaphylaxis and how is it managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Anaphylaxis with no improvement after 2 appropriate doses of IM adrenaline; it requires an IV adrenaline infusion given with expert (senior/critical care) help.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: Which drugs are no longer given routinely in acute anaphylaxis, and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone — they do not treat the ABC problem (Resuscitation Council UK). Management focuses on adrenaline, oxygen and fluids. An oral non-sedating antihistamine may help residual skin symptoms afterwards, and a steroid may still be considered after initial resuscitation in refractory anaphylaxis or where there is coexisting asthma or ongoing shock.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What is a biphasic reaction, and why does it matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
A recurrence of anaphylaxis symptoms hours after the initial reaction without re-exposure. Because of this risk, every child under 16 given emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis is ADMITTED under a paediatric medical team (NICE). Observation is then risk-stratified:
  • 2 h from resolution if a single IM dose given within 30 min of onset gave a good response and observations are normal;
  • at least 6 h if 2 doses were needed or there is a previous biphasic reaction;
  • at least 12 h if more than 2 doses were needed, severe asthma or respiratory compromise, possible continuing allergen absorption, or difficult access to emergency care.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: Which blood test helps confirm anaphylaxis, and when is it indicated in a child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
Mast cell tryptase — but it is of limited value in children (NICE). In under-16s take timed samples ONLY if the trigger is thought to be venom, a drug, or idiopathic — not for food-triggered anaphylaxis, where tryptase is often normal. When indicated:
  • one sample as soon as possible after treatment starts,
  • another at about 1–2 hours (within 4 hours of onset),
  • and a baseline later at follow-up.
Anaphylaxis remains a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What should be prescribed and arranged after an episode of anaphylaxis in a child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
• Two adrenaline auto-injectors (MHRA), which the child and carers must carry at all times and replace before they expire, with training for the child, carers and school;
  • a written allergy action plan;
  • trigger identification and avoidance;
  • admission under a paediatric team for any child under 16;
  • referral to a paediatric allergy specialist;
  • and consideration of medical alert identification.
Safety-net: after using a device, call 999 and say “anaphylaxis” even if the child seems better.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: Why are TWO adrenaline auto-injectors prescribed rather than one?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: A second dose may be needed if there is no improvement after 5 minutes, and a device may misfire or be unavailable — so a spare ensures a repeat dose can always be given.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What auto-injector strengths are available and roughly how are they chosen?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: 150 microgram and 300 microgram devices, prescribed by weight — roughly 150 mcg for about 7.5–25 kg and 300 mcg above that.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What are the major complications of anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back:
• Airway obstruction,
  • respiratory failure and cardiac arrest (death, especially with delayed adrenaline),
  • a biphasic reaction,
  • hypoxic-ischaemic injury from prolonged shock,
  • and psychological impact.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: Why must adrenaline not be delayed while giving antihistamines or steroids?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Adrenaline is the only treatment that reverses the airway, breathing and circulation compromise; antihistamines and steroids do not, and delaying adrenaline is linked to fatal outcomes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What co-factors can lower the threshold for or worsen anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Exercise, intercurrent viral illness, and NSAIDs can act as co-factors that increase the severity or likelihood of a reaction to a given allergen.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: A child eats a peanut and rapidly develops wheeze and stridor but no rash. Is this anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Yes — sudden airway/breathing compromise after a likely allergen is anaphylaxis even without skin changes; give IM adrenaline immediately.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What concentration of adrenaline is used for the IM route in anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) adrenaline for the intramuscular route; 1:10,000 is reserved for IV use (e.g. cardiac arrest or specialist IV infusion), not routine IM anaphylaxis treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.front: What should be done with the trigger during acute management of anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.back: Remove or stop the trigger where possible (e.g. stop a drug/blood infusion, remove a stinger) — but never delay adrenaline to do so.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What two tools underpin the assessment of childhood growth and puberty?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: The growth chart (serial plotting, centiles, and mid-parental/target height) and bone age (left-wrist X-ray) — delayed in constitutional delay and hypothyroidism, advanced in precocious puberty and CAH.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How is mid-parental (target) height calculated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Boys = (mother's + father's height)/2 + 7 cm; girls = (mother's + father's height)/2 − 7 cm, with a target range of roughly ± 8–10 cm.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Define short stature.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Height below the 2nd centile — with the 0.4th centile line on UK growth charts (RCPCH) the usual threshold prompting referral — or crossing centiles downward, or well below the mid-parental (target) height. The growth pattern over time matters more than a single measurement.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How does familial short stature differ from constitutional delay on bone age?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Familial short stature has a NORMAL bone age (the child is simply short like the parents)
  • constitutional delay of growth and puberty has a DELAYED bone age and reaches a normal final height.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What is constitutional delay of growth and puberty?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: A common, benign 'late bloomer' pattern (especially in boys, often with a family history) with delayed bone age; the child is short and enters puberty late but reaches a normal final adult height.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Which endocrine causes of short stature should you consider?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Growth hormone deficiency
  • hypothyroidism
  • and Cushing's syndrome / exogenous steroids (a short but often overweight child).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Which syndrome must always be excluded in a short girl?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Turner syndrome — check a karyotype.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Which chronic diseases commonly cause faltering growth / short stature?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Coeliac disease
  • inflammatory bowel disease
  • chronic kidney disease and other chronic illness
  • also undernutrition, psychosocial deprivation, and being small for gestational age (IUGR).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What investigations are used in the work-up of short stature?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Bone age
  • TFTs
  • coeliac serology
  • U&E
  • FBC/CRP
  • karyotype in girls (Turner)
  • and IGF-1 with a GH stimulation test if GH deficiency is suspected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How is GH deficiency treated, and in which other conditions is growth hormone approved?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
Recombinant human growth hormone, specialist-initiated and monitored. It is also approved (NICE) for growth failure in
  • Turner syndrome
  • Prader-Willi syndrome
  • chronic renal insufficiency
  • SHOX deficiency
  • and children born small for gestational age with persistent growth failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Define precocious puberty.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls or before age 9 in boys.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Distinguish central from peripheral precocious puberty.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Central (gonadotrophin-dependent, 'true') = early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis with consonant puberty and raised LH/FSH.
  • Peripheral (gonadotrophin-independent) = sex steroids from gonads/adrenals independent of the axis, with suppressed LH/FSH.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Why is precocious puberty in a boy more concerning than in a girl?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: In girls central precocious puberty is usually idiopathic, but in boys it is more often pathological (e.g. a CNS lesion) — so an MRI brain is important.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Name causes of peripheral (gonadotrophin-independent) precocious puberty.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
  • adrenal or gonadal tumours
  • McCune-Albright syndrome (café-au-lait patches, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia)
  • and exogenous steroids.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What are premature thelarche and premature adrenarche?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Benign normal variants: premature thelarche is isolated breast development, and premature adrenarche is isolated early pubic hair — without other progressing pubertal signs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How is central precocious puberty managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: With GnRH analogues, which halt pubertal progression and help preserve final adult height; treat any underlying cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What investigations are used in precocious puberty?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Bone age (advanced)
  • basal and GnRH-stimulated LH/FSH
  • sex steroids
  • 17-OHP
  • pelvic ultrasound in girls
  • and MRI brain in all boys with central precocious puberty, and in girls under 6 or with rapid progression or neurological signs — in girls aged 6–8 it is usually idiopathic, so imaging is selective.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Define delayed puberty.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Absence of secondary sexual characteristics by age 13 in girls or age 14 in boys.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What is the commonest cause of delayed puberty?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty, particularly in boys (family history, delayed bone age) — a benign self-limiting variant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Give causes of hypogonadotrophic (low LH/FSH) delayed puberty.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Constitutional delay
  • chronic illness
  • undernutrition
  • excessive exercise / low weight / anorexia
  • hypothalamic-pituitary disease
  • and Kallmann syndrome (isolated GnRH deficiency with anosmia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Give causes of hypergonadotrophic (high LH/FSH) delayed puberty.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
Primary gonadal failure —
  • Turner syndrome (girls)
  • Klinefelter syndrome (boys)
  • and gonadal damage from chemotherapy/radiotherapy, torsion or infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What is Kallmann syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (GnRH deficiency) associated with anosmia (loss of smell), causing delayed puberty with low LH/FSH.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How is delayed puberty due to constitutional delay managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Reassurance is the mainstay. If the young person is distressed, a short course of low-dose sex steroids can be used to induce puberty — low-dose testosterone in boys, low-dose oestrogen in girls — which kick-starts puberty without costing final height. Otherwise treat any underlying cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Why is congenital hypothyroidism screened for at birth?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: It is one of the commonest preventable causes of intellectual disability — early levothyroxine ensures normal neurodevelopment. It is detected on the newborn blood-spot screen (still often called the Guthrie test), taken at around day 5, which measures TSH (raised in primary disease).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What is the commonest cause of congenital hypothyroidism?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Thyroid dysgenesis — an absent (agenesis) or ectopic thyroid gland. Other causes include dyshormonogenesis (enzyme defects), iodine deficiency, and rarely central TSH deficiency. Because the UK screen measures TSH, it detects primary disease but MISSES central (secondary) hypothyroidism, where TSH is low or normal — so a normal screen does not exclude it.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What are the clinical features of congenital hypothyroidism if it is missed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Prolonged neonatal jaundice
  • poor feeding
  • constipation
  • hypotonia
  • lethargy
  • a large tongue (macroglossia)
  • coarse features
  • an umbilical hernia
  • a large posterior fontanelle
  • and later developmental delay.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How is congenital hypothyroidism treated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Levothyroxine started urgently once a screen-positive result is confirmed — aim to be on treatment by about 2 weeks of age. Typical starting dose 10–15 micrograms/kg once daily (BNFC), titrated against thyroid function and growth. The earlier treatment starts, the better the neurodevelopmental outcome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What is congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), and what is the commonest enzyme defect?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: An autosomal recessive disorder of adrenal steroid synthesis; the commonest form is 21-hydroxylase deficiency, causing reduced cortisol (± aldosterone) with precursors shunted into androgens, and raised ACTH driving adrenal hyperplasia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How does CAH present in girls at birth?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: With virilisation / ambiguous genitalia (clitoromegaly, labial fusion) due to excess androgens.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Describe the salt-losing crisis in CAH.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Typically at ~1–3 weeks (especially boys, who look normal at birth): vomiting, poor feeding, weight loss, dehydration and shock, with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia — potentially fatal.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What is the diagnostic biochemical marker of 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP); the salt-losing picture shows low sodium, high potassium, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How is an adrenal (salt-losing) crisis in CAH managed acutely?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Resuscitate with IV hydrocortisone — give it IM if there is no IV access, rather than delaying while cannulating — plus IV 0.9% saline and glucose, and correct the electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: What is the long-term management of CAH?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) replacement, plus mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) and salt supplements in salt-losers
  • monitor growth and bone age
  • sick-day rules (increase the oral hydrocortisone when febrile or unwell), a steroid emergency card, and an emergency intramuscular hydrocortisone kit at home with parental training — a vomiting child cannot absorb oral steroid
  • and MDT input on genital surgery decisions.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: How can CAH present in a non-classic/milder form later in childhood?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: With premature pubic hair (peripheral, gonadotrophin-independent precocious puberty), hirsutism and acne, and in adolescent girls oligomenorrhoea; plus a growth pattern of a tall child who becomes a short adult (early growth spurt with early epiphyseal fusion from excess androgens).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: In which conditions is bone age delayed versus advanced?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• Delayed in constitutional delay of growth and puberty and in hypothyroidism
  • advanced in precocious puberty and in CAH (androgen excess).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Why can excess androgens in CAH or precocious puberty ultimately reduce final adult height?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: They cause an early growth spurt but also advance bone age and cause early epiphyseal fusion, so the child stops growing sooner — tall as a child but short as an adult.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: A short girl with delayed puberty has high LH/FSH. Which diagnosis should you actively exclude and how?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: Turner syndrome (primary gonadal failure) — confirm with a karyotype.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Which childhood endocrine conditions are considered emergencies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back:
• An adrenal (salt-losing) crisis in CAH
  • and untreated congenital hypothyroidism (an emergency for the developing brain, hence early treatment).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.front: Where are Type 1 diabetes and DKA covered, and why not here?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.back: They are covered in the Endocrinology resource; this paediatric umbrella focuses on growth, puberty and congenital endocrine disorders to avoid duplication.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What are the birth injuries covered here, and the organising principle?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
Brachial plexus injuries sustained during delivery (often with shoulder dystocia), classified by the nerve roots involved. The root level predicts the deformity:
  • upper roots (C5-6) = Erb's palsy ('waiter's tip')
  • lower roots (C8-T1) = Klumpke's (claw hand).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What is the prognosis and general management of brachial plexus birth injuries?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: Most recover spontaneously with physiotherapy; refer early to a specialist brachial plexus service and physiotherapy, with assessment for nerve surgery if no recovery by ~3 months. They are associated with shoulder dystocia and large babies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Contrast Erb's and Klumpke's palsy in one line each.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
• Erb's (C5-6): arm adducted/internally rotated, pronated ('waiter's tip'); associated with shoulder dystocia/macrosomia.
  • Klumpke's (C8-T1): claw hand +/- Horner's; rarer.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What is Erb's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: The commonest neonatal brachial plexus birth injury — paralysis of the upper arm and shoulder from injury to the C5-C6 nerve roots during delivery, producing the classic 'waiter's tip' posture.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What is the mechanism of Erb's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: During a difficult delivery, excessive lateral traction / widening of the head-to-shoulder angle stretches (or ruptures/avulses) the upper trunk (C5-C6), which supplies the shoulder abductors/external rotators and elbow flexors. The hand (C8-T1) is spared.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Describe the 'waiter's tip' posture of Erb's palsy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: Arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist and fingers flexed (palm facing backward/outward).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Which movements are lost in Erb's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
• Shoulder abduction/external rotation
  • elbow flexion
  • and forearm supination.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What is the reflex pattern in Erb's palsy, and why is it useful?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: Moro absent on the affected side; grasp reflex PRESERVED (C8-T1 spared) — this distinguishes Erb's from Klumpke's/total palsy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: List the risk factors for Erb's palsy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
• Shoulder dystocia (classic)
  • macrosomia/large-for-dates (often maternal/gestational diabetes)
  • instrumental delivery
  • breech
  • prolonged/difficult labour
  • high maternal BMI
  • and a previous baby with a brachial plexus injury.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Which associated injuries should you check for in Erb's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
• Clavicle/humeral fracture (co-exist with shoulder dystocia) — confirm on X-ray if suspected, but management is conservative with analgesia and gentle handling, uniting in a couple of weeks with a callus lump that resolves
  • Facial nerve palsy (compression, classically after forceps) — unilateral lower-motor-neurone weakness most obvious on crying, managed with eye protection and observation, almost all resolving in weeks
  • Phrenic nerve palsy (C3-5 → ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paralysis → respiratory distress).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What does the presence of Horner's syndrome indicate in a brachial plexus birth injury?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: T1 involvement → a more extensive injury and worse prognosis (Horner's is classically associated with Klumpke's/lower-plexus injury).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: How is Erb's palsy managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
Mostly CONSERVATIVELY:
  • physiotherapy/OT (gentle passive range-of-movement + positioning to prevent contractures)
  • parental support
  • early referral to a specialist brachial plexus MDT
  • and watchful waiting
Surgery (nerve grafting/reconstruction, ~3-6 months) only if no meaningful recovery by ~3 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What is the prognosis of Erb's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
Good — ~80-90% recover fully or nearly fully within the first year (especially milder stretch injuries). Poorer prognosis:
  • no recovery by 3 months
  • Horner's (T1 involvement/avulsion)
  • or total plexus (C5-T1) involvement.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: How does correct shoulder dystocia management prevent Erb's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: The injury is linked to excessive traction on the fetal head; the correct response to shoulder dystocia is the McRoberts manoeuvre + suprapubic pressure, NOT traction on the head.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What is Klumpke's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: A lower brachial plexus birth injury (C8-T1) paralysing the intrinsic hand muscles and long finger flexors — the classic 'claw hand'. It is the rarer, more severe counterpart to Erb's palsy and is classically associated with Horner's syndrome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: What is the mechanism of Klumpke's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: Traction on an ABDUCTED/overhead arm (classically the arm pulled upward, or a difficult breech), stretching/avulsing the lower trunk (C8-T1) which supplies the intrinsic hand muscles and finger/wrist flexors. T1 carries sympathetic fibres to the eye — hence Horner's.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Describe the 'claw hand' of Klumpke's palsy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: Paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals/interossei) → hyperextension at the MCP joints + flexion at the IP joints; forearm may be supinated, wrist extended.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Which movements/reflexes are lost in Klumpke's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: Intrinsic hand muscles + wrist/finger flexors (fine hand function) are lost, and the grasp reflex is ABSENT. Shoulder and elbow movement are preserved (upper plexus intact — distinguishes from Erb's).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Where is the sensory loss in Klumpke's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: Over the medial (ulnar) aspect of the forearm and hand (C8-T1 dermatomes).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Why is Horner's syndrome important in Klumpke's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: Ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis (+/- enophthalmos) indicates T1 root avulsion — a marker of severe injury and a poor prognostic sign.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: List the risk factors for Klumpke's palsy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
• Traction on an abducted/hyperabducted arm (pulled over the head)
  • difficult breech delivery (classic)
  • shoulder dystocia
  • instrumental delivery
  • and macrosomia/large-for-dates (maternal/gestational diabetes).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: How is Klumpke's palsy managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back:
Conservative first-line:
  • physiotherapy/OT with passive range-of-movement
  • splinting (wrist/hand, given the claw deformity)
  • and positioning to prevent contractures
  • early referral to a specialist brachial plexus MDT
Surgery (nerve reconstruction, ~3-6 months) is needed more often than in Erb's.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.front: Why is Klumpke's palsy prognosis worse than Erb's?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.back: The lower roots (especially T1) are more frequently avulsed (rather than stretched), so spontaneous full recovery is less likely and surgery is more often required. Horner's syndrome marks a severe (T1 avulsion) injury with poorer prognosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back: A permanent disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive lesion of the developing brain (motor pathways). It is the commonest cause of physical disability in childhood (~2-2.5 per 1000 births), often accompanied by disturbances of sensation, cognition, communication, behaviour and epilepsy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: Why is the brain lesion 'static but evolving', and what does regression imply?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back: The brain injury is non-progressive (doesn't worsen), but its clinical manifestations evolve as the child grows — presenting as delayed/abnormal motor milestones, not regression. Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) is NOT cerebral palsy — think a neurodegenerative/metabolic disorder.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: What is the timing distribution of CP causes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back:
• Antenatal ~80% (commonest): cerebral malformations, congenital (TORCH) infection, vascular events, genetic
  • Perinatal ~10%: HIE (birth asphyxia), prematurity (PVL/IVH), kernicterus
  • Postnatal ~10%: meningitis/encephalitis, head injury (incl. NAI), intracranial haemorrhage, hypoglycaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: Which lesion classically underlies spastic diplegia, and its key risk factor?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) — white-matter damage; the key risk factor is prematurity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: How is CP classified by motor type, and what does each localise to?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back:
• Spastic (~70%) — UMN/motor cortex & pyramidal tracts (increased tone, hyperreflexia, clonus)
  • Dyskinetic (~10%) — basal ganglia (athetosis, chorea, dystonia, oro-motor problems; often kernicterus/HIE)
  • Ataxic (~5%) — cerebellum (incoordination, intention tremor, ataxic gait, hypotonia)
  • Mixed.

• Hemiplegia (one side, arm often > leg; may present as early hand preference <12 months)
  • Diplegia (all four limbs but LEGS >> arms — classic of prematurity/PVL; scissoring/tiptoe gait)
  • Quadriplegia (all four limbs + trunk, most severe; highest rate of seizures, cognitive impairment, feeding problems).

• Delayed motor milestones (not sitting by 8 months, not walking by 18 months, no hand function by 1 year)
  • abnormal tone (early hypotonia → later spasticity/dystonia)
  • abnormal movements/posture/asymmetry
  • persistent primitive reflexes
  • feeding difficulties/faltering growth
  • delayed speech
  • and gait abnormalities (tiptoe/scissoring).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: What are the NICE motor red flags for CP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back:
• Not sitting by 8 months (corrected)
  • not walking by 18 months
  • hand preference before 1 year
  • and persistent toe-walking.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: List the key neuro/sensory comorbidities of CP.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back:
• Learning disability (~half)
  • epilepsy (~a third)
  • visual impairment (squint, cortical visual impairment)
  • hearing impairment
  • speech & language/communication difficulties
  • behavioural/emotional problems
  • sleep disturbance
  • and chronic pain.

• Feeding difficulties
  • GORD
  • aspiration
  • faltering growth (may need gastrostomy)
  • drooling
  • constipation
  • and orthopaedic problems — hip subluxation/dislocation, scoliosis, contractures (secondary to spasticity).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: What is the role of MRI in CP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back: To investigate the aetiology (PVL, malformation, HIE) — recommended if the cause isn't clear. It won't accurately date a hypoxic-ischaemic injury, and subtle changes may not appear until ~2 years. Diagnosis is largely clinical.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: When should genetic/metabolic testing be considered in suspected CP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back: If the presentation is atypical or there is regression — to exclude a progressive (neurodegenerative/metabolic) disorder, which is not CP.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: What is the overarching approach to CP management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back: MDT approach — no cure; the goal is to maximise function, participation and quality of life and manage comorbidities. Team: paediatrician, physiotherapist, OT, SALT, dietitian, orthotist, orthopaedics, neurology, social care, education.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: Outline the management of spasticity in CP.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back:
• Physiotherapy + OT (mainstay)
  • Oral baclofen first for ongoing generalised spasticity, started low and titrated over about 4 weeks
  • oral diazepam as a bedtime dose for painful spasm, switching to baclofen if long-term treatment is needed (NICE)
  • Botulinum toxin A for focal spasticity, always with continued physiotherapy and an orthosis
  • Intrathecal baclofen for severe generalised spasticity
  • selective dorsal rhizotomy for selected AMBULANT children with spastic diplegia (GMFCS II–III, aged 3–9)
  • orthopaedic surgery for contractures, hips and scoliosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.front: Besides spasticity, what other management does CP require?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.back: Antiseizure medication for epilepsy; analgesia for pain; and management of comorbidities — feeding (SALT, gastrostomy for unsafe swallow), GORD, drooling (glycopyrronium, licensed over age 3 in chronic neurological disorders), constipation, hip surveillance (a UK-wide programme of clinical review plus a pelvic X-ray to measure migration percentage, at intervals set by GMFCS level — negligible risk at level I, around 90% at level V), bone health, vision/hearing support, communication aids — plus family/carer support, education and social care.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the organising principle for the childhood exanthems?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Pattern recognition — recognise the classic (mostly viral) infectious rashes by their rash pattern, prodrome and associated features.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Match each classic exanthem to its hallmark: measles, rubella, slapped cheek, roseola, hand-foot-mouth, scarlet fever, chickenpox.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Measles — Koplik spots, 3 C's, descending rash.
  • Rubella — mild, post-auricular nodes.
  • Slapped cheek — parvovirus B19.
  • Roseola — high fever then rash.
  • Hand-foot-mouth — Coxsackie.
  • Scarlet fever — Strep A, sandpaper rash.
  • Chickenpox — vesicular crops.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Which childhood exanthems are notifiable, and which carry special risks in pregnancy or specific groups?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Measles, rubella and scarlet fever are notifiable, and chickenpox is now notifiable in England and Northern Ireland (not Scotland or Wales). Beware parvovirus B19 in sickle cell (aplastic crisis) and pregnancy (hydrops), and varicella/measles in the immunocompromised or a non-immune pregnant contact (rubella too → congenital rubella syndrome).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What causes measles and why does it matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: A highly contagious paramyxovirus (RNA virus); one of the most communicable diseases (R0 ~15). It causes serious complications (pneumonia, encephalitis, fatal SSPE), is vaccine-preventable (MMR) yet resurging in the UK, and is a notifiable disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the clinical rhythm of measles?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Prodrome of high fever + the '3 C's' (Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis) → Koplik spots (pathognomonic, in the mouth) → rash starting behind the ears/on the face, spreading down. Incubation ~10 days.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What are Koplik spots?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Small white/bluish-white spots on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa (opposite the lower molars) — pathognomonic of measles. They appear 1-2 days before the rash and fade as it emerges; absence does NOT exclude measles.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Describe the measles rash.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Erythematous, maculopapular, blotchy
  • starts behind the ears/on the face → spreads cephalocaudally (downward), becomes confluent
  • spares palms and soles
  • fades after ~5 days with brownish staining/desquamation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the infectious period of measles?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: From ~4 days before to 4 days after the rash.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is measles notified and confirmed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Notify the Health Protection Team by phone the SAME DAY on clinical suspicion (don't wait for labs). Confirm with an oral fluid (saliva) sample for measles IgM/IgG and/or RNA (PCR). Isolate immediately.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is measles managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Supportive (rest, fluids, antipyretics)
  • isolate/exclude until at least 4 days after rash onset
  • antibiotics only for secondary bacterial infection.
Vitamin A is NOT routine in the UK — do not prescribe it in the community; in hospital it is considered only for selected admitted children (under 2 years, malnourished, or with diarrhoea) after paediatric infectious diseases advice.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is post-exposure prophylaxis for a susceptible measles contact?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure (if immunocompetent and not pregnant), OR human normal immunoglobulin (HNIG) within 6 days for those in whom the live vaccine is contraindicated — pregnant women, the immunosuppressed, and infants up to 8 months (MMR can be offered from 6 months in an outbreak). Always discuss with the Health Protection Team.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: List the complications of measles.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Otitis media (commonest), diarrhoea, febrile convulsions
  • pneumonia (commonest cause of measles death)
  • encephalitis (~1 in 1000)
  • SSPE (rare, fatal, ~7-10 years later; worse if infected <2y)
  • keratoconjunctivitis/blindness
  • and 'immune amnesia'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the MMR schedule, and its key contraindication?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Live attenuated, two doses at 12 months and 18 months (the second dose moved earlier from 3 years 4 months; now given as MMRV, with varicella, for eligible children). Being live, it is contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromise. Two doses give ~99% protection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Why does rubella matter, given it is a mild childhood illness?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Because of its devastating effect in pregnancy — congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). In a child it is mild/often subclinical; every rubella question is really a pregnancy/vaccination question. It is notifiable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the characteristic clinical feature of acquired rubella?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Tender lymphadenopathy — postauricular, suboccipital and posterior cervical nodes — which precedes the rash by days and persists ~1-2 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Describe the rubella rash.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Pink/light-red, fine maculopapular
  • starts on the face → spreads to trunk/limbs
  • fainter and more transient than measles
  • lasts ~3 days ('three-day measles')
  • no palm/sole involvement.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What are Forchheimer spots, and how common is asymptomatic rubella?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Petechiae on the soft palate (~20%) — supportive but not diagnostic. ~25-50% of rubella is asymptomatic/subclinical — important, as silent infection can still infect a pregnant contact.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the triad of congenital rubella syndrome, and the highest-risk window?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
Sensorineural deafness + cataracts + congenital heart disease (classically PDA).
  • Risk is highest with infection <11-12 weeks' gestation (~85-90% affected)
  • between 11 and 16 weeks the main risk is deafness alone
  • damage is rare after 16 weeks
  • and congenital rubella syndrome is essentially not reported after 20 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is rubella diagnosed and managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Notifiable; clinical diagnosis is unreliable → confirm serologically (rubella IgM, rising IgG or IgG avidity, oral fluid). Management is supportive; exclude until 4-5 days after rash onset and keep away from pregnant women.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is rubella prevented, and what happened to antenatal screening?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Live attenuated MMR, two doses (12 months + 18 months, given as MMRV for eligible children); contraindicated in pregnancy/immunocompromise. The goal is herd immunity to protect pregnant women. UK antenatal rubella screening was stopped in April 2016.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What causes hand, foot and mouth disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
Enteroviruses —
  • most often Coxsackievirus A16
  • enterovirus 71 (EV71) causes more severe/neurological disease
  • Coxsackie A6 causes more extensive rash + later onychomadesis
It is unrelated to animal 'foot-and-mouth disease'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What are the clinical features of hand, foot and mouth disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: A young child (<5-10y) with a mild prodrome, then painful oral vesicles/ulcers and a vesicular/papulovesicular rash on the palms, soles and often buttocks/perineum — 'the name is the distribution'. Self-limiting in ~7-10 days.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the main practical problem in hand, foot and mouth disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Dehydration — the painful oral ulcers reduce drinking (risk in toddlers).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is hand, foot and mouth disease managed, and is school exclusion needed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
Supportive only —
  • analgesia/antipyretics and encourage fluids (prevent dehydration)
  • good hand hygiene
  • no antivirals/antibiotics
School exclusion is NOT required (UK) — attend when well (exclusion doesn't reduce spread; stool shedding continues for weeks).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is hand, foot and mouth disease distinguished from chickenpox and herpangina?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Chickenpox is more widespread/truncal with crops of different stages
  • herpangina is mouth-only (same virus family)
HFMD = oral ulcers + vesicles on hands/feet (+ buttocks).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is onychomadesis in hand, foot and mouth disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Nail shedding occurring weeks later (especially with Coxsackie A6) — a benign, self-resolving sequela.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What causes slapped cheek syndrome, and its other names?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Parvovirus B19 — also called erythema infectiosum or 'fifth disease'. Usually a mild childhood exanthem, but dangerous in specific vulnerable groups.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the mechanism behind parvovirus B19's dangerous complications?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: It targets and destroys erythroid progenitor cells in the marrow (binds the P antigen on red-cell precursors), halting red-cell production. Harmless (brief) in health, but catastrophic in those dependent on rapid red-cell turnover or in a fetus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Describe the three phases of slapped cheek syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• (1) Prodrome (mild fever/headache)
  • (2) bright red 'slapped cheek' erythema on both cheeks with circumoral pallor
  • (3) lacy/reticular body rash (proximal arms/trunk) that waxes and wanes over 1-3 weeks, worse with heat/sun/exercise

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the key infectivity rule for parvovirus B19?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Infectious BEFORE the rash appears; once the 'slapped cheek' rash is present, they are NO LONGER infectious → no school exclusion needed. Exception: patients in aplastic crisis (still viraemic, no rash) ARE infectious → isolate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What happens with parvovirus B19 in a patient with chronic haemolytic anaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: A transient aplastic crisis — sudden severe anaemia with reticulocytopenia (e.g. sickle cell, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia) → may need transfusion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What happens with parvovirus B19 in a non-immune pregnant woman?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Fetal anaemia → hydrops fetalis and fetal loss (especially <20 weeks). B19 is the commonest infective cause of non-immune hydrops. Management: fetal medicine referral, serial ultrasound + MCA Doppler, and intrauterine transfusion if severe.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is parvovirus B19 managed in the healthy host and the immunocompromised?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Healthy host: supportive only, self-limiting
  • Immunocompromised (chronic red-cell aplasia/persistent anaemia): IVIG (contains anti-B19 antibodies)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What causes scarlet fever, and what is the core mechanism?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep) strains producing erythrogenic (pyrogenic) exotoxins — essentially 'strep throat PLUS a rash-producing toxin'. It is common in school-age children, resurging in the UK, and notifiable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Describe the rash of scarlet fever.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Fine, blanching, erythematous, 'sandpaper' texture (easier to feel than see)
  • starts on the trunk → spreads outward
  • with circumoral pallor and Pastia's lines (accentuated in skin creases)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the strawberry tongue of scarlet fever?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Initially a white coating with red papillae ('white strawberry tongue') → the coating peels → a red, swollen tongue with prominent papillae ('red strawberry tongue').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is a late clue to scarlet fever as the rash fades?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Desquamation (skin peeling), classically on the fingertips, palms and soles (~1 week later).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is scarlet fever diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Primarily clinical — don't wait to treat; a throat swab/rapid antigen test confirms GAS. It is notifiable → notify UKHSA/Health Protection Team on clinical suspicion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is scarlet fever treated, and what is the exclusion rule?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
First-line: oral phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) for 10 days —
  • 62.5 mg (1-11 months)
  • 125 mg (1-5 years)
  • 250 mg (6-11 years)
  • 500 mg (12-17 years)
each four times a day (BNFC). Amoxicillin is an alternative if penicillin V is not tolerated, but it is still a penicillin and must NOT be used in penicillin allergy — for that, clarithromycin (5-day course). Exclude from school until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics (and until well).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: List the suppurative and non-suppurative complications of scarlet fever.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Suppurative: otitis media (commonest), sinusitis, quinsy, cervical lymphadenitis, pneumonia; invasive GAS (necrotising fasciitis, toxic shock)
  • Non-suppurative (immune): acute rheumatic fever (2-4 weeks) and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (1-3 weeks)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Which serious differential shares a strawberry tongue with scarlet fever, and how is it distinguished?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Kawasaki disease — but it has >=5 days of fever, conjunctivitis, cracked lips, and typically affects children <5 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is chickenpox, and its key latency feature?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: The primary infection with varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a herpesvirus — a widespread, intensely itchy vesicular rash with fever. After primary infection VZV becomes latent in dorsal root/cranial nerve ganglia and can reactivate later as shingles (incl. Ramsay Hunt).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Describe the chickenpox rash and its key distinguishing feature.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Starts on the face/trunk (central) → spreads to limbs; evolves macule → papule → vesicle ('dewdrop on a rose petal') → pustule → crust, in successive crops so lesions of DIFFERENT stages are present at once. Intensely itchy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the infectious period of chickenpox, and the exclusion rule?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Infectious from ~2 days before the rash until ALL lesions have crusted over (~5 days after onset). Exclude from school for at least 5 days from rash onset AND until all lesions have crusted (UKHSA).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is chickenpox managed in a healthy child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Supportive only — do NOT routinely give aciclovir. Paracetamol (AVOID ibuprofen/NSAIDs — linked to severe skin/soft-tissue infection); calamine/chlorphenamine for itch; keep cool, nails short, hydrate. AVOID aspirin in under-16s (Reye's syndrome).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: When is aciclovir used in chickenpox?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
It works only if started within ~24 hours of rash onset.
  • Oral aciclovir: consider in adolescents/adults presenting within 24h
  • IV aciclovir: immunocompromised, neonates, and severe/complicated disease (pneumonia, encephalitis)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the approach in high-risk chickenpox contacts (post-exposure)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Check immunity (VZV IgG); if susceptible → prophylactic antivirals (aciclovir/valaciclovir), typically days 7-14 post-exposure (now first-line PEP), OR VZIG where antivirals are unsuitable (up to ~10 days post-exposure).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: List the complications of chickenpox.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Secondary bacterial skin infection (commonest; GAS/Staph — can progress to necrotising fasciitis, worsened by NSAIDs)
  • dehydration
  • varicella pneumonia (adults, smokers, pregnant, immunocompromised)
  • encephalitis/cerebellitis (ataxia)
  • Reye's (with aspirin)
  • haemorrhagic/disseminated varicella (immunocompromised)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What are the pregnancy and prevention issues in chickenpox?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• In pregnancy: congenital varicella syndrome (<28 weeks) and neonatal varicella — if the mother develops chickenpox from 7 days before to 7 days after delivery, give the baby VZIG without waiting for antibody testing
  • Prevention: varicella vaccine (live attenuated), now routine in the UK as MMRV at 12 and 18 months; contraindicated in pregnancy/immunocompromise

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What causes roseola infantum, and its other names?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) (less often HHV-7). Also called exanthem subitum ('sudden rash') or 'sixth disease' / 'three-day fever'. It affects infants 6 months-2 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the characteristic two-phase rhythm of roseola?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: High fever for ~3-5 days in a relatively WELL child → the fever suddenly resolves → THEN a rose-pink rash appears (~12-24h later). The rash is the 'all-clear' that appears after the fever has gone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: Describe the roseola rash.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• Rose-pink macules and papules, often with pale halos
  • starts on the trunk → spreads to neck/limbs
  • non-itchy, non-tender, blanching
  • fades in 1-2 days with no desquamation

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is roseola distinguished from measles?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back:
• In roseola the rash appears AFTER the fever resolves and the child is often well
  • in measles the rash appears DURING the fever (with the 3 C's) in a miserable child
Roseola has Nagayama spots (palate); measles has Koplik spots.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: What is the commonest complication of roseola?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Febrile convulsions — roseola is a classic trigger, due to the high fever in the vulnerable age group; usually benign/self-limiting.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.front: How is roseola managed, and what is the key clinical pitfall?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.back: Clinical diagnosis; supportive only (antipyretics, fluids) — benign and self-limiting. Pitfall: during the febrile phase (before the rash), a high-fever infant must be assessed for serious bacterial infection (the rash, once it appears, is reassuring).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What are chromosomal disorders (aneuploidies), and the organising principle?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Disorders of abnormal chromosome number with characteristic phenotypes and associated anomalies. The principle: recognise the pattern, then screen for the associated conditions. Trisomy 21 (Down) is commonest; Turner (45,X) affects girls.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: Give the karyotype and key associations for Down syndrome and Turner syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Down (trisomy 21): hypotonia, characteristic facies, single palmar crease; AVSD, duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, leukaemia
  • Turner (45,X): short stature, webbed neck; coarctation/bicuspid valve, ovarian failure — treated with growth hormone and oestrogen.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What is the commonest genetic mechanism of the trisomies, and the biggest risk factor?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Meiotic non-disjunction (a chromosome fails to separate → gamete gets two copies → zygote has three). The single biggest risk factor is advancing maternal age.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: Give the three trisomies with their chromosome and survival.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Down (T21) — commonest (~1/700), often survives into adulthood
  • Edwards (T18) — ~1/5000, most die <1 year
  • Patau (T13) — ~1/10,000, most die <1 year.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What are the three genetic mechanisms of Down syndrome and their proportions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Non-disjunction (~94%) — sporadic, risk rises with maternal age
  • Robertsonian translocation (~4%) — can be inherited from a balanced-carrier parent (recurrence risk → parental karyotyping)
  • mosaicism (~2%) — milder phenotype.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: List the craniofacial features of Down syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Round/flat face
  • flat occiput (brachycephaly)
  • small low-set ears
  • epicanthic folds + upslanting palpebral fissures
  • Brushfield spots (speckled iris)
  • protruding tongue (relative macroglossia)
  • small mouth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: List the limb/other features of Down syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Single palmar (simian) crease
  • hypotonia (floppy baby — often the first sign)
  • sandal gap (wide 1st-2nd toe gap)
  • clinodactyly (incurved 5th finger)
  • short stature.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What cardiac defects occur in Down syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Congenital heart disease in ~50% — atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) is the classic/most characteristic; also VSD, ASD, tetralogy of Fallot. All need echocardiography.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: List the GI associations of Down syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Duodenal atresia ('double bubble')
  • Hirschsprung's disease
  • imperforate anus
  • coeliac disease
  • oesophageal atresia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: List the other key associations of Down syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Learning disability (commonest genetic cause)
  • conductive (glue ear) + sensorineural hearing loss
  • cataracts/refractive errors/squint
  • leukaemia (ALL and AML) + transient abnormal myelopoiesis
  • hypothyroidism (screen), diabetes
  • atlantoaxial instability (symptom-based — no routine screening X-rays)
  • early-onset Alzheimer's (APP gene on chromosome 21)
  • OSA
  • epilepsy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What is offered in antenatal screening, and what does the combined test measure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: All women are offered screening for T21, T18 and T13 (gives a chance/risk, not a diagnosis). The combined test (11+2 to 14+1 weeks): increased nuchal translucency, increased beta-hCG, decreased PAPP-A (+ maternal age).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What is the quadruple test and its pattern for Down syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Offered at 14+2 to 20+0 weeks if the combined-test window is missed — it screens for Down's syndrome only (Edwards' and Patau's are then looked for at the 18+0-20+6 week anomaly scan). Pattern: AFP decreased, uE3 (oestriol) decreased, hCG increased, inhibin-A increased.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What is the 'higher chance' threshold, and the roles of NIPT and diagnostic tests?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: 'Higher chance' = risk >=1 in 150 → offered further testing. NIPT (cell-free fetal DNA) has ~99% detection for T21 but is still a screening test. Definitive diagnosis (karyotype): chorionic villus sampling (from 11w) or amniocentesis (from 15w) — procedure-related miscarriage risk about 1 in 200.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: How is Down syndrome managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
No cure — MDT support and health surveillance:
  • echocardiography for every baby, cardiac status established by 6 weeks
  • thyroid function annually from 1 year (newborn bloodspot first)
  • hearing + vision checks on a defined schedule
  • growth on the Down syndrome charts (RCPCH)
  • developmental support
  • consider coeliac serology.
Life expectancy now ~60 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: Give the key features of Edwards (T18).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Micrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, overlapping/clenched fingers, prominent occiput, cardiac/renal malformations, severe learning disability — most die within the first year. ('E for Extremities'.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: Give the key features of Patau (T13).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Microcephaly, small/abnormal eyes (microphthalmia), cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, scalp defects (cutis aplasia), holoprosencephaly, cardiac/renal defects — most die within days to the first year. ('P for Polydactyly, Palate, holoProsencephaly'.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What is Turner syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: A chromosomal disorder of females caused by complete or partial absence of one X chromosome (45,X) — the commonest sex-chromosome abnormality in females (~1/2500). Key features: short stature, gonadal dysgenesis (ovarian failure), and cardiac/renal anomalies. NOT associated with maternal age.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What are the genetic variants of Turner syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Monosomy 45,X (~50%)
  • mosaicism (45,X/46,XX)
  • or a structural X abnormality (Xp deletion, isochromosome, ring X).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: Explain the endocrine mechanism in Turner syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Streak (dysgenetic) ovaries → primary ovarian failure → low oestrogen → loss of negative feedback → HIGH FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) → primary amenorrhoea, absent/incomplete puberty, infertility. (A classic cause of primary amenorrhoea with a HIGH FSH.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: List the growth/skeletal features of Turner syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Short stature (most consistent — SHOX haploinsufficiency)
  • shield chest with widely-spaced nipples
  • short 4th metacarpal
  • cubitus valgus (increased carrying angle)
  • scoliosis
  • high-arched palate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: List the neck/lymphatic features of Turner syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Webbed neck (from a resolved cystic hygroma)
  • low posterior hairline
  • antenatal cystic hygroma
  • and lymphoedema of the hands and feet in the neonate (a classic newborn presentation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What are the cardiac features of Turner syndrome, and the key life-threatening risk?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Bicuspid aortic valve (~15-30%, commonest)
  • and coarctation of the aorta (~5-10%).
The key risk is aortic dilatation and dissection — the leading cause of premature death (needs lifelong echo/MRI surveillance and BP control).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What is the commonest renal anomaly in Turner syndrome, and its autoimmune associations?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Horseshoe kidney. Autoimmune associations: hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's), coeliac disease, type 1 diabetes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What is the intellectual profile in Turner syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back: Normal intelligence (mean IQ ~90) but difficulties with non-verbal/spatial skills and social cognition (verbal skills preserved).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: How is Turner syndrome diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Karyotype (45,X or variant) — definitive
  • gonadotrophins (FSH/LH) elevated, low oestradiol
  • echocardiography +/- cardiac MRI (valve, coarctation, aortic root)
  • renal ultrasound
  • autoimmune/hearing/growth screening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: What are the two hormonal pillars of Turner syndrome management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Growth hormone (to improve final adult height)
  • and oestrogen replacement (to induce/maintain puberty and protect bone, then combined HRT to ~51).
Plus lifelong cardiac surveillance, BP control, and screening for thyroid/coeliac/hearing/renal problems.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.front: Contrast Turner syndrome with Noonan syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Chromosomal Dis.back:
• Turner: 45,X (chromosomal), females only, left-sided cardiac lesions (bicuspid AV, coarctation), abnormal karyotype, infertile
  • Noonan: autosomal dominant (PTPN11 etc.), both sexes, right-sided lesions (pulmonary stenosis, HCM), normal karyotype, usually fertile ('male Turner's').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How is congenital heart disease broadly classified?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Acyanotic (left→right shunt) — VSD, ASD, PDA — often a murmur +/- heart failure; and cyanotic (right→left shunt) — ToF, TGA — causing cyanosis. Innocent murmurs are common and benign.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is a duct-dependent lesion, and the emergency response?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: A lesion where systemic or pulmonary flow depends on the ductus arteriosus; the baby collapses/becomes cyanotic as the duct closes. Response: start a prostaglandin E1 (PGE) INFUSION to keep the duct open and get urgent cardiology. Give it as a continuous IV infusion, started low and titrated, and watch for APNOEA — the key side effect, worst in the first hour; support the airway rather than stopping the infusion. Take cultures and give IV antibiotics in parallel — a shocked neonate is indistinguishable from early-onset sepsis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Give the key auscultatory signs of VSD, ASD and PDA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• VSD — pansystolic murmur
  • ASD — ejection systolic murmur with fixed split S2
  • PDA — continuous 'machinery' murmur (NSAIDs — ibuprofen or indometacin — close it in preterm infants; device closure in term infants and older children)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What defines an acyanotic (left-to-right shunt) heart defect?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Blood shunts left-to-right (oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs) so the child is NOT cyanosed. Examples: VSD, ASD, PDA, AVSD. Extra blood floods the lungs → heart failure and pulmonary hypertension over time.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is Eisenmenger syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Chronic high pulmonary flow from a large L→R shunt → pulmonary arterial hypertension → pulmonary vascular resistance rises → the shunt REVERSES to right→left → cyanosis. Once established, closing the defect is CONTRAINDICATED (management is supportive/pulmonary vasodilators +/- heart-lung transplant). This is why large shunts are closed early.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is the commonest congenital heart defect, and its associations?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) — a hole in the interventricular septum. Associations: Down, Edwards, Patau, fetal alcohol syndrome; often isolated.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Describe the VSD murmur, and the counterintuitive rule about size.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur at the LEFT LOWER STERNAL EDGE +/- a thrill. Counterintuitively, a SMALL VSD gives a LOUDER, harsher murmur (more turbulence through the tiny hole).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How does a large VSD present?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
Heart failure at ~4-6 weeks as pulmonary vascular resistance falls (increasing the L→R shunt):
  • poor feeding
  • sweating with feeds
  • tachypnoea
  • faltering growth
  • recurrent chest infections
  • hepatomegaly

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How is a VSD managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Small VSDs often close spontaneously (watchful waiting). Large/symptomatic: treat heart failure (a loop diuretic such as furosemide 0.5–1 mg/kg 12-hourly +/- an ACE inhibitor), high-calorie feeds, then surgical or transcatheter closure. Endocarditis risk → dental hygiene and regular dental review; routine antibiotic prophylaxis is NOT recommended in the UK (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is an atrial septal defect, and its commonest type?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: A hole in the interatrial septum. Ostium secundum is commonest (central/fossa ovalis). Ostium primum is part of an AVSD (strongly associated with Down syndrome + AV valve regurgitation); sinus venosus and coronary sinus are rarer.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How does an ASD often present, and what are its complications?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
Often presents in ADULTHOOD —
  • dyspnoea
  • palpitations (AF/flutter)
  • recurrent chest infections
  • or paradoxical embolism → stroke
Frequently asymptomatic in childhood.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Describe the ASD murmur and its hallmark heart sound.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: An ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge (pulmonary area) — from increased flow across the pulmonary valve (not across the defect) — with FIXED splitting of S2 (the split doesn't vary with respiration because the ASD equalises the respiratory effect between the atria).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How is an ASD managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Small secundum ASDs (esp. <8 mm) often close spontaneously; primum and sinus venosus do NOT. Significant (RV overload): transcatheter device closure (secundum) or surgical closure (primum/sinus venosus).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What are the signs of established Eisenmenger syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Cyanosis
  • clubbing
  • polycythaemia
  • right heart failure
  • loud P2

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What are the investigations for VSD/ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Echocardiography is diagnostic (defect, shunt direction, RV overload)
  • ECG: VSD → LVH/biventricular; ASD → RV hypertrophy, RBBB, right axis (primum → left axis)
  • CXR: cardiomegaly + increased pulmonary vascular markings ('plethora') with large shunts

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What defines a cyanotic congenital heart defect, and the two most important examples?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: A right-to-left shunt sends deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation → a blue (cyanotic) baby. Most important: Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) — commonest cyanotic CHD overall — and Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) — commonest cyanotic CHD presenting in the newborn.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What are the '5 T's' of cyanotic CHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Tetralogy of Fallot
  • Transposition
  • Truncus arteriosus
  • Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
  • Tricuspid atresia

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is the life-saving holding measure in duct-dependent cyanotic lesions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) — a continuous IV infusion, started low (commonly 5 nanograms/kg/minute) and titrated, maintaining a patent ductus arteriosus as a 'mixing point' until surgery. Apnoea is the key side effect — be ready to intubate, but do NOT stop the infusion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How is central cyanosis assessed, including the hyperoxia test?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Central cyanosis is clinically apparent when reduced haemoglobin >5 g/dL (distinguish from benign acrocyanosis). The nitrogen washout (hyperoxia) test: give 100% O2 for ~10 min then ABG → PaO2 <15 kPa suggests cyanotic CHD (fails to correct because the problem is shunting, not the lungs).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What are the four features of Tetralogy of Fallot ('PROVe')?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Pulmonary stenosis / RV outflow tract obstruction (the key determinant of severity)
  • Right ventricular hypertrophy
  • Overriding aorta (over the VSD)
  • Ventricular septal defect (large)
Caused by anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What determines how cyanotic a child with Tetralogy of Fallot is?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: The degree of pulmonary stenosis / RVOT obstruction — more obstruction → more right-to-left shunt → more cyanosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is a hypercyanotic 'tet spell', and how does an older child self-relieve it?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Sudden severe cyanosis from RV infundibular spasm increasing the right-to-left shunt (often on crying/feeding/waking); can cause loss of consciousness/death. An older child squats (a baby is put knee-to-chest) → increases systemic vascular resistance → reduces the R→L shunt → improves cyanosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How is an acute tet spell managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Knee-to-chest position, high-flow O2, morphine 50–100 micrograms/kg (calms the child and relaxes the infundibulum), an IV fluid bolus, and an IV beta-blocker (propranolol or esmolol, specialist-directed — reduces infundibular spasm) +/- phenylephrine; correct acidosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Give the murmur, CXR and definitive treatment of Tetralogy of Fallot.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Murmur: ejection systolic (pulmonary area), from the pulmonary stenosis (not the VSD)
  • CXR: 'boot-shaped heart' (coeur en sabot)
  • Duct-dependent neonate → prostaglandin E1; Blalock-Taussig shunt (temporising); definitive: total surgical repair (close VSD + relieve RVOTO), usually in infancy

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: The aorta arises from the RIGHT ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the LEFT ventricle → two parallel, separate circulations, incompatible with life unless there is mixing (PDA, ASD/PFO, or VSD). Associated with infants of diabetic mothers.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How does TGA present, and what is its CXR sign?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Severe cyanosis within the first day(s) of life — the commonest cyanotic lesion in the neonate; profound, unresponsive to oxygen; worsens as the duct closes. Often no murmur. CXR: 'egg on a string' (narrow superior mediastinum + egg-shaped silhouette).
