conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How is TGA managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion immediately (maintain the PDA for mixing; watch for apnoea) → balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) (tears the atrial septum to allow mixing) → definitive arterial switch operation (first ~2 weeks of life).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Persistence of the ductus arteriosus beyond the neonatal period — the fetal vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta fails to close. It is a common acyanotic left-to-right shunt (aorta → pulmonary artery), especially in premature infants.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Why does the duct normally close after birth, and why do NSAIDs vs prostaglandin have opposite effects?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: After birth, the rise in PaO2 and fall in prostaglandins makes the duct constrict and close (~1-3 days). Therefore NSAIDs (ibuprofen/indometacin) lower prostaglandins → close it, whereas prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) keeps it open. Prematurity/hypoxia keep it open.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: List the risk factors for PDA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Prematurity (the biggest — immature ductal tissue, common with RDS)
  • hypoxia/respiratory distress syndrome
  • congenital rubella (PDA is part of the triad)
  • female sex
  • high altitude
  • and genetic syndromes

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Distinguish isolated PDA from a duct-dependent lesion in terms of the goal and drug.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Isolated PDA (otherwise normal heart, PDA causes L→R shunt/HF): goal = CLOSE the duct with ibuprofen or indometacin in the preterm. Duct-dependent lesion: goal = KEEP the duct OPEN with a prostaglandin E1 infusion. Duct-dependent SYSTEMIC flow (critical coarctation, interrupted aortic arch, critical aortic stenosis, hypoplastic left heart) presents with collapse/shock; duct-dependent PULMONARY flow (pulmonary atresia, critical pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid atresia) presents with cyanosis; TGA needs the duct for mixing.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How does a large PDA present?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
A left-to-right shunt → pulmonary overcirculation + heart failure:
  • poor feeding
  • sweating with feeds
  • faltering growth
  • tachypnoea
  • recurrent chest infections
In preterm infants: difficulty weaning off ventilation and associations with NEC, IVH, chronic lung disease.Small PDAs are often asymptomatic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Describe the murmur and pulses of a PDA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: A continuous 'machinery' murmur, best at the left upper sternal edge / below the left clavicle, running through systole and diastole; with bounding/collapsing pulses and a wide pulse pressure (diastolic run-off into the pulmonary circuit).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How is an isolated PDA closed in a preterm infant vs a term infant/older child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Preterm: ibuprofen (usually first choice in UK practice) 10 mg/kg IV then 5 mg/kg at 24 and 48 hours, or indometacin 200 micrograms/kg IV repeated twice (+/- paracetamol) + fluid restriction +/- diuretics. Term/older: NSAIDs don't work → transcatheter (device) closure (or surgical ligation) if symptomatic/persistent; small asymptomatic PDAs often close spontaneously.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What are the complications of an untreated large PDA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Heart failure
  • faltering growth
  • recurrent chest infections
  • pulmonary hypertension → Eisenmenger syndrome (L→R reverses to R→L → cyanosis, differential clubbing of the toes)
  • infective endocarditis
  • and (preterm) NEC, IVH, chronic lung disease

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is an innocent (functional/flow) murmur?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: A murmur from normal blood flow through a structurally NORMAL heart. Murmurs are heard in ~50-80% of children, while structural heart disease affects only ~1% - so most murmurs in a well child are innocent, but the proportion that is pathological is far higher in neonates. The skill is distinguishing innocent from pathological murmurs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: List the 'S' features of an innocent murmur.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Soft
  • Systolic (never purely diastolic)
  • Single (no added sounds/clicks/gallops)
  • Sensitive (varies with posture/respiration - louder lying down, softer standing)
  • Short
  • Small (no radiation, localised)
  • often Sweet/musical and aSymptomatic with a normal exam

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is Still's murmur?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: The commonest innocent murmur — a low-pitched, vibratory/musical systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge/apex, loudest lying down and softer on standing; peak age 3-6 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is a venous hum, and how is it distinguished from a PDA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: The only innocent murmur with a diastolic (continuous) component — a soft continuous murmur below the clavicle/neck that disappears on lying down or turning/compressing the neck (distinguishing it from a PDA, whose continuous murmur is fixed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is a pulmonary flow murmur?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: A soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge (pulmonary area), common in infants/adolescents; louder lying down.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: List the red-flag features of a murmur that warrant referral/echocardiography.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Any diastolic murmur
  • a continuous murmur (except venous hum)
  • loud (>=grade 3) or a thrill (a thrill means grade 4 or above)
  • harsh quality
  • radiation
  • abnormal/added sounds (clicks, gallops, abnormal or fixed-split S2)
  • symptoms (cyanosis, breathlessness, poor feeding, faltering growth, syncope)
  • abnormal pulses (weak femorals/radio-femoral delay)
  • family history
  • and a neonatal murmur, which needs specialist cardiac assessment before discharge

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What factors accentuate an innocent flow murmur?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Fever, anaemia, exercise, and a thin chest wall — all increase flow/turbulence (a murmur during a febrile illness may disappear on recovery).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is the role of ECG, CXR and echocardiography in assessing a murmur?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: ECG and CXR are NO LONGER routinely recommended to distinguish innocent from pathological murmurs (poor sensitivity/specificity). Echocardiography is the definitive test if pathology is suspected (red flags) — not needed for a clearly innocent murmur. Pulse oximetry (pre-ductal right hand and post-ductal foot) is used in many UK units to pick up critical CHD — positive if either saturation is <95% or the pre-/post-ductal difference is >2% — but it is not part of the UK national newborn screening programme.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is coarctation of the aorta?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: A congenital narrowing of the aorta, usually just distal to the left subclavian artery (at the aortic isthmus, near the ductus insertion). It is an acyanotic obstructive lesion with a bimodal presentation and is the classic cause of radio-femoral delay.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Explain the 'high above, low below the block' mechanism of coarctation.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
The narrowing obstructs flow to the lower body:
  • upstream (heart, arms, head) → high pressure (upper-limb hypertension)
  • downstream (abdomen, legs) → low pressure/reduced flow (weak femoral pulses)
Collateral intercostal vessels develop → rib notching.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Why can critical neonatal coarctation cause differential cyanosis and collapse?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Critical neonatal coarctation is duct-dependent — the lower body is perfused via the PDA. When the duct closes → differential cyanosis (pink upper body, blue lower body) + shock.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Contrast the neonatal and older-child/adult presentations of coarctation.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Neonate (critical, duct-dependent): collapse/SHOCK as the duct closes (grey, floppy, poor feeding, acidosis, absent femorals, differential cyanosis) → prostaglandin E1 infusion + resuscitation + IV antibiotics for possible sepsis, then urgent repair
  • Older child/adult: asymptomatic hypertension, headache, epistaxis, leg claudication, radio-femoral delay → elective repair + BP control

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What are the key associations of coarctation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Turner syndrome (45,X)
  • and bicuspid aortic valve (in up to ~two-thirds of infants with coarctation)
  • also male sex
  • family history
  • and other left-heart lesions (VSD, PDA, aortic stenosis, Shone complex)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: Describe the signs of coarctation in an older child/adult.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Upper-limb hypertension with lower BP in the legs (measure BP in all four limbs)
  • radio-femoral delay
  • an ejection systolic murmur best at the left infraclavicular area / between the scapulae (back) +/- a systolic click (bicuspid valve)
  • LV heave
  • underdeveloped legs/cold feet

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What is the key bedside test and the diagnostic investigation for coarctation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: Bedside: four-limb BP + pulse examination (arm-leg gradient, radio-femoral delay). Echocardiography is diagnostic (narrowing, gradient, associated lesions/bicuspid valve).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What are the classic CXR signs of coarctation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back: The 'Figure 3 sign' (aortic contour: pre-stenotic dilatation + indentation + post-stenotic dilatation) and rib notching (dilated collateral intercostals eroding the ribs — usually only after ~age 5, not in neonates).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: How is coarctation managed in the neonate vs the stable older child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Neonate (critical/duct-dependent): a prostaglandin E1 infusion to reopen/maintain the duct (watch for apnoea; do not stop it) + resuscitation, with blood cultures and IV antibiotics in parallel → urgent surgical repair
  • Older child/stable: elective repair (surgery or balloon angioplasty +/- stent) + antihypertensive control

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.front: What are the lifelong follow-up issues after coarctation repair?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.back:
• Re-coarctation (esp. after neonatal repair)
  • persistent/late hypertension (even after successful repair)
  • aneurysm at the repair site
  • aortic dissection
  • and (if bicuspid valve) aortic valve disease + endocarditis

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What is Fragile X syndrome, and its significance?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: The commonest inherited (single-gene) cause of learning disability and the commonest known monogenic cause of autism, caused by a CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome (Xq27.3).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Explain the molecular mechanism of Fragile X syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: An unstable CGG repeat expansion in the 5'-UTR of FMR1. A full mutation (>200 repeats) → hypermethylation → FMR1 is silenced → loss of FMRP (needed for synaptic development) → intellectual disability. It is a trinucleotide-repeat disorder showing anticipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What is the CGG repeat-size spectrum in Fragile X?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• ~5-44 = normal
  • 45-54 = intermediate
  • 55-200 = premutation (carrier) — usually normal intellect but risk of FXTAS/FXPOI, can expand to full mutation via the mother
  • >200 = full mutation → Fragile X syndrome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Describe the inheritance pattern of Fragile X syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: X-linked (FMR1 on the X) — males more severely affected (one X, no back-up); females variably/more mildly affected (~50% have some learning disability). Full-mutation expansion occurs only through MATERNAL transmission.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the cognitive/behavioural features of Fragile X?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Intellectual disability/developmental delay (often language delay first)
  • autism spectrum features (commonest monogenic cause of autism), social anxiety, poor eye contact, hand-flapping/biting
  • ADHD/hyperactivity, sensory hypersensitivity, anxiety
  • hypotonia in infancy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the physical features of Fragile X syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Long, narrow face with prominent forehead and jaw (prognathism)
  • large, protruding ears
  • macro-orchidism (large testes) after puberty (a specific male hallmark)
  • high-arched palate, joint hypermobility, mitral valve prolapse, macrocephaly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the two premutation-carrier disorders in Fragile X?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• FXTAS (Fragile X-associated Tremor/Ataxia Syndrome) — older male premutation carriers (>50y) → intention tremor, cerebellar ataxia, cognitive decline (misdiagnosed as Parkinson's)
  • FXPOI (Fragile X-associated Primary Ovarian Insufficiency) — ~20% of female carriers → premature ovarian failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How is Fragile X diagnosed and managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis (PCR + Southern blot for methylation) — definitive. No cure: MDT supportive care (education, SALT, OT, behavioural support), treat comorbidities (ADHD, anxiety, seizures), and genetic counselling + cascade testing.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What causes Prader-Willi syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Loss of function of PATERNALLY-inherited genes at 15q11-q13, producing an evolving phenotype (neonatal hypotonia → later hyperphagia/obesity). It is the classic teaching example of genomic imprinting. Much of the picture reflects hypothalamic dysfunction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the three genetic mechanisms of Prader-Willi syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Paternal deletion of 15q11-q13 (~65-75%, commonest)
  • maternal uniparental disomy (~20-30%) (both chromosome 15s from the mother)
  • and an imprinting defect (~1-3%).
All result in no paternal expression.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How does Prader-Willi syndrome present in infancy (Phase 1)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Severe central hypotonia ('floppy infant') with a weak cry, poor suck/feeding difficulty → FAILURE TO THRIVE (counterintuitively, they can't feed well early), reduced fetal movements, lethargy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How does Prader-Willi syndrome present in later childhood (Phase 2)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: HYPERPHAGIA — insatiable appetite/lack of satiety → food-seeking → OBESITY (the central problem and main cause of morbidity/mortality: type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea). Also short stature (GH deficiency), small hands/feet, hypogonadism/hypogenitalism, mild-moderate learning disability, behavioural problems (skin-picking, tantrums).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Contrast Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
Same locus (15q11-q13).
  • Prader-Willi = loss of PATERNAL genes (paternal deletion/maternal UPD): hypotonia, hyperphagia/obesity, hypogonadism
  • Angelman = loss of MATERNAL UBE3A (maternal deletion/paternal UPD): severe LD, ataxic 'puppet' gait, seizures, inappropriate laughter ('hAppy', mAternal).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How is Prader-Willi syndrome diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 — first-line/definitive (detects >99% across all mechanisms and separates PWS from Angelman); FISH/microarray (deletion) and UPD studies define the mechanism for recurrence-risk counselling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How is Prader-Willi syndrome managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Strict dietary control / supervised eating environment is the cornerstone (prevent life-threatening obesity)
  • growth hormone (somatropin) — height, body composition, motor function: assess for severe obesity, upper-airway obstruction and sleep apnoea BEFORE starting, and interrupt if snoring or new apnoea appears (sudden deaths have occurred in children with these risk factors) (MHRA)
  • sex hormone replacement
  • MDT (dietitian, endocrinology, physio, SALT, psychology)
  • treat OSA/scoliosis
  • genetic counselling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What is Noonan syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: A common autosomal dominant multisystem disorder caused by overactivation of the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway (a 'RASopathy') — short stature, characteristic facies, congenital heart disease (classically pulmonary stenosis), webbed neck, and a bleeding tendency. Often called 'the male Turner syndrome' but is a distinct disorder.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What is the commonest gene mutated in Noonan syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: PTPN11 (~50%); others include SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, KRAS — all activating the RAS-MAPK pathway.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Contrast Noonan and Turner syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Noonan: autosomal dominant RASopathy, both sexes, NORMAL karyotype, right-sided (pulmonary stenosis, HCM) heart disease, usually fertile
  • Turner: 45,X, females only, abnormal karyotype, left-sided (bicuspid AV, coarctation), infertile.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the craniofacial/skeletal features of Noonan syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Broad forehead, hypertelorism (wide-spaced eyes), down-slanting palpebral fissures, ptosis, low-set posteriorly-rotated ears, high-arched palate, short/webbed neck
  • short stature
  • pectus excavatum/carinatum, cubitus valgus
  • cryptorchidism (males)
  • lymphoedema.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the cardiac and haematological features of Noonan syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Pulmonary (valve) stenosis — commonest/classic (~50%, may be dysplastic)
  • hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
  • also ASD/VSD/PDA
  • Bleeding tendency/coagulation defects (check clotting before surgery)
  • increased risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (JMML).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How is Noonan syndrome diagnosed and managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by genetic testing (RASopathy gene panel); karyotype is NORMAL (distinguishes from Turner). Echo + ECG (pulmonary stenosis, HCM), coagulation screen. MDT: manage pulmonary stenosis (balloon valvuloplasty)/HCM, growth hormone, bleeding precautions before surgery, genetic counselling (AD, 50% transmission; many de novo).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What causes Williams syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: A microdeletion on chromosome 7q11.23 (a contiguous-gene deletion of ~26-28 genes, including the elastin gene, ELN). Usually de novo (sporadic). Elastin haploinsufficiency → the arteriopathy; neighbouring genes account for the neurocognitive profile.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the cardiovascular features of Williams syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
An elastin arteriopathy:
  • supravalvular aortic stenosis (SVAS) — classic/commonest (~75%)
  • peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis
  • renal artery stenosis (→ hypertension)
  • systemic hypertension.
The arteriopathy is PROGRESSIVE → lifelong cardiac surveillance, with a risk of sudden death (coronary ostial stenosis, especially with anaesthesia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the metabolic and behavioural features of Williams syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Transient infantile hypercalcaemia (irritability, feeding difficulty, constipation, failure to thrive); hypothyroidism; later glucose intolerance. Mild-moderate learning disability with strong verbal/social but weak visuospatial skills; an overly friendly 'cocktail-party personality'; hyperacusis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Describe the 'elfin' facies of Williams syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Broad forehead
  • periorbital fullness
  • stellate (star-like) iris
  • short upturned nose
  • long philtrum
  • full lips/wide mouth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How is Williams syndrome diagnosed and managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: FISH or chromosomal microarray showing the 7q11.23 (ELN) deletion. Echo + regular cardiovascular surveillance (progressive), serum calcium, TFTs, glucose, BP, renal US. MDT: manage SVAS/arterial stenoses, treat hypertension, cautious anaesthesia; avoid vitamin D and calcium supplementation (hypercalcaemia); educational support.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What causes Cri du Chat syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Loss of the short (p) arm of chromosome 5 (5p-) — one of the commonest deletion (contiguous-gene) syndromes (22q11.2 deletion is the commonest). Usually a de novo terminal deletion (~80-90%); ~10-15% from an unbalanced parental translocation. The deletion size determines severity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What is the signature feature of Cri du Chat syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: A high-pitched, monotonous, 'cat-like' cry in infancy (from laryngeal + neurological abnormalities) — which tends to fade with age (a diagnostic clue mainly in infancy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Give the classic triad and craniofacial features of Cri du Chat.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Triad: cat-like cry + microcephaly + severe learning disability. Craniofacial: a round 'moon' face (in infancy), hypertelorism, micrognathia, epicanthic folds, down-slanting palpebral fissures, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What other features occur in Cri du Chat syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Feeding difficulties + failure to thrive, hypotonia in infancy (poor suck/swallow), severe psychomotor and intellectual disability with marked speech/language delay
  • less often congenital heart defects, renal anomalies, scoliosis, and recurrent respiratory infections (a major cause of infant death).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How is Cri du Chat diagnosed and managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Karyotype (visualises the 5p deletion); FISH/microarray for small deletions. No specific therapy: MDT supportive care + early intervention (physio, SALT, OT, special education), feeding support. Genetic counselling — usually de novo (low recurrence), but check parental karyotype to exclude a balanced translocation carrier.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What is Pierre Robin sequence?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: A triad of micrognathia (small lower jaw), glossoptosis (tongue falling backwards), and upper-airway obstruction, usually with a U-shaped cleft palate (~90%). It is a neonatal airway emergency.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Why is Pierre Robin a 'sequence' rather than a syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: A sequence is a chain of malformations from a single initiating event: the primary defect is mandibular hypoplasia (micrognathia) → the small jaw forces the tongue up/back (glossoptosis) → the elevated tongue blocks the palatal shelves from fusing → cleft palate + airway obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the two categories of Pierre Robin sequence, and the commonest syndromic association?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Isolated (non-syndromic) — often the more airway-severe group; and syndromic (~half) — the commonest association is Stickler syndrome (collagen disorder → myopia/retinal detachment, hearing loss, joint problems); also 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge), Treacher Collins. ~20% have congenital heart disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the dangers/complications of Pierre Robin sequence?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Airway obstruction/respiratory distress from birth (stridor, retractions, desaturation, apnoea, OSA) — life-threatening in the first hours
  • and feeding difficulties (poor suck/swallow, worsened by the cleft palate) → aspiration and failure to thrive.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How is the airway managed in Pierre Robin sequence (stepwise)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• PRONE (or lateral) positioning first-line (gravity pulls the tongue forward — many need nothing more); this is a monitored, hospital-initiated airway treatment, not a change to safer-sleep advice
  • Then nasopharyngeal airway
  • CPAP/non-invasive ventilation
  • rarely intubation (difficult airway)
  • Surgical (if severe): tongue-lip adhesion (glossopexy), mandibular distraction osteogenesis, or tracheostomy (last resort).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What is the longer-term management and outlook in Pierre Robin sequence?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Specialised feeding techniques/cleft feeding devices (NG/gastrostomy if aspiration/failure to thrive)
  • cleft palate repair later (~6-12 months)
  • the jaw often 'catches up' with age, improving the airway.
MDT: neonatology, ENT, plastics/maxillofacial, SALT, genetics, ophthalmology (for Stickler).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What is Klinefelter syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: A sex-chromosome disorder in males caused by >=1 extra X chromosome (usually 47,XXY) from meiotic non-disjunction — the commonest sex-chromosome disorder and the commonest genetic cause of male hypogonadism and infertility. Often underdiagnosed until puberty or an adult infertility clinic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Explain the endocrine mechanism in Klinefelter syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: The extra X causes primary testicular failure — small, fibrotic testes → low testosterone + impaired spermatogenesis. Low testosterone → loss of negative feedback → HIGH FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) — analogous to Turner's, but male.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: What are the classic pubertal features of Klinefelter syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Small, firm testes (a key sign — fail to grow despite puberty)
  • delayed/incomplete puberty, incomplete virilisation (reduced facial/body hair)
  • gynaecomastia (~50%)
  • tall stature with a eunuchoid habitus (long limbs from delayed epiphyseal fusion).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How does Klinefelter syndrome commonly present in adults?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
• Infertility (azoospermia/oligospermia — often diagnosed here)
  • androgen deficiency (reduced libido, low energy, osteoporosis)
  • small testes/penis, sparse body hair
  • Increased risk of breast cancer (rare in absolute terms but many times the risk in other men), osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome/type 2 diabetes, VTE.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: Contrast Klinefelter and Turner syndromes.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back:
Both cause hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and are usually infertile.
  • Klinefelter: male, extra X (47,XXY), TALL, small firm testes
  • Turner: female, missing X (45,X), SHORT, streak ovaries.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.front: How is Klinefelter syndrome diagnosed and managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.back: Karyotype (47,XXY) — definitive; low testosterone, high FSH/LH. Testosterone replacement is the mainstay (virilisation, muscle/bone, libido — but does NOT restore fertility); sperm retrieval (micro-TESE) + ICSI can achieve fatherhood in some (discuss before testosterone therapy); manage gynaecomastia, osteoporosis, metabolic risk; genetic counselling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the defining triad of haemolytic uraemic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (a thrombotic microangiopathy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the commonest cause of acute kidney injury in children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Which organism classically precedes typical HUS, and via what toxin?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: E. coli O157:H7 (STEC) — Shiga toxin. (Shigella can also cause it.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Describe the core mechanism of HUS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Shiga toxin damages vascular endothelium (especially renal microvasculature) → platelet activation and microthrombi in small vessels (thrombotic microangiopathy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How does the HUS mechanism explain each part of the triad?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back:
• MAHA — red cells sheared through clogged microvasculature (schistocytes)
  • thrombocytopenia — platelets consumed in microthrombi
  • AKI — microthrombi occlude the glomerular microvasculature

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Typical vs atypical HUS — frequency and trigger?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Typical (STEC-HUS/D+HUS) ~90%, triggered by Shiga toxin after bloody diarrhoea. Atypical (aHUS) ~10%, complement (alternative-pathway) dysregulation, often no diarrhoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How does treatment differ between typical and atypical HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Typical STEC-HUS: supportive. Atypical HUS: eculizumab (anti-C5).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How does prognosis differ between typical and atypical HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Typical usually recovers; atypical has a worse, often relapsing course.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Name a further recognised form of HUS beyond STEC and complement-mediated.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Streptococcus pneumoniae-associated HUS — about 5% of all childhood HUS (but a large share of non-STEC cases), after invasive pneumococcal disease/pneumonia. It is the Coombs-POSITIVE exception (T-antigen exposure), and plasma-containing products are avoided.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Describe the typical prodrome of STEC-HUS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back:
A diarrhoeal illness — classically BLOODY diarrhoea (haemorrhagic colitis), abdominal pain, vomiting — from
  • undercooked beef
  • unpasteurised milk
  • petting farms
  • or person-to-person spread

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How long after diarrhoea onset does STEC-HUS typically develop, and in what proportion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: ~5–14 days after the diarrhoea starts, in ~10–15% of infected children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What clinical features appear when the HUS triad develops?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back:
• Anaemia (pallor, lethargy, jaundice)
  • thrombocytopenia (bruising, petechiae, bleeding)
  • AKI (reduced urine output/oliguria-anuria, oedema, hypertension, rising creatinine)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What extra-renal complications occur in severe HUS (~20%)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: CNS involvement (irritability, seizures, encephalopathy — worse prognosis), cardiac, and pancreatic (glucose) involvement.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What blood film and FBC findings are expected in HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back:
• Anaemia with schistocytes (fragmented RBCs)
  • thrombocytopenia
  • reticulocytosis

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What haemolysis screen findings are seen in HUS, and what is the Coombs result?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: ↑ LDH, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin, and a NEGATIVE Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test — non-immune haemolysis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Why is the coagulation screen important in suspected HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: It is NORMAL in HUS — the key distinction from DIC, where it is deranged.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What stool tests are used in suspected STEC-HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Stool culture / PCR for STEC / E. coli O157 and Shiga toxin.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How does TTP differ from HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: TTP is a pentad (MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI + neurological signs + fever), caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency; more neuro/less renal, adults > children; treated with plasma exchange.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How is DIC distinguished from HUS on labs?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: HUS has a NORMAL coagulation screen; DIC is deranged — ↑PT/APTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the mainstay of management for STEC-HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Supportive care — there is no specific treatment; most children recover. Before HUS declares itself, a child with bloody diarrhoea and suspected or confirmed STEC should be volume-expanded early with IV 0.9% sodium chloride without waiting for the stool result, which reduces the risk of oligo-anuric HUS and the need for dialysis. Then careful fluid/electrolyte management, BP control and nutrition, with early discussion with the regional paediatric nephrology unit.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: When are blood and platelet transfusions used in HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Blood transfusion for symptomatic anaemia; platelets are generally AVOIDED unless active bleeding/surgery (can fuel microthrombi).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What proportion of HUS children need dialysis, and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back:
~50% — for
  • AKI
  • hyperkalaemia
  • fluid overload
  • or uraemia

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Which agents must be AVOIDED in suspected STEC-HUS and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Antibiotics and anti-motility/antidiarrhoeal agents — they increase Shiga toxin release/absorption and the risk of HUS.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the treatment for atypical (complement-mediated) HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Eculizumab (anti-C5 monoclonal antibody) — has transformed its outcome (NICE). It is NOT routinely used in STEC-HUS, where randomised evidence has not shown benefit in the acute illness. Because it blocks terminal complement, meningococcal vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis are mandatory.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What public health action is required in STEC/E. coli O157 HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Notify the local health protection team on clinical SUSPICION, without waiting for the stool result — HUS and infectious bloody diarrhoea are both notifiable diseases, and laboratories separately notify E. coli O157/STEC. Source tracing and household screening follow. Young children (and food handlers, healthcare and childcare staff) are excluded until two consecutive negative stool samples — the usual 48-hour symptom-free rule is not enough for STEC (UKHSA).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the prognosis of STEC-HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Acute mortality now <5%; most recover, but ~1/3 have long-term renal sequelae (CKD, hypertension, proteinuria) → long-term renal follow-up. CNS involvement worsens outcome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: An acquired autoimmune disorder in which antibodies destroy platelets, causing isolated thrombocytopenia with bruising and a petechial/purpuric rash.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the commonest cause of acute-onset thrombocytopenia in an otherwise-well child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the key management principle in childhood ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Treat the BLEEDING, not the platelet number — most children need only watchful waiting, not treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Describe the core mechanism of ITP.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Antibodies against the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex → type II hypersensitivity → antibody-coated platelets destroyed by the spleen (± impaired production).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What typically triggers acute childhood ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: It is typically acute and post-viral — often 1–2 weeks after a viral infection (or, less often, vaccination); a transient immune response, which is why it usually resolves.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Why is ITP described as a diagnosis of exclusion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: The assessment confirms isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child and excludes marrow failure/malignancy (leukaemia, aplastic anaemia); there is no confirmatory test.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Which features on other cell lines reassure you it is ITP rather than leukaemia/aplastic anaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Normal Hb and WCC (isolated ↓platelets). Anaemia or abnormal WCC (pancytopenia) is a red flag.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What systemic and examination red flags suggest a sinister cause rather than ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back:
• Fever, weight loss, bone pain, malaise
  • lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly
In ITP the child is well with no organomegaly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What blood film finding would point away from ITP toward malignancy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Blasts or abnormal cells. In ITP the film is normal apart from few (often large/young) platelets.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: If a red flag is present, what must be done before giving steroids and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Bone marrow examination to exclude leukaemia — steroids could partially treat/mask leukaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the classic age range for childhood ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: 2–7 years, often 1–2 weeks after a viral illness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What are the typical skin findings in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Bruising (ecchymoses) and a petechial or purpuric rash — non-blanching, often on the legs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What types of bleeding occur in ITP, and which marks higher risk?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Bleeding is less common — typically epistaxis or gingival (gum) bleeding; mucosal bleeding ('wet purpura') is a marker of higher bleeding risk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: How common is serious bleeding such as intracranial haemorrhage in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Rare — intracranial haemorrhage occurs in well under 1% (~0.2–0.8%); the risk is concentrated in children with platelets <20, head trauma, or haematuria. Remember that a non-blanching rash is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise, and unexplained bruising in a non-mobile infant is a safeguarding presentation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the central FBC pattern in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Isolated thrombocytopenia — normal haemoglobin and white cell count.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What does the blood film help exclude in suspected ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back:
• Blasts (leukaemia)
  • fragments (HUS/TTP)
  • and pseudothrombocytopenia (platelet clumping)
it confirms low platelets, often large/young.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: When is bone marrow examination indicated in suspected ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back:
Only if atypical:
  • lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly
  • failure to respond to treatment
  • abnormal other cell lines
  • or before starting steroids if leukaemia is a concern

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Is anti-platelet antibody testing routine in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: No — ITP is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion with no confirmatory test; anti-platelet antibody testing is not routine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: How is ITP classified by duration?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back:
• Newly diagnosed: <3 months
  • persistent: 3–12 months
  • chronic: >12 months

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What proportion of children develop chronic ITP, and who is more at risk?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back:
~20–30%; more likely in
  • older children/adolescents
  • insidious onset
  • and girls

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is first-line management for most children with ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Watchful waiting — for no or only minor bleeding (bruising/petechiae only), regardless of how low the count is; ~80% resolve spontaneously within ~6 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What safety advice is given during watchful waiting for ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back:
• Avoid contact sports and trauma
  • avoid NSAIDs/aspirin and IM injections (paracetamol is safe)
  • seek urgent assessment after ANY head injury, or for headache, vomiting, drowsiness, visual change, or bleeding that will not stop
  • written safety-net with a direct contact number
Do NOT withhold routine immunisations — normally-IM vaccines are given subcutaneously or with a fine needle and firm pressure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the first-line drug treatment when there is significant/mucosal bleeding?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) — a SHORT course only: 4 mg/kg/day (max 200 mg/day) in divided doses for 4 days, or 1–2 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg/day) for up to 14 days with a taper. Longer courses add toxicity without extra benefit.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: When is IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) used in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: When a faster rise is needed (active bleeding, before a procedure), or if steroids are unsuitable — 0.8–1 g/kg as a single dose, which may be repeated once.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is a role for IV anti-D immunoglobulin in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Historically an alternative in D-positive, non-splenectomised children with a negative direct antiglobulin test — but now rarely used in the UK because of the risk of severe intravascular haemolysis; haemoglobin and urine must be monitored after the dose.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: When are platelet transfusions used in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Only for life-threatening bleeding — transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed too, so they are used with IVIG/steroids as rescue, not routinely.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: How is life-threatening bleeding (e.g. intracranial haemorrhage) in ITP managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Combination rescue: platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG (± tranexamic acid; emergency splenectomy as last resort).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What are the second-line options for chronic/refractory ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back:
• Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim)
  • rituximab
  • splenectomy

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Why is splenectomy generally deferred/avoided in children with ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: High spontaneous-resolution rate plus infection risk — reserved for chronic, refractory disease, usually age >5.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the key differential of ITP and its red flags?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back:
Acute leukaemia — red flags:
  • unwell child
  • other cytopenias
  • organomegaly
  • bone pain

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What two common feeding-related presentations are grouped under infant feeding & reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA) and gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR/GORD).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the organising principle distinguishing benign from concerning infant feeding presentations?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Physiological reflux (posseting, otherwise thriving) usually resolves by ~1 year; red flags (poor weight gain, distress, blood) suggest GORD or CMPA.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What clues point to cow's milk protein intolerance, and how is it managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Vomiting, diarrhoea/blood in stool, eczema, poor weight gain → exclude cow's milk (extensively hydrolysed formula / maternal dairy exclusion).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How do you distinguish infant reflux GOR from GORD, and how is each managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: GOR = effortless posseting → reassure. GORD = distress/faltering growth → thickened feeds, alginates, and a PPI only if there is feeding difficulty, distressed behaviour or faltering growth — never for regurgitation alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When should reflux be treated as GORD rather than simple posseting?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: When there is faltering growth, marked distress or respiratory symptoms — investigate/treat; consider CMPA in refractory reflux + atopy. Haematemesis is a red flag needing assessment for an alternative cause, not a GORD label.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: An immune-mediated adverse reaction to the proteins in cow's milk (mainly casein and whey); one of the commonest food allergies of infancy (~1–3% of infants).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Why is CMPA both over- and under-diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Its GI, skin and respiratory symptoms overlap with reflux, colic and infection, and there is no single confirmatory test for non-IgE disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How does 'allergy' differ from 'intolerance' in this context?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Allergy = immune-mediated (IgE or non-IgE) — what CMPA refers to. True intolerance is non-immune (e.g. lactose intolerance — an enzyme/sugar problem), a completely different entity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the timing of IgE-mediated vs non-IgE-mediated CMPA reactions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: IgE-mediated: <2 hours after ingestion (immediate). Non-IgE-mediated: after 4 hours, up to 24–48 h/days (delayed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the mechanism of IgE-mediated vs non-IgE-mediated CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: IgE-mediated: immediate hypersensitivity (mast cell/IgE). Non-IgE-mediated: cell-mediated (delayed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What are the typical features of IgE-mediated CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Urticaria, wheeze, stridor, angioedema; acute; can progress to anaphylaxis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What are the typical features of non-IgE-mediated CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Rectal bleeding, mucus in stool, vomiting, diarrhoea; GI-predominant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What testing helps in IgE-mediated vs non-IgE-mediated CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: IgE-mediated: skin prick / specific IgE (RAST) helpful. Non-IgE-mediated: no useful blood test — diagnosis is clinical (elimination + reintroduction).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When do IgE-mediated vs non-IgE-mediated CMPA typically resolve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: IgE-mediated: later, ~by 5 years. Non-IgE-mediated: earlier, ~by 3 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When and in whom does CMPA usually present?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Usually in the first 3 months of life, in formula-fed infants — but can occur in exclusively breastfed babies from maternal dairy passing into breast milk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: List the GI features of CMPA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back:
• Regurgitation/vomiting
  • diarrhoea
  • colic (irritability, crying)
  • rectal bleeding/mucus (non-IgE)
  • constipation
  • faltering growth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: List the skin and respiratory features of CMPA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back:
• Skin: urticaria, atopic eczema, angioedema.
  • Respiratory: wheeze, chronic cough, stridor (IgE).
Anaphylaxis is rare but possible in IgE-mediated disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the cornerstone of diagnosing CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: It is primarily clinical — improvement on removing cow's milk protein and recurrence on reintroduction (especially for non-IgE disease where tests don't help).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Which unproven test should be avoided in CMPA and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Food-specific IgG panels — not validated, cause overdiagnosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the first-line formula for mild–moderate CMPA in a formula-fed infant?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Extensively Hydrolysed Formula (EHF) — cow's-milk protein broken down so it's not recognised; tolerated by ~90%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When is Amino Acid Formula (AAF) used in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: If severe, or no response to EHF — fully non-allergenic; only ~10% of infants need it.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Which milks/formulas should NOT be used in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Soya formula (cross-reacts in ~10–15% of CMPA, and not for infants under 6 months because of its phytoestrogen content) or other mammalian milks (goat/sheep — cross-react).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How is CMPA managed in a breastfed infant?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Continue breastfeeding; eliminate cow's milk protein from the maternal diet and prescribe the mother calcium 1000 mg and vitamin D 10 micrograms daily. When breastfeeding stops, use EHF.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How long is EHF continued after breastfeeding stops in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Until ~12 months of age and for at least 6 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Why is dietitian involvement important in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back:
• To ensure nutritional adequacy (calcium/vitamin D)
  • avoid hidden allergens
  • and prevent unnecessary long-term restriction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the 'milk ladder' in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Planned staged reintroduction starting with small amounts of BAKED milk (e.g. malted-milk biscuit) → progressing up, to confirm resolution and build tolerance (supervised/specialist for IgE-mediated).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When should a child with CMPA be referred to paediatrics/allergy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: If severe — failure to thrive, anaphylaxis, or severe symptoms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR) in babies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: The passage of stomach contents up into the oesophagus — effortless posseting/regurgitation of milk after feeds; extremely common and physiological (≥40% of infants).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How is physiological GOR in a thriving baby managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Reassurance only, not treatment — it is often over-medicalised.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Why is reflux so common in babies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back:
• Short narrow oesophagus
  • relatively incompetent/immature lower oesophageal sphincter
  • large fluid milk volume
  • and much time lying flat
→ milk easily flows back up.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When does physiological GOR usually resolve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: As the baby matures, sits up and takes solids — ~90% by 12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How does GOR differ from GORD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: GOR is normal, effortless regurgitation in a well, thriving 'happy spitter'. GORD is reflux causing symptoms/complications in a distressed, unwell or faltering baby.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the key teaching point about GOR and crying?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: GOR does NOT cause crying/irritability in an otherwise healthy, thriving infant — if a baby is genuinely distressed or not growing, think GORD or an alternative diagnosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What are the clinical features of GORD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back:
Regurgitation/vomiting WITH
  • poor weight gain
  • feeding difficulties (refusal, pulling off, distress/pain)
  • marked unexplained irritability (especially with arching)
  • Sandifer syndrome
  • respiratory symptoms and oesophagitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is Sandifer syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Episodic dystonic posturing — torticollis (neck twisting) + back arching — associated with GORD; can be mistaken for seizures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What respiratory and oesophageal complications can GORD cause?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Chronic cough, wheeze (aspiration), recurrent chest infections, apnoea/BRUE; oesophagitis (haematemesis, pain), dental erosion in older children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Which vomiting red flag suggests intestinal obstruction and needs urgent surgical referral?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Bilious (green) vomiting → intestinal obstruction (e.g. malrotation/volvulus) — urgent, same-day surgical referral. Never ignore green vomit.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What does projectile, non-bilious vomiting in a 2–8-week-old suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Pyloric stenosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: List reflux red flags that mean 'not simple reflux — investigate/refer'.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back:
• Bilious vomiting
  • projectile non-bilious vomiting (2–8 wks)
  • haematemesis/melaena
  • abdominal distension/tenderness
  • bulging fontanelle/altered consciousness
  • blood in stool
  • onset after 6 months or persisting beyond 1 year
  • fever/lethargy
  • faltering growth
  • chronic diarrhoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What should prompt consideration of CMPA in a baby with reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Eczema, family history of atopy, or other GI symptoms — CMPA can present as/with reflux.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Is GORD usually diagnosed clinically or with investigations?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Usually a clinical diagnosis — investigations are rarely needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What investigations may be considered in GORD, and when?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back:
Urinalysis (exclude UTI if faltering growth/late onset); and only if diagnostic doubt/complications/red flags:
  • pH/impedance monitoring
  • upper GI endoscopy (suspected oesophagitis)
  • contrast study (if anatomical/obstruction suspected).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the first step of stepped-care management (NICE) for reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Feeding review — assess technique/volume, avoid overfeeding (smaller, more frequent feeds); breastfeeding assessment if breastfed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the stepped-care approach for a breastfed infant with troublesome reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Breastfeeding assessment → if it persists, a trial of alginate (infant sachets) for 1–2 weeks — 1 dose if under 4.5 kg, 2 doses if 4.5 kg or over, with each feed, maximum 6 doses in 24 hours (BNFC).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the stepped-care approach for a formula-fed infant with troublesome reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Review feed volumes → thickened (anti-reflux) formula → if unsuccessful, stop thickener and trial alginate for 1–2 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When should acid suppression (PPI/H2RA) be offered in infant reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back:
NOT for overt regurgitation alone in an otherwise-well infant (NICE). Consider a 4-week trial of a PPI or H2RA when overt regurgitation is accompanied by one or more of:
  • unexplained feeding difficulties
  • distressed behaviour
  • or faltering growth.
Reassess at 4 weeks; refer for specialist assessment ± endoscopy if symptoms persist or recur on stopping.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How is endoscopy-proven reflux oesophagitis treated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: PPI/H2RA treatment. Do NOT use prokinetics (metoclopramide/domperidone/erythromycin) without specialist advice.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When is specialist referral / fundoplication considered for GORD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: For severe, intractable GORD unresponsive to medical treatment, or complications.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the safe-sleep caveat when managing infant reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Do NOT use positional (head-up/prone/side) management to treat reflux in sleeping infants — babies must be placed on their BACK to sleep (SIDS prevention overrides reflux positioning).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What three conditions are grouped under lower respiratory infection & wheeze in young children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Bronchiolitis, whooping cough (pertussis), and viral-induced (pre-school) wheeze.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the organising principle for these conditions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
Age + pattern:
  • bronchiolitis in under-2s but overwhelmingly under 1 year, peak 3–6 months (RSV coryza → cough/wheeze/feeding difficulty)
  • pertussis = paroxysmal cough + whoop/apnoea + post-tussive vomiting
  • viral-induced wheeze = episodic wheeze with viral URTIs and no interval symptoms (not asthma).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Give the clue and management for bronchiolitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Under 2 years, overwhelmingly under 1 (peak 3–6 months), RSV; coryza then wheeze/crackles, poor feeding → supportive (oxygen, feeding support); admit if severe/apnoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Give the clue and management for pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Paroxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop, apnoea in infants, post-tussive vomiting → macrolide; notifiable; vaccine-preventable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Give the clue and management for pre-school/viral-induced wheeze.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Episodic wheeze with viral URTI, well between episodes → SABA; distinguish from asthma (atopy, interval symptoms).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: An acute viral lower respiratory tract infection of the small airways (bronchioles) in infants, causing inflammation, mucus and airway obstruction → coryza then cough, wheeze/crackles and feeding difficulty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why does bronchiolitis matter clinically?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is the commonest LRTI and commonest cause of hospital admission in infants under 1 year; RSV is the main cause; and management is a 'less is more' point — it is supportive (bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics don't work).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the core mechanism of bronchiolitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A virus (usually RSV) infects and inflames the bronchiolar epithelium → oedema, mucus and sloughed cells plug the tiny airways; because infant airways are small, minor narrowing causes big obstruction → air trapping/hyperinflation, wheeze, crackles, work of breathing → feeding difficulty and, in the youngest, apnoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What organism causes most cases of bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) — ~70–85% of cases; others include parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, influenza, adenovirus, rhinovirus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the typical age and season for bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Under 2 years, peak ~3–6 months; winter epidemics; spread by droplets/contact (very contagious).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is bronchiolitis distinguished from viral-induced wheeze/asthma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Bronchiolitis: <1–2 yrs, widespread crackles ± wheeze, low-grade fever, first episode with coryzal prodrome. Viral wheeze/asthma: usually >1 yr, wheeze without crackles, recurrent, atopy/family history (both unusual under 1 year).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is bronchiolitis distinguished from pneumonia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Pneumonia has focal crackles, high/persistent fever (>39°C) and persistent focal signs; bronchiolitis has widespread crackles and low-grade fever. High fever or focal crackles → think pneumonia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the typical clinical course of bronchiolitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Coryzal prodrome (runny nose, mild fever) for 1–3 days, then persistent cough, tachypnoea and increased work of breathing (recession, nasal flaring, head bobbing, grunting), wheeze and/or fine bibasal crackles, and feeding difficulty. Signs peak days 3–5 then improve; cough can linger ~3 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why is feeding difficulty important in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is a key marker of severity (from respiratory effort/nasal blockage) and guides admission.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is a crucial, potentially life-threatening presenting feature of bronchiolitis in young/preterm infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Apnoea — especially in infants <6 weeks/preterm; it may be the presenting feature and is life-threatening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is bronchiolitis diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is a CLINICAL diagnosis — do NOT routinely do blood tests or a chest X-ray (CXR can mimic pneumonia → unnecessary antibiotics).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the role of pulse oximetry and nasopharyngeal aspirate in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Pulse oximetry — for hypoxia, guides admission
  • Nasopharyngeal aspirate/viral PCR (RSV) — mainly for cohorting/infection control, not diagnosis
  • Capillary blood gas only if severe/impending respiratory failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the mainstay of bronchiolitis management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Supportive care (NICE) — most are managed at home.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What oxygen thresholds guide supplemental O2 in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Give supplemental O2 if SpO2 <90% in children ≥6 weeks (or <92% if <6 weeks/comorbid).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What feeding/fluid support is used in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Smaller/more frequent feeds
  • nasogastric/orogastric or IV fluids if not feeding adequately
  • nasal suctioning if secretions/apnoea
  • minimal handling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is respiratory failure escalated in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: High-flow humidified oxygen (Optiflow)/CPAP → ventilation for respiratory failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Which treatments do NOT work in bronchiolitis and should not be used routinely?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Bronchodilators (salbutamol)
  • nebulised adrenaline
  • corticosteroids
  • nebulised hypertonic saline
  • montelukast
  • and antibiotics.
(Antibiotics only if genuine evidence of secondary bacterial infection.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What features warrant immediate emergency referral to hospital in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Apnoea
  • looks seriously unwell
  • severe respiratory distress (grunting, marked recession, RR >70)
  • central cyanosis
  • or SpO2 persistently <92% in air.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What features should prompt considering referral in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• RR >60
  • difficulty feeding/inadequate oral intake (50–75% of normal)
  • clinical dehydration.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Which risk factors lower the threshold for admission in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Age <3 months
  • prematurity (especially <32 weeks)
  • chronic lung disease
  • congenital heart disease
  • immunodeficiency
  • neuromuscular disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is nirsevimab and its role in RSV prevention?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A long-acting anti-RSV monoclonal antibody; a single injection covers the whole RSV season (unlike palivizumab, which is monthly). In the UK the routine offer for healthy term/late-preterm babies is the maternal RSV vaccine in pregnancy from 28 weeks; nirsevimab is targeted at high-risk infants and those whose mothers were not vaccinated, replacing palivizumab.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What other RSV prevention measure is part of the new UK programme?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Maternal RSV vaccination (given in pregnancy to protect the newborn); plus general measures — breastfeeding, hand hygiene, avoiding smoke exposure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is pertussis and what causes it?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis (a Gram-negative coccobacillus), characterised by a prolonged paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory 'whoop'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why does pertussis matter now?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Despite being vaccine-preventable it is resurgent, with recent major UK and global outbreaks
  • it is most dangerous in young infants (under 6 months), causing apnoea, pneumonia and death
  • prevention hinges on maternal vaccination in pregnancy
  • and it is notifiable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the core mechanism of pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: B. pertussis infects the ciliated respiratory epithelium and releases toxins (pertussis toxin) that paralyse mucociliary clearance → mucus accumulates and can't be cleared → the violent repetitive coughing paroxysms (the '100-day cough').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the three stages of pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Catarrhal (~1–2 weeks)
  • paroxysmal (~2–6 weeks)
  • convalescent (weeks–months).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the catarrhal stage of pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: ~1–2 weeks of coryzal symptoms indistinguishable from a cold (runny nose, mild cough, low-grade fever); the MOST infectious phase.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the paroxysmal stage of pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: ~2–6 weeks of paroxysms — bursts of coughing ending in an inspiratory 'whoop' (forced inspiration against a closed glottis); post-tussive vomiting; worse at night; cyanosis/exhaustion. The whoop is often ABSENT in infants (→ apnoea instead) and in adults.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the convalescent stage of pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Weeks–months of gradual improvement; cough can linger for months, recurring with later URTIs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the classic clinical features of pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Coryzal prodrome → paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting (vomiting after a coughing fit); typically afebrile/low-grade; the child often looks WELL between fits.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What can coughing paroxysms in pertussis cause?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Cyanosis
  • subconjunctival haemorrhages
  • petechiae
  • syncope.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How does pertussis present in infants <6 months?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Atypically and dangerously — may have NO whoop; present with apnoea, cyanosis, poor feeding or a brief resolved unexplained event rather than the classic cough. This is the group to worry about.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is first-line investigation for pertussis in the early weeks?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: B. pertussis PCR (nasopharyngeal swab/aspirate) — most sensitive early.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What investigation is used for pertussis in patients coughing >2 weeks?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Anti-pertussis toxin IgG serology / oral fluid testing — the mainstay of confirmation later, when PCR/culture sensitivity falls.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What classic FBC finding occurs in pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Marked lymphocytosis (especially in infants).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: When should UKHSA be notified about pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: On clinical suspicion — don't wait for confirmation (it is a notifiable disease).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What do antibiotics achieve in pertussis, and when should they be given?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A macrolide if within 21 days of cough onset — they reduce infectivity/transmission but do little for symptoms once the paroxysmal (toxin-mediated) stage is established.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the antibiotic choice for pertussis by group?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
A macrolide, and only worth giving within 21 days of cough onset.
  • Under 1 month: clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days.
  • Over 1 month and non-pregnant adults: azithromycin or clarithromycin.
  • Pregnant women: erythromycin.
  • Macrolide-intolerant/contraindicated: co-trimoxazole (NOT in pregnancy or in infants under 6 weeks).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Who should be admitted with pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
Infants —
  • <6 months
  • apnoea/cyanosis
  • severe paroxysms
  • feeding difficulty
  • or complications
(for oxygen, monitoring, feeding/fluid support, sometimes ICU).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the exclusion rules for pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Stay off school/nursery/work until 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics (or 21 days from cough onset if untreated).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Who receives chemoprophylaxis for pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A macrolide for close contacts, but only if the cough started within the last 21 days AND the household contains a vulnerable person — an infant under 1 year, a woman in the last month of pregnancy, or someone in close contact with them (UKHSA). Contacts should also be offered vaccination if not up to date.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the main complications of pertussis in infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Apnoea, secondary pneumonia (commonest cause of death), pulmonary hypertension, seizures, encephalopathy (hypoxia) and death
  • and from the force of coughing: subconjunctival/nasal haemorrhage, rib fracture, hernia, syncope, pneumothorax.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is pertussis prevented by vaccination?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Routine childhood immunisation — pertussis is in the 6-in-1 vaccine (2, 3, 4 months) and the pre-school (4-in-1) booster; plus maternal vaccination in pregnancy (~16–32 weeks) — the key intervention to protect newborns via passive antibody transfer.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why do older children and adults matter in pertussis epidemiology?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Immunity (vaccine or natural) wanes → they get milder disease and act as a reservoir for infants.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Recurrent wheezing in children under ~5 years, most commonly triggered by viral upper respiratory tract infections ('episodic viral wheeze').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why does preschool wheeze matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is extremely common (up to a third of preschoolers wheeze), a frequent cause of GP/ED attendance and admission, and the key challenges are distinguishing it from asthma (can't confidently diagnose asthma under 5) and managing acute episodes without over-treating.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the core concept behind preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Small preschool airways narrow easily when inflamed by a virus → wheeze during colds; most children grow out of it as their airways enlarge (usually by ~6), but ~1 in 3 who wheeze persistently develop asthma (especially with atopy/sensitisation and a family history).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is episodic viral wheeze (EVW)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Wheeze ONLY with viral URTIs
  • symptom-free between episodes
  • with less underlying inflammation
  • often resolves by ~6.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is multiple-trigger wheeze (MTW)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Wheeze with viral URTIs PLUS other triggers (exercise, allergens, cold air, smoke)
  • with interval symptoms (cough/wheeze between colds) and more underlying inflammation (closer to asthma)
  • more likely to become asthma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the current caveat about the EVW/MTW distinction?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is less rigid than once taught — children move between phenotypes over time and parental reporting is imperfect; it is a useful framework but treatment is increasingly guided by frequency/severity and atopy risk rather than the label alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What features favour asthma / higher risk of progression in a preschool wheezer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Interval (between-episode) symptoms — cough/wheeze when well, night cough, exercise-induced wheeze
  • personal/family history of atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis, food allergy, parental asthma — the Asthma Predictive Index)
  • a clear response to a bronchodilator/ICS trial
  • frequent/severe exacerbations.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why do you generally NOT formally diagnose asthma under 5?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Can't do reliable spirometry and many will grow out of it — use a 'watch, treat, and review' approach and reassess with age.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the typical clinical features of preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
