• Wheeze + cough + increased work of breathing appearing WITH a viral cold (coryzal prodrome → wheeze)
  • expiratory polyphonic wheeze, tachypnoea, recession
  • recurrent self-limiting episodes
  • well between episodes (EVW) or interval symptoms (MTW).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What red flags suggest an alternative diagnosis rather than simple preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Symptoms from birth/very early
  • failure to thrive
  • wet/productive chronic cough (CF, bronchiectasis)
  • focal signs/stridor
  • choking episode (inhaled foreign body)
  • finger clubbing
  • cardiac signs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Is preschool wheeze usually investigated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: No — it is a clinical diagnosis; consider CXR if atypical/red flags (exclude foreign body, structural/cardiac cause), sweat test if CF suspected. Spirometry is not reliable under ~5.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the mainstay of treating an acute preschool wheeze exacerbation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Inhaled SABA (salbutamol) via a spacer, 2–10 puffs titrated to response (burst therapy, then spacing out)
  • oxygen if hypoxic to keep saturations 94–98%
  • oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg once daily for up to 3 days (about 10 mg under 2 years, 20 mg at 2–5 years) for moderate–severe exacerbations
  • escalate as for acute asthma if severe.
Do not apply adult asthma severity numbers to a young child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: When should a child with acute preschool wheeze be admitted?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: If poor response, hypoxia, severe distress, or unable to feed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the preventer approach for episodic viral wheeze (EVW)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• First-line: SABA via a spacer as needed for episodes — ipratropium is an add-on in severe acute episodes, not an equal first-line reliever.
  • Second-line (if frequent/severe): intermittent LTRA (montelukast) and/or intermittent ICS started at the onset of a viral episode.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the preventer approach for multiple-trigger wheeze (MTW)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A trial of twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS with a SABA reliever for 8–12 weeks, then REVIEW; continue only if there is clear benefit (a treatment trial, not open-ended). Montelukast is an add-on if still uncontrolled on ICS — its own 8–12 week trial — not an equal first choice.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What general measures are advised in preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back:
• Avoid tobacco smoke exposure (a major modifiable trigger)
  • inhaler technique/spacer education
  • and a written action plan.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What safety counselling is needed for montelukast?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Counsel about neuropsychiatric side effects — sleep disturbance, mood/behaviour change, nightmares (a recent safety emphasis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What conditions are grouped under neonatal GI & abdominal wall?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Congenital gut and abdominal-wall anomalies plus the acquired bowel emergency of prematurity (NEC).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the organising principle for neonatal GI & abdominal wall conditions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Many present with neonatal bowel obstruction (vomiting, distension, failure to pass meconium) or are seen at birth (abdominal-wall defects); NEC is an acquired emergency in preterm/formula-fed neonates.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Give the clue for duodenal atresia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Bilious vomiting, 'double bubble' on X-ray; associated with Down syndrome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Give the clue and management for biliary atresia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Prolonged conjugated jaundice, pale stools/dark urine; Kasai portoenterostomy early.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How do gastroschisis and omphalocele differ at a glance?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis (no sac, right of cord, isolated) vs omphalocele (sac, associated anomalies).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Give the clue and management for necrotising enterocolitis (NEC).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Preterm; feeding intolerance, distension, bloody stool, pneumatosis → stop feeds, antibiotics, surgery if perforation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What does prolonged conjugated jaundice with pale stools mean until proven otherwise?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Biliary atresia → urgent referral (Kasai success depends on early surgery).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A congenital complete obstruction of the duodenal lumen — the commonest cause of congenital (proximal) small-bowel obstruction in the neonate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the core mechanism of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Failure of recanalisation of the duodenal lumen during the ~8th week of fetal development (the duodenum normally becomes a solid cord then re-hollows; if it doesn't → an atretic blind-ending segment).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How does duodenal atresia's mechanism differ from distal (jejunal/ileal) atresias?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Duodenal atresia is failure of recanalisation, whereas distal atresias have an ischaemic/vascular cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why is most duodenal atresia vomiting bilious?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Because ~85% of obstructions are distal to the ampulla of Vater, so bile enters above the obstruction (green vomit); a proximal one (~15%) is non-bilious.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the key rule about any bilious vomiting in a neonate?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: It is a surgical emergency until obstruction is excluded — the key differential being malrotation with volvulus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: When does duodenal atresia present and how?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Vomiting within the first day of life (complete obstruction presents early); usually bilious (distal to ampulla), non-bilious if proximal.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the abdomen typically like in duodenal atresia, and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Often scaphoid/flat distally with only epigastric (or no) distension — the obstruction is high so distal bowel is empty/gasless, unlike distal obstructions which distend the whole abdomen. Failure to pass meconium may occur; excessive salivation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How may duodenal atresia be picked up antenatally?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Polyhydramnios (fetus can't swallow/absorb amniotic fluid past the obstruction) plus a double bubble on the fetal ultrasound.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the classic association of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — ~1/3 of cases; karyotyping is indicated.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: List other associations of duodenal atresia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Congenital heart disease (~half); annular pancreas, malrotation, oesophageal atresia/TOF, imperforate anus, renal anomalies, biliary anomalies (VACTERL-type) — the same VACTERL work-up applies; in oesophageal atresia, polyhydramnios antenatally and an NG tube that will not pass are the giveaways. Also prematurity and maternal polyhydramnios.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the 'double bubble' sign?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Two gas-filled bubbles (dilated stomach + dilated proximal duodenum) with no/little gas distally on abdominal X-ray — usually diagnostic of duodenal atresia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What does gas distal to the double bubble suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Duodenal stenosis (partial) or, importantly, malrotation/volvulus rather than complete atresia — a crucial distinction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What investigations are done for the associations of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Echocardiography and karyotype (screen the associations)
  • electrolytes for dehydration/losses
  • upper GI contrast study + ultrasound for equivocal cases/to exclude malrotation

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the immediate/supportive management of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Nasogastric tube (decompress the stomach), IV fluid resuscitation, and correct electrolyte disturbance (vomiting → hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis) — stabilise first.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the definitive treatment of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Surgical repair — duodenoduodenostomy (bypass the atretic segment, joining the two duodenal ends); good outcomes. Screen/manage associated anomalies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A progressive, obliterative cholangiopathy of the newborn — inflammatory destruction and fibrosis of the bile ducts blocking bile flow (obstructive cholestasis); if untreated leads to cirrhosis, liver failure and death by ~2 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why does biliary atresia matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: It is the commonest surgical cause of neonatal cholestasis and the leading indication for paediatric liver transplantation; outcome depends entirely on early diagnosis and surgery (Kasai works far better before ~60 days).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Describe the core mechanism of biliary atresia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Progressive inflammation and fibrosis obliterate the extrahepatic (± intrahepatic) bile ducts → bile can't drain → conjugated (direct) bilirubin backs up → progressive hepatic fibrosis → cirrhosis. Cause unknown (likely immune/inflammatory ± viral/genetic).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What causes of jaundice does a conjugated (direct) picture suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, infection, metabolic (galactosaemia, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency) — pathological, needs urgent work-up.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What causes of jaundice does an unconjugated (indirect) picture suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Physiological jaundice, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis — usually benign.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the stool and urine findings in biliary atresia (obstructive) vs benign unconjugated jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Biliary atresia: pale stools + dark urine (obstructive). Benign unconjugated: normal-coloured stools/urine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is THE rule for prolonged neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Any term infant still jaundiced at >14 days (or preterm >21 days) → do a jaundice screen including a SPLIT bilirubin. Do not wait for day 14 if there are pale chalky stools or dark urine staining the nappy — measure the conjugated bilirubin the same day. A conjugated bilirubin above 25 micromol/L means biliary atresia until proven otherwise, and needs urgent referral to a specialist centre.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the presenting feature of biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Persistent (prolonged) neonatal jaundice beyond 2 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why can pale/acholic stools be a missed clue in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Pale clay-coloured stools mean no bile pigment reaches the gut, but they can be overlooked → false reassurance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why is urine dark in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble → excreted renally, darkening the urine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why is the early presentation of biliary atresia a trap?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: The baby often initially looks well and thrives early on; hepatomegaly develops, and only later (if untreated, >3 months) come hepatosplenomegaly, faltering growth, ascites, coagulopathy (vitamin K malabsorption) and cirrhosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is BASM syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Biliary Atresia Splenic Malformation syndrome (~10–15%) — polysplenia/asplenia, situs inversus, cardiac defects, intestinal malrotation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the key first test in suspected biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A SPLIT (conjugated/unconjugated) bilirubin — showing a raised conjugated (direct) fraction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What LFT findings occur in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Raised transaminases and especially raised GGT; plus a coagulation screen (vitamin-K-dependent factors; bleeding risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What does the jaundice screen include for biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• TFTs (hypothyroid)
  • FBC/blood film
  • urine MC&S (UTI)
  • U&E
  • galactosaemia screen
  • infection/TORCH
  • alpha-1-antitrypsin
  • metabolic tests

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What ultrasound findings suggest biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Absent/abnormal gallbladder and the 'triangular cord' sign; ultrasound also excludes a choledochal cyst.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What do HIDA scan and liver biopsy show in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• HIDA (hepatobiliary) scan — no excretion of tracer into the bowel, but it is now largely superseded: too non-specific and it delays surgery.
  • Liver biopsy — bile duct proliferation, fibrosis.
  • Intra-operative cholangiogram is the definitive/confirmatory test.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the first-line surgical treatment of biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Kasai portoenterostomy — a Roux loop of jejunum anastomosed to the porta hepatis to allow bile drainage, bypassing the obliterated extrahepatic ducts.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why is the timing of the Kasai procedure critical?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Best outcomes if done before ~60 days of life (some say <45 days); the older the infant, the worse the result — age at surgery is the single most important prognostic factor.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What supportive management is needed in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (A, D, E, K)
  • nutritional support (MCT-based feeds)
  • ursodeoxycholic acid
  • and treating/preventing cholangitis (a common post-Kasai complication)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the definitive treatment if Kasai fails or cirrhosis develops?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Liver transplantation — biliary atresia is the commonest indication for paediatric liver transplant; many children ultimately need one even after a successful Kasai.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are gastroschisis and omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: The two congenital anterior abdominal wall defects in which abdominal contents herniate out through the wall at birth; usually diagnosed antenatally.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What single feature separates gastroschisis from omphalocele and drives everything?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
The presence of a covering sac:
  • gastroschisis has NO sac (bowel exposed)
  • omphalocele has a sac (amnion + peritoneum).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Where is the defect in gastroschisis vs omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Gastroschisis: lateral to the cord (usually to the right).
  • Omphalocele: at/through the umbilicus itself.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How do the associations differ between gastroschisis and omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Gastroschisis: few/none (usually isolated).
  • Omphalocele: strong chromosomal and syndromic associations.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What happens to the bowel in gastroschisis vs omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Gastroschisis: exposed → inflamed, matted, at risk of ischaemia/atresia.
  • Omphalocele: protected by the sac (unless it ruptures).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How does the delivery plan differ between gastroschisis and omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Gastroschisis: vaginal delivery can be attempted.
  • Omphalocele: vaginal delivery is usually possible too — caesarean is reserved for a giant/liver-containing sac or for obstetric indications.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How does the repair differ between gastroschisis and omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Gastroschisis: urgent — theatre ASAP (± silo).
  • Omphalocele: primary closure if minor; giant/major defects are dressed and left to epithelialise ('paint and wait') with delayed closure over 6–12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Describe gastroschisis in detail.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A full-thickness defect lateral to the cord (usually right) with NO covering sac → bowel exposed to amniotic fluid → inflamed, thickened, matted ('peel'), at risk of ischaemia, atresia and heat/fluid loss.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the risk factors for gastroschisis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Young maternal age (<20), maternal smoking, alcohol and recreational drug use; incidence is rising. Usually isolated with few associated anomalies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How is gastroschisis managed after birth?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Newborn to theatre ASAP — primary closure if possible, or a 'silo' (bowel suspended and gradually reduced over days before closure).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Describe omphalocele (exomphalos).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Protrusion of abdominal contents through the abdominal wall at the umbilicus, covered by a sac of amniotic membrane and peritoneum; may contain bowel, liver and other viscera.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What chromosomal associations does omphalocele have?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Trisomy 13 (Patau), 18 (Edwards), 21 (Down) → karyotyping is essential.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and its link to omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Exomphalos + macroglossia + gigantism/overgrowth + neonatal hypoglycaemia (+ Wilms'/hepatoblastoma risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What other associations does omphalocele have?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Cardiac defects (common — echo needed)
  • Pentalogy of Cantrell
  • cloacal exstrophy
  • renal anomalies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How is omphalocele managed (delivery and repair)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
Vaginal delivery is usually possible; caesarean is reserved for a giant/liver-containing sac or obstetric indications. Repair depends on size:
  • exomphalos minor (small defect, no liver) is closed primarily in the neonatal period
  • a giant/major defect is dressed and left to epithelialise with delayed closure over 6–12 months, because forcing a large volume back suddenly causes respiratory compromise and abdominal compartment syndrome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How are both abdominal wall defects usually diagnosed antenatally, and what marker is raised?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Both are usually detected on the routine 20-week ultrasound; maternal serum AFP is raised in both (higher in gastroschisis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What antenatal investigations does omphalocele need vs gastroschisis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Omphalocele → karyotyping (amniocentesis) + echocardiography + renal ultrasound (screen associations).
  • Gastroschisis → fewer investigations (usually isolated), serial growth scans (IUGR risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the immediate neonatal management of an abdominal wall defect?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Cover the exposed bowel/defect (clingfilm/clear occlusive covering or 'bowel bag')
  • fluid resuscitation (large insensible losses)
  • thermoregulation
  • nasogastric tube (decompress bowel)
  • IV antibiotics
monitor bowel perfusion, then surgical closure (primary or staged/silo).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How do the prognoses of gastroschisis and omphalocele compare?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis is generally good (isolated); omphalocele prognosis depends on associated anomalies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is necrotising enterocolitis (NEC)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A devastating inflammatory bowel disease of the neonate — inflammation, ischaemia and bacterial invasion of the bowel wall → necrosis, which can progress to perforation, peritonitis and death.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why does NEC matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: It is the commonest GI emergency in the neonatal unit and one of the leading causes of death in premature infants; strongly linked to prematurity and enteral (especially formula) feeding, with breast milk protective. Survivors risk short bowel syndrome, strictures and neurodevelopmental impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Describe the core mechanism ('perfect storm') of NEC.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Immature intestinal barrier + abnormal bacterial colonisation (dysbiosis) + mucosal ischaemia/hypoperfusion + enteral feed as substrate → bacteria breach the fragile bowel wall → inflammation and ischaemic necrosis → gas tracks into the bowel wall (pneumatosis) and portal system → perforation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: When does NEC typically cluster?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: In preterm, formula-fed babies after feeds are established (typically weeks 2–4).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the biggest risk factors for NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Prematurity + very low birth weight (the more preterm, the higher the risk); formula feeding (breast milk is protective).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: List other risk factors for NEC.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: IUGR/placental insufficiency, hypoxia/perinatal asphyxia; anything reducing gut perfusion — congenital heart disease (especially duct-dependent/PDA), polycythaemia, exchange/RBC transfusion, sepsis, hypotension; rapid advancement of enteral feeds.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the early clinical features of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Feeding intolerance (increased/bilious gastric aspirates, vomiting often bile-stained)
  • abdominal distension (often the first sign, ± tenderness/visible loops)
  • and bloody stools (blood/mucus per rectum).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the systemic and late/severe features of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Systemic: lethargy, temperature instability, apnoea/bradycardia, poor perfusion → sepsis/shock, DIC.
  • Severe/late: abdominal wall discolouration (erythema), perforation, peritonitis — needing surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the key investigation in NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Abdominal X-ray.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What abdominal X-ray findings occur in NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Dilated bowel loops
  • bowel wall oedema (thickened wall)
  • pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas — the pathognomonic sign)
  • portal venous gas (more severe)
  • pneumoperitoneum → perforation (Rigler's sign — gas both sides of the bowel wall; 'football sign').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the pathognomonic X-ray sign of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Pneumatosis intestinalis — gas within the bowel wall.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What blood findings occur in NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Thrombocytopenia (a useful early clue), anaemia, leukocytosis/leukopenia
  • metabolic acidosis
  • raised CRP
  • blood culture (sepsis)
  • coagulation/DIC screen
  • blood gas.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is Bell staging used for in NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Staging NEC I (suspected) → II (definite) → III (advanced/perforation) on clinical + radiological features, guiding management.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the medical (Bell I–II) management of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Stop enteral feeds (bowel rest/nil by mouth) and NG tube on free drainage
  • typically bowel rest ~7–14 days with parenteral nutrition
  • broad-spectrum IV antibiotics after blood cultures — typically benzylpenicillin 25 mg/kg 12-hourly + gentamicin 5 mg/kg + metronidazole, per local neonatal protocol (BNFC)
  • supportive care (IV fluids, correct acidosis/electrolytes, respiratory/circulatory support, treat DIC/thrombocytopenia)
  • serial X-rays and examinations.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the surgical (Bell III) management of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: For perforation or deterioration despite medical management: laparotomy with resection of necrotic bowel (± stoma); peritoneal drain in the very small/unstable. Pneumoperitoneum is an indication for surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the complications of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Perforation/peritonitis
  • sepsis/DIC
  • strictures (later)
  • short bowel syndrome (after resection → long-term parenteral nutrition)
  • neurodevelopmental impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the single most important protective factor against NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Breast milk (maternal or donor).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What other measures help prevent NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back:
• Antenatal corticosteroids (if preterm delivery anticipated — gut maturation)
  • cautious/standardised feeding protocols
  • and probiotics (increasingly used to reduce NEC in preterms).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the organising principle for neonatal medicine problems?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
Prematurity and perinatal events drive most neonatal illness; approach by system —
  • breathing (RDS, meconium aspiration),
  • metabolic (jaundice, hypoglycaemia),
  • infection (sepsis)
  • and brain (HIE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for neonatal RDS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Preterm surfactant deficiency; grunting, ground-glass X-ray; antenatal steroids, surfactant, CPAP.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for meconium aspiration syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Term/post-term, meconium-stained liquor; respiratory distress; supportive/ventilation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key rule for neonatal jaundice.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: <24h = always pathological (haemolysis/sepsis); phototherapy/exchange by threshold; kernicterus risk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for neonatal sepsis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Non-specific (temperature instability, poor feeding); cultures + empirical antibiotics promptly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Perinatal hypoxia; encephalopathy; therapeutic cooling within 6h.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for neonatal hypoglycaemia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Jittery, poor feeding, seizures; at-risk (IUGR, IDM, preterm); feed / IV dextrose.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: An acute lung disease of the newborn caused by insufficient pulmonary surfactant → alveolar collapse and stiff, poorly-inflated lungs (also called surfactant deficient lung disease / hyaline membrane disease).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does RDS matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is the commonest cause of respiratory distress in premature infants, its incidence rises the more preterm the baby, and antenatal corticosteroids and exogenous surfactant have transformed survival.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe the core mechanism of RDS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes (mature ~weeks 24–34). In prematurity, insufficient surfactant + structural lung immaturity → high alveolar surface tension → alveolar collapse (atelectasis) → stiff/non-compliant lungs; blood passing collapsed alveoli isn't oxygenated (intrapulmonary shunt) → hypoxaemia + increased work of breathing.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is surfactant's job?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: To lower surface tension and stop alveoli collapsing — so its absence is the whole disease of RDS.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the biggest risk factor for RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Prematurity — risk is inversely proportional to gestational age (very common <28 weeks, uncommon at term).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List other risk factors for RDS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Male sex;
  • maternal diabetes (fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant production);
  • caesarean section (especially without labour);
  • second twin, perinatal asphyxia/hypothermia, family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: When does RDS present and how does it evolve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Onset within minutes–hours of birth (typically <4 hours), worsening over the first ~48–72 h.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the clinical signs of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Tachypnoea,
  • intercostal (± subcostal) recession,
  • expiratory grunting (auto-PEEP against a closed glottis),
  • cyanosis,
  • nasal flaring,
  • apnoea in the very preterm.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the chest X-ray appearance of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: 'Ground-glass' appearance — diffuse fine reticulogranular shadowing + air bronchograms + reduced lung volumes, with an indistinct heart border (from widespread atelectasis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What blood gas findings occur in RDS, and what must be excluded?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, respiratory ± metabolic acidosis. Screen for/exclude sepsis (congenital pneumonia e.g. Group B Strep can look identical).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the antenatal prevention of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Maternal (antenatal) corticosteroids to induce fetal lung maturation — given to mothers at risk of preterm delivery (e.g. <34–36 weeks); reduces RDS, IVH and neonatal death.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the first-line postnatal respiratory support for RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: CPAP — keeps alveoli open and often avoids intubation, escalating to mechanical ventilation if needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is exogenous surfactant given in RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Via an endotracheal tube — replacing the missing surfactant; increasingly given by minimally invasive techniques (LISA/MIST — a thin catheter without full intubation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What supportive care is needed in RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Thermoregulation,
  • fluids/nutrition,
  • treat sepsis,
  • gentle handling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the complications of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Pneumothorax/air leak (stiff lungs + positive-pressure ventilation);
  • bronchopulmonary dysplasia (oxygen need beyond 36 weeks corrected age);
  • IVH, patent ductus arteriosus, retinopathy of prematurity, NEC, infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Chronic lung disease of prematurity — an oxygen requirement persisting beyond 36 weeks corrected age (from lung injury + oxygen/ventilation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the key differentials of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN — term/C-section, self-resolves ~24–48h) and congenital pneumonia (Group B Strep).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Respiratory distress in a newborn caused by aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid (MSAF) into the lungs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does MAS matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is an important cause of respiratory distress in TERM and POST-TERM infants (opposite end of the spectrum to RDS), causes disease through multiple mechanisms at once, and is strongly linked to persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe the core sequence leading to MAS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Fetal distress/hypoxia (or maturity) → the fetus passes meconium into the amniotic fluid AND gasps → meconium is inhaled into the airways.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the four ways meconium causes disease in the lungs?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• (1) Airway obstruction — 'ball-valve' → air trapping/hyperinflation (pneumothorax) and atelectasis;
  • (2) chemical pneumonitis/inflammation;
  • (3) surfactant inactivation (free fatty/bile acids);
  • (4) persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is PPHN in the context of MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Hypoxia → pulmonary vasoconstriction → the circulation reverts to a right-to-left (fetal-type) shunt → refractory hypoxaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the single most important risk factor for MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Fetal distress / intrapartum hypoxia-asphyxia (hypoxia → meconium passage + gasping).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List other risk factors for MAS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Post-term/post-maturity (mature gut passes meconium more readily),
  • small-for-gestational-age/IUGR,
  • placental insufficiency,
  • difficult/prolonged labour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What does meconium-stained liquor in preterm labour suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is rare in preterm labour — if present, think chorioamnionitis/infection or cord compression.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the clinical features of MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Onset immediately/soon after birth in a term/post-term baby;
  • meconium-stained (green) liquor and staining of skin/nails/cord;
  • respiratory distress (tachypnoea, grunting, flaring, recession, cyanosis);
  • often a barrel/hyperinflated chest;
  • crackles/rhonchi;
  • may be depressed/asphyxiated at birth (low Apgars).
Watch for PPHN — severe/labile hypoxaemia out of proportion to lung findings.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the chest X-ray appearance of MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Patchy infiltrates and atelectasis, with hyperinflation and areas of consolidation/collapse; ± pneumothorax/air leak.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What investigations are used if PPHN is suspected in MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Pre-/post-ductal saturations + echocardiography (right-to-left shunt); plus blood gas and a sepsis screen (MAS mimics/co-exists with congenital pneumonia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the current delivery-room approach to meconium-stained babies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Routine deep endotracheal suctioning is NO LONGER recommended — even non-vigorous infants: follow normal neonatal resuscitation (airway, breathing). Suction only if the airway is obstructed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the mainstay of postnatal management of MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Supportive — oxygen and respiratory support (CPAP/mechanical ventilation as needed; HFOV in severe cases); careful because air trapping + atelectasis make ventilation tricky.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the role of surfactant in MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Exogenous surfactant and/or surfactant lavage in moderate–severe MAS, because meconium inactivates surfactant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is PPHN treated in MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) — a pulmonary vasodilator; ECMO as rescue in refractory PPHN/respiratory failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What additional supportive measures are used in MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Antibiotics (can't exclude infection),
  • thermoregulation,
  • fluids,
  • treat air leaks (chest drain for pneumothorax),
  • monitor for hypoxic-ischaemic injury.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Yellow discolouration of the skin/sclera from raised bilirubin (hyperbilirubinaemia) in a newborn; extremely common (>50% of term, most preterm babies) — usually benign/physiological, but a minority is pathological and dangerous.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does neonatal jaundice matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause kernicterus (permanent brain injury); the clinical skill is using the TIMING to separate benign from serious.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why are newborns predisposed to jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• High red-cell mass with a short lifespan (rapid breakdown of fetal Hb → more bilirubin)
  • + an immature liver (low UGT enzyme activity → can't conjugate fast enough)
  • + increased enterohepatic circulation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is jaundice at <24 hours interpreted, and what are the causes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: ALWAYS pathological — usually haemolysis: Rhesus & ABO haemolytic disease, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency; plus congenital infection/sepsis (TORCH). Check serum bilirubin urgently (within ~2 hours).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is jaundice at day 2–14 usually interpreted?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Usually physiological (or breastfeeding/breast-milk jaundice) — unconjugated, benign; peaks day 3–5, resolves by ~day 10–14, baby is well and feeding. A diagnosis of exclusion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is jaundice at >14 days (>21 days if preterm) interpreted?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
Prolonged — pathological until proven otherwise → jaundice screen. Causes:
  • biliary atresia,
  • hypothyroidism,
  • galactosaemia,
  • UTI,
  • breast-milk jaundice,
  • prematurity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the difference between breastfeeding jaundice and breast-milk jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Breastfeeding jaundice — early, from suboptimal intake/dehydration → more enterohepatic circulation. Breast-milk jaundice — later/prolonged, benign, from breast-milk factors (a common cause of prolonged jaundice in a thriving baby).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How does prematurity affect physiological jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It exaggerates and prolongs it (immature liver + shorter red-cell survival).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What does a jaundice screen include for prolonged jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Conjugated + unconjugated (split) bilirubin, Coombs (DAT), TFTs, FBC (± film), urine MC&S, U&E, LFTs (+ blood group, G6PD, infection/metabolic screen).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why is the split bilirubin the key branch point in prolonged jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Conjugated (>~25 µmol/L or >20%) → pathological → biliary atresia until proven otherwise (pale stools/dark urine), neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, metabolic. Unconjugated → hypothyroidism, UTI/infection, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis, galactosaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is bilirubin measured in a jaundiced newborn?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Transcutaneous bilirubinometer (screening, ≥35 weeks & >24h) → serum bilirubin (SBR) to confirm/if high-risk; always SBR if <24 hours old or <35 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What decides treatment in neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Plotting the SBR against age (hours) on the gestational-age-specific NICE treatment threshold chart, comparing the level to the phototherapy and exchange lines.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is first-line treatment for neonatal jaundice, and how does it work?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Phototherapy — blue light (~450 nm) converts unconjugated bilirubin in the skin to water-soluble isomers excreted without conjugation. Escalate to multiple/intensified phototherapy if rising fast or nearing the exchange threshold.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: When is IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) used in neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: As an adjunct in Rhesus/ABO haemolytic disease when bilirubin keeps rising despite intensive phototherapy — IVIG 500 mg/kg over 4 hours.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: When is exchange transfusion used in neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: For very high/rapidly rising bilirubin (above the exchange line, or signs of bilirubin encephalopathy) — removes bilirubin and antibody-coated red cells; prevents kernicterus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Which type of bilirubin causes kernicterus and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Only UNCONJUGATED (fat-soluble) bilirubin — it crosses the blood-brain barrier; conjugated is water-soluble and doesn't. This is why the split matters and why unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is treated aggressively.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia → then irritability, hypertonia, arching (opisthotonos), high-pitched cry, seizures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the chronic (permanent) sequelae of kernicterus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Choreoathetoid cerebral palsy,
  • sensorineural hearing loss,
  • upward-gaze palsy,
  • dental enamel dysplasia,
  • learning difficulty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: A systemic bacterial infection in the first 28 days of life — a medical emergency; newborns have an immature immune system, deteriorate rapidly, and present with vague, non-specific signs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does neonatal sepsis matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is a major cause of neonatal death and disability; Group B Streptococcus and E. coli are the leading organisms; the approach is 'treat first, ask questions later' — take cultures and start antibiotics within 1 hour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is early-onset vs late-onset neonatal sepsis defined by timing?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Early-onset: <72 hours (often <24 h) of life. Late-onset: >72 hours to 28 days.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the sources and organisms of early-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Source: vertical — from the mother (birth canal/ascending infection). Organisms: Group B Strep + E. coli (also Listeria).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the sources and organisms of late-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Source: environmental/nosocomial (hands, lines, ventilators). Organisms: coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (esp. lines), Staph aureus, Gram-negatives, Group B Strep, fungal (Candida).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List the maternal/early-onset risk factors for neonatal sepsis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Maternal Group B Strep (colonisation, GBS bacteriuria, or a previous baby with invasive GBS disease)
  • prolonged rupture of membranes (>18–24 h)
  • preterm labour/prematurity
  • chorioamnionitis/maternal intrapartum fever (>38°C) or confirmed maternal infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the risk factors for late-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Preterm
  • low birth weight
  • indwelling lines/devices
  • prolonged neonatal-unit stay.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the non-specific clinical features of neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Respiratory (grunting, tachypnoea, apnoea, increased O2 need, cyanosis)
  • temperature instability (fever OR — more commonly — hypothermia)
  • poor feeding/vomiting/distension
  • lethargy/irritability/hypotonia/seizures/bulging fontanelle
  • poor perfusion/mottling/hypotension
  • jaundice (especially <24 h)
  • hypo-/hyperglycaemia
  • metabolic acidosis
  • DIC/bleeding.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the NICE 'red flag' signs of neonatal sepsis prompting immediate treatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Signs of shock, seizures, need for mechanical ventilation, or respiratory distress starting >4 h after birth. The rule that connects the lists: start empirical antibiotics for ONE red flag, or for TWO OR MORE non-red-flag risk factors or clinical indicators.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the key investigation in neonatal sepsis, and when is it taken?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Blood culture — BEFORE the first antibiotic dose (but don't delay antibiotics for it).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What other investigations are used in neonatal sepsis (NICE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• FBC (neutropenia/neutrophilia, thrombocytopenia), CRP (baseline and repeated ~18–24 h to trend)
  • lumbar puncture if strong suspicion/meningitis signs/culture-positive
  • blood gas, glucose, U&E
  • surface/urine cultures, CXR as indicated
  • late-onset → sample lines.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the empirical antibiotic regimen for early-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Benzylpenicillin 25 mg/kg IV 12-hourly (consider 8-hourly if the baby appears very ill) + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV, the second dose usually at 36 hours — the standard UK regimen, covering Group B Strep, E. coli and Listeria.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the empirical antibiotic regimen for late-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Flucloxacillin + gentamicin (or per local policy — cover coagulase-negative staph/line infection; add Gram-negative/Listeria cover as needed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How quickly must antibiotics be started in neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Within 1 hour of deciding to treat — don't wait for results (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What supportive care is needed in neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Respiratory support (O2/ventilation)
  • fluids/inotropes for shock
  • glucose
  • correct acidosis/coagulopathy (DIC)
  • thermoregulation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How are antibiotics reviewed in neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: At ~36 hours: stop if the baby is well, blood cultures are negative and CRP is normal/falling; continue (≥7 days, longer for meningitis) if culture-positive or ongoing suspicion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is early-onset Group B Strep sepsis prevented?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) — IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.5 g every 4 hours until delivery, for at-risk mothers (GBS colonisation/bacteriuria, previous GBS baby, preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, intrapartum fever).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Neonatal brain injury caused by insufficient oxygen and blood flow to the brain (perinatal asphyxia), usually around the time of birth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does HIE matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is a major cause of neonatal death and long-term neurodisability (cerebral palsy, epilepsy, cognitive/sensory impairment), and therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) started within 6 hours is the one intervention proven to reduce death and disability.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe the 'two-phase' injury of HIE and why the 6-hour window exists.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Primary energy failure during the insult (cells can't make ATP → ion pumps fail → cell death) → a latent phase (~6 hours) as circulation is restored (the therapeutic window) → secondary energy failure (~6–48 h) of excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation and apoptosis causing delayed neuronal death. Cooling slows this secondary cascade, so it must start within ~6 hours.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List causes of HIE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Placental abruption
  • cord prolapse/compression
  • uterine rupture
  • shoulder dystocia
  • maternal hypotension/shock
  • prolonged/obstructed labour
  • failure to breathe at birth
  • severe anaemia (feto-maternal haemorrhage)
  • maternal hypoxia
  • meconium aspiration.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What evidence of perinatal asphyxia supports HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Low Apgar scores (≤5 at 10 min), need for prolonged resuscitation, and metabolic acidosis (cord pH <7.0 or base deficit ≥16).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the features of encephalopathy in HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Altered consciousness (irritability → lethargy → coma)
  • abnormal tone (hypo-/hypertonia)
  • poor feeding/weak suck
  • abnormal/primitive reflexes
  • seizures
  • apnoea
  • abnormal posturing/movements.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What multi-organ involvement supports HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Acute kidney injury
  • hepatic dysfunction (deranged LFTs)
  • cardiac dysfunction
  • DIC
(hypoxia hits other organs too).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe modified Sarnat grade 1 (mild) HIE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Irritable/hyperalert consciousness, normal/slightly increased tone, exaggerated startle, no seizures; usually good prognosis (recovers ~24–48 h); no cooling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe modified Sarnat grade 2 (moderate) HIE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Lethargic consciousness, hypotonia, weak suck, seizures common; variable prognosis (~1/3 have long-term problems); cool.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe modified Sarnat grade 3 (severe) HIE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Comatose, flaccid tone, absent suck/reflexes, frequent/prolonged seizures; poor prognosis (high death/severe disability); cool.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Which Sarnat grades receive therapeutic cooling?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Grades 2–3 (moderate–severe).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What investigations are used in HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Cord/arterial blood gas (acidosis), glucose, U&E, LFTs, FBC, coagulation (multi-organ screen)
  • aEEG/EEG (background activity + detect often-subclinical seizures, prognostic)
  • MRI brain (usually days 5–14, defines injury pattern, prognostic)
  • cranial ultrasound.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the key intervention in HIE and its parameters?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) — cool to ~33–34°C for 72 hours, started within 6 hours of birth, for moderate–severe (Sarnat 2–3) HIE in infants ≥36 weeks; reduces death and disability; then rewarm slowly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What supportive intensive care is needed alongside cooling in HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Ventilation as needed (maintain normal oxygenation/CO2)
  • treat seizures (phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV first-line)
  • maintain normoglycaemia, normal BP/perfusion, fluid/electrolyte balance
  • treat multi-organ dysfunction
  • avoid hyperthermia (worsens injury)
  • monitor for infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the first-line treatment for seizures in HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV, loaded over about 20 minutes (a further 10 mg/kg may be given).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What determines prognosis in HIE, and what are the sequelae?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Severity (Sarnat grade): grade 1 usually normal, grade 2 variable, grade 3 high mortality/severe disability. Sequelae: cerebral palsy (especially dyskinetic/spastic quadriplegic), epilepsy, learning disability, sensorineural hearing loss, visual impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: A low blood glucose in the newborn — the commonest metabolic problem in neonates.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does neonatal hypoglycaemia matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Transient mild hypoglycaemia in the first hours is common and usually benign (transition from constant placental glucose to intermittent feeds), but persistent or symptomatic hypoglycaemia can cause permanent brain injury (the brain depends on glucose).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe the core physiology of neonatal hypoglycaemia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: At birth the placental glucose supply is suddenly cut off → the newborn must mobilise its own glucose (glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis) and establish feeding. A transient dip is normal; problems arise when demand outstrips supply, stores are low, or consumption is high.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why do infants of diabetic mothers get hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia (from maternal hyperglycaemia) persists after birth → the baby keeps over-secreting insulin.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List the at-risk groups for persistent neonatal hypoglycaemia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Infant of a diabetic mother (fetal hyperinsulinaemia)
  • prematurity (low glycogen stores)
  • IUGR/SGA (low stores)
  • large-for-dates
  • hypothermia (increased consumption)
  • neonatal sepsis
  • perinatal asphyxia/stress
  • polycythaemia
  • inborn errors of metabolism
  • congenital hyperinsulinism (nesidioblastosis)
  • Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
  • endocrine deficiency (hypopituitarism, cortisol/growth hormone deficiency).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the autonomic features of neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Jitteriness (the classic sign)
  • irritability
  • tachypnoea
  • pallor
  • sweating.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the neuroglycopenic features of neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Poor feeding/sucking
  • weak/high-pitched cry
  • drowsiness/lethargy
  • hypotonia
  • seizures
  • apnoea
  • coma (severe).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why must at-risk babies be screened for hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Because hypoglycaemia may be asymptomatic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is blood glucose measured/confirmed in neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Screen at-risk infants with pre-feed capillary glucose; confirm low readings with a laboratory glucose (bedside glucometers are unreliable at low values).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the operational treatment threshold for neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
<2.6 mmol/L is the figure commonly used in UK teaching. The BAPM operational thresholds are
  • <2.0 mmol/L in an at-risk baby with no abnormal signs (and still <2.0 on the next measurement)
  • <2.5 mmol/L where there ARE abnormal clinical signs
  • and <1.0 mmol/L at any time, which needs immediate IV glucose.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is a hypoglycaemia screen and when is it taken?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Taken WHEN glucose is low, for persistent/severe hypoglycaemia: insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones, free fatty acids, lactate, ammonia, and metabolic/acylcarnitine studies — to identify hyperinsulinism, endocrine deficiency or an inborn error of metabolism.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is asymptomatic/mildly low neonatal hypoglycaemia managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Encourage normal/early feeding and monitor blood glucose — frequent feeds (breast/formula), keep warm, recheck pre-feeds; add buccal 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (= 0.5 mL/kg) massaged into the cheek alongside feeding (reduces neonatal-unit admissions, supports breastfeeding).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is symptomatic or very low neonatal hypoglycaemia managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Admit to the neonatal unit and give IV 10% glucose — a 2 mL/kg bolus then an infusion of about 60–100 mL/kg/day (roughly 4–6 mg/kg/min); escalate concentration/rate as needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is refractory/persistent neonatal hypoglycaemia managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back:
• Investigate the cause (hypoglycaemia screen)
  • hyperinsulinism → diazoxide (± octreotide)
  • treat endocrine deficiency
  • specialist metabolic/endocrine input.
Aim to maintain glucose in a safe range and avoid recurrent/prolonged hypoglycaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is the triad of nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema — caused by increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier to protein.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Why does paediatric nephrotic syndrome matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: It is the commonest glomerular disorder of childhood; unlike adults it is overwhelmingly minimal change disease (~90%), which is steroid-responsive, so children are treated empirically with steroids WITHOUT a biopsy; and its complications (infection, thrombosis) can be life-threatening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Describe the core mechanism of nephrotic syndrome (minimal change).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Podocyte foot-process effacement makes the glomerular barrier leaky → massive protein (mainly albumin) leaks into urine → proteinuria → hypoalbuminaemia → reduced plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shifts into tissues → oedema. (In minimal change the glomeruli look 'normal' on light microscopy — effacement is seen only on electron microscopy.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: How is nephrotic-range proteinuria defined in children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Heavy proteinuria — >40 mg/m²/hour or a very high urine protein:creatinine ratio (adult equivalent >3.5 g/day); 'frothy urine'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What albumin level defines hypoalbuminaemia in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Serum albumin <25 g/L (albumin lost in urine).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Describe the oedema of nephrotic syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Periorbital classically (puffy eyes in the morning), then peripheral, ascites, scrotal/labial, ± anasarca.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is the common fourth feature of nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Hyperlipidaemia — the liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low albumin.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is the dominant cause of nephrotic syndrome in children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Minimal change disease (~90%) — steroid-responsive, often following a viral URTI (contrast adults, where membranous is common).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is FSGS and how does it behave?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — more often steroid-resistant; commoner in older children/certain ethnicities.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Name secondary causes of nephrotic syndrome to consider if atypical.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back:
• Henoch-Schönlein purpura
  • SLE (lupus nephritis)
  • infection (HIV, hepatitis)
  • diabetes
  • also membranoproliferative and (rarely in kids) membranous GN.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is congenital nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Nephrotic syndrome presenting <3 months (e.g. NPHS1/nephrin mutations) — severe and not steroid-responsive.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is the classic age and sex distribution of minimal change nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Age 2–5 years; boys > girls.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is often the first sign of nephrotic syndrome, and what is it mistaken for?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Periorbital puffiness — often mistaken for allergy — then generalised oedema (ascites, peripheral, scrotal) and frothy urine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What are the typical renal findings in minimal change disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Usually normotensive with normal renal function; weight gain and reduced urine output. Features suggesting otherwise are atypical → biopsy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What atypical features suggest NOT minimal change disease and warrant biopsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back:
• Hypertension
  • haematuria
  • low complement (low C3)
  • impaired renal function
  • age <1 or >12 years
  • or steroid resistance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What urine investigations are used in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Urine dipstick + urine protein:creatinine ratio (uPCR) on a first morning sample — heavy proteinuria (3+/4+; nephrotic-range uPCR >200 mg/mmol).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What blood/other investigations are done in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Serum albumin (low <25), U&E/creatinine, FBC, lipids; look for cause/complications — complement (C3/C4), ASO/anti-DNase, ANA/anti-dsDNA, hepatitis/HIV, ± varicella immunity before steroids.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: When is renal biopsy indicated in childhood nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: NOT routine in typical cases — reserved for atypical features or steroid resistance (the empirical steroid trial IS the 'test' in typical minimal change).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is first-line treatment for typical childhood nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Oral prednisolone — WITHOUT a biopsy: 60 mg/m² once daily (max 80 mg) for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m² on alternate days for 4 weeks, then withdraw by reducing the dose gradually (BNFc) — the final phase is a gradual taper, not an abrupt stop. ~80–90% of minimal change disease responds ('steroid-sensitive').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What supportive management is used in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back:
• Refer for same-day paediatric assessment
  • salt and fluid restriction
  • diuretics (careful — intravascular depletion) for severe oedema
  • IV albumin (20%, usually with IV furosemide) for severe symptomatic oedema or hypovolaemia — a specialist decision with close observation for fluid overload, hypertension and pulmonary oedema
  • phenoxymethylpenicillin prophylaxis while oedematous
  • treat/prevent complications.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: How are steroid-resistant/frequent-relapsing/steroid-dependent cases managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Biopsy + second-line agents — calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/ciclosporin), levamisole, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab; ACE inhibitors (reduce proteinuria).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: How is paediatric nephrotic syndrome classified (not by biopsy)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back:
By steroid response:
  • steroid-sensitive (remission with steroids, ~90%, usually minimal change)
  • steroid-resistant (no remission after ~4 weeks → biopsy, often FSGS)
  • and relapsing/frequently-relapsing/steroid-dependent (relapses on tapering/stopping).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Why do children with nephrotic syndrome get infections, and how is this managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Loss of immunoglobulins + complement in urine (and immunosuppression) → risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and pneumococcal/encapsulated-organism infection → phenoxymethylpenicillin prophylaxis while oedematous (stopped once oedema resolves) + pneumococcal vaccination; care with live vaccines on steroids. A non-immune child on steroids exposed to chickenpox or measles needs urgent same-day advice on post-exposure prophylaxis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Why are children with nephrotic syndrome hypercoagulable?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Loss of antithrombin in urine + haemoconcentration → VTE, renal vein thrombosis, and rarely cerebral sinus thrombosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: List the main complications of nephrotic syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back:
• Infection (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, pneumococcus)
  • thromboembolism (VTE/renal vein thrombosis)
  • hypovolaemia (fluid in tissues not vessels → shock; care with diuretics)
  • hyperlipidaemia
  • acute kidney injury
  • growth impairment/steroid side effects.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: How does nephritic syndrome contrast with nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back:
• Nephritic: haematuria + hypertension + mild proteinuria + acute kidney injury (inflammatory)
  • Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What conditions are grouped under neurodevelopmental & behavioural?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Global developmental delay and the neurodevelopmental conditions ADHD and autism spectrum disorder.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is the organising principle for neurodevelopmental & behavioural disorders?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Distinguish global delay (multiple domains — needs investigation) from specific patterns: ASD = social-communication + restricted/repetitive behaviours; ADHD = inattention + hyperactivity/impulsivity across settings. Assess against developmental milestones.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give the features and management of developmental delay.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Delay across gross/fine motor, speech, social → screen for cause (hearing, vision, genetic, metabolic); MDT.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give the features and management of ADHD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Inattention + hyperactivity/impulsivity in ≥2 settings, impairing → behavioural strategies; methylphenidate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give the features and management of autism spectrum disorder.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Persistent social-communication difficulty + restricted/repetitive behaviours → MDT diagnosis and support.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What developmental red flags warrant prompt referral?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Loss of skills/regression (most serious, at any age)
  • no social smile by 8 weeks
  • not sitting unsupported by 9 months
  • not walking by 18 months.
Always check hearing and vision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is developmental delay?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: When a child fails to reach expected developmental milestones at the expected age.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why does developmental delay matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Development is the paediatric equivalent of a vital sign — deviation flags underlying pathology (genetic, neurological, sensory, metabolic, environmental); early identification → early intervention improves outcomes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is the 'limit age' concept?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: The age by which a skill should have appeared; failure to reach it (not the average age) is what triggers action.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the four developmental domains?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• (1) Gross motor
  • (2) Fine motor & vision
  • (3) Speech, language & hearing
  • (4) Social, emotional & behavioural.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is isolated (specific) developmental delay?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Delay in one domain (e.g. isolated speech delay) — often has a specific, sometimes reversible cause (e.g. hearing loss → speech delay).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is global developmental delay (GDD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Delay in ≥2 domains in a child <5 years (formally, ≥2 standard deviations below the mean) — suggests a broader/underlying cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is developmental regression and why does it matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Loss of previously acquired skills — a serious red flag always warranting investigation (suggests a neurodegenerative/metabolic condition, e.g. a leukodystrophy or Rett syndrome).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How do you correct for prematurity when assessing development?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Subtract the weeks of prematurity from chronological age (until ~2 years): milestone age = age − weeks born early.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: By what age should a child sit without support, and when do you refer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Sits without support ~7–8 months; refer at 9 months (the limit age).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: By what age should a child walk unsupported, and when do you refer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Walks unsupported ~13–15 months; refer at 18 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the key gross-motor memory hooks '6, 9, 12'?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: 6 = sits with support, 9 = sits with no support (refer if not sitting unsupported by 9 months). Also '3, 6, 9, 12 — heads, shoulders, knees and toes': 3 mo head control, 6 mo sitting (supported), 9 mo crawling, 12 mo walking.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why is hand preference before 12 months abnormal?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: It may indicate a contralateral hemiplegia/cerebral palsy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the speech/language limit ages for first words and 2-word phrases?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: 2–6 words by 12–15 months (refer at 18 months); combines 2 words by 2 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: When does a baby smile, and when do you refer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Smiles at 6 weeks; refer at 8 weeks — no social smile by 8 weeks is a red flag.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: List the developmental red flags warranting referral.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Loss of any acquired skill (regression — most serious)
  • no smile by 8 weeks
  • no eye contact by ~3 months
  • no reaching by 6 months
  • no sitting by 9 months
  • no walking by 18 months
  • no words by 18 months
  • no 2-word phrases by 2 years
  • hand preference before 12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: List genetic/antenatal causes of developmental delay.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Genetic/chromosomal: Down syndrome, Fragile X, other syndromes
  • Antenatal: congenital infection (TORCH), fetal alcohol syndrome, teratogens.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: List perinatal/postnatal causes of developmental delay.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Perinatal: prematurity, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, kernicterus
  • Postnatal: meningitis/encephalitis, head injury, non-accidental injury, hypothyroidism, metabolic disorders.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: List neurological, sensory and environmental causes of developmental delay.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Neurological: cerebral palsy, neuromuscular disease (e.g. Duchenne), neural tube defects
  • Sensory: hearing impairment (→ speech delay), visual impairment
  • Environmental/social: neglect, understimulation, safeguarding concerns
Often idiopathic — much isolated delay is time-limited with a good prognosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What does assessment of developmental delay involve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Detailed history (pregnancy/birth, milestones, family history, hearing/vision, social)
  • examination (growth, head circumference, neuro, dysmorphism)
  • development assessment
always check hearing and vision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What investigations may be used in developmental delay?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
Guided by findings:
  • genetic testing (chromosomal microarray, Fragile X)
  • TFTs
  • creatine kinase (if motor delay — Duchenne)
  • metabolic screen
  • ± MRI/EEG.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How is developmental delay managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• MDT — community paediatrics, SALT (speech), physiotherapy (gross motor), occupational therapy (fine motor), audiology, orthoptics, portage, health visitor, educational support
  • treat any reversible cause
  • safeguarding referral if neglect suspected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that is developmentally inappropriate and impairs functioning across multiple settings (home and school/work).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why does ADHD matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: It is common (~5% of children); untreated it causes academic underachievement, low self-esteem and secondary problems (conduct disorder, anxiety, depression, substance misuse); and it is very treatable.
