conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What makes ADHD a disorder rather than normal behaviour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Symptoms are persistent (≥6 months), present before age 12, occur in ≥2 settings, and cause real impairment — so diagnosis requires observation across settings and cannot be made on a rating scale alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the three presentations of ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Predominantly inattentive (the 'daydreamer'; easily missed, commoner in girls)
  • predominantly hyperactive-impulsive
  • and combined (both — the commonest).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the DSM-5 diagnostic requirements for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Symptoms persistent for ≥6 months, onset before age 12, in ≥2 settings, causing ≥moderate impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How many symptoms are needed for ADHD by age?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Children/young people (<17 years): ≥6 features from a domain
  • Adults (≥17 years): ≥5 features (the threshold drops for adults).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give examples of inattention symptoms in ADHD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Doesn't follow through on instructions
  • reluctant to engage in mentally-intense tasks
  • easily distracted
  • difficulty sustaining attention
  • difficulty organising tasks
  • forgetful
  • loses things
  • doesn't seem to listen when spoken to.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give examples of hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms in ADHD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Unable to play quietly
  • talks excessively
  • doesn't wait their turn
  • leaves seat when expected to sit
  • often 'on the go'
  • interrupts/intrudes
  • answers prematurely
  • runs/climbs inappropriately.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What conditions commonly co-occur with ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Autism spectrum disorder
  • oppositional defiant/conduct disorder
  • tic disorders/Tourette's
  • learning disability/dyslexia
  • anxiety and depression
  • attachment/sleep problems
  • epilepsy
Consider safeguarding, attachment disorder and hearing/vision as mimics.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How is ADHD diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: By a specialist after a full clinical and psychosocial assessment, developmental and psychiatric history, and observer reports from ≥2 settings (e.g. school).Do NOT diagnose on rating scales or observation alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What role do rating scales play in ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Conners' rating scales and the Strengths & Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) are useful adjuncts; QbTest may aid diagnosis in 6–17s — but they don't replace clinical assessment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is first-line management of ADHD before medication (NICE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
Watchful waiting (up to 10 weeks) for mild symptoms; do NOT offer medication first-line for pre-school children — offer a group parent-training/education programme. Medication must NOT be offered to any child under 5 without a second specialist opinion from an ADHD service with expertise in young children (NICE). Also:
  • education about ADHD
  • environmental modifications
  • sleep and exercise advice
  • ADHD-focused group parent-training (children) and CBT (older children/adults).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is first-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Methylphenidate (a stimulant; short- or long-acting) for children ≥5 and young people, if there is persistent significant impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is second-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Lisdexamfetamine if a 6-week trial of methylphenidate at an adequate dose gives insufficient benefit — 30 mg once daily in the morning, adjusted in steps of 20 mg weekly to a maximum of 70 mg daily (BNFC).Dexamfetamine is reserved for a child who responds to lisdexamfetamine but cannot tolerate its longer duration of effect (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the non-stimulant options for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Atomoxetine (a selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor — not an SNRI) or guanfacine (an alpha-2A agonist) — if stimulants are ineffective/not tolerated/contraindicated, or where diversion/misuse is a concern.Atomoxetine 6–17 years under 70 kg: 500 micrograms/kg daily for 7 days, then 1.2 mg/kg daily; guanfacine: 1 mg once daily, increased in steps of 1 mg weekly (BNFC).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What baseline checks are needed before starting stimulants for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Plot height and weight on a centile chart
  • record baseline BP and HR
  • and take a full cardiovascular history and examination.
An ECG is NOT needed routinely — obtain one, and a cardiology opinion before starting, if there is known cardiac disease, a murmur, syncope on exertion, exertional breathlessness out of keeping with peers, or a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What monitoring is required on stimulants for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Monitor height every 6 months and weight every 3–6 months (stimulants suppress appetite and growth — plot on centile charts); record BP and HR before and after every dose change and at least 6-monthly (NICE). If height falls away from the expected centile, consider a planned break in treatment over the school holidays to allow catch-up growth, or a change of medication.Watch for reduced appetite, insomnia, tics and mood changes; with atomoxetine, monitor for suicidal ideation and hepatic toxicity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why are SSRIs/antipsychotics NOT used for core ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: They describe autism/challenging-behaviour management — for ADHD itself the drug is a stimulant (methylphenidate).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is autism spectrum disorder (ASD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
A lifelong neurodevelopmental condition defined by two core domains:
  • (1) persistent deficits in social communication and interaction
  • and (2) restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why does ASD matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: It is common (~1–2%), early recognition and support markedly improve function and quality of life, and it is frequently missed or misattributed — especially in girls and those with normal/high intelligence.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What does 'spectrum' mean in ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: It spans from profound impairment with intellectual disability and no speech to highly able individuals with subtle social difficulties (formerly Asperger's, now subsumed into ASD in DSM-5) — hence variable presentation and individualised management.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What does DSM-5 require for an ASD diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Deficits in BOTH domains (the 'dyad'), present from early childhood, causing functional impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give examples of social communication & interaction deficits in ASD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Poor social-emotional reciprocity (back-and-forth conversation, sharing interests/emotions)
  • impaired non-verbal communication (reduced eye contact, gestures, facial expression)
  • difficulty developing/maintaining relationships
  • lack of interest in peers
  • absent imaginative/shared play.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give examples of restricted, repetitive behaviours (RRBs) in ASD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• Stereotyped/repetitive movements or speech (hand-flapping, lining up toys, echolalia)
  • insistence on sameness, inflexible routines, distress at change
  • highly restricted fixated interests of abnormal intensity
  • hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the early features/red flags of ASD prompting referral (NICE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• No babble/pointing/gesture by ~12 months
  • no single words by 16 months
  • no 2-word phrases by 24 months
  • reduced/absent eye contact
  • not responding to their name
  • lack of protodeclarative pointing/joint attention
  • not showing objects to others
  • limited pretend play
  • loss of language or social skills at any age (regression)
  • repetitive behaviours, unusual sensory responses, preference for being alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What conditions are associated with ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
Strongly genetic/heritable (polygenic); associated with
  • Fragile X syndrome
  • tuberous sclerosis
  • Rett syndrome
  • Down syndrome
  • fetal valproate/alcohol exposure
  • prematurity/SGA.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Is ASD caused by the MMR vaccine?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: No — the alleged link is comprehensively discredited/fraudulent; ASD is NOT caused by MMR(a high-yield public-health point).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are common comorbidities of ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• ADHD (very common overlap)
  • intellectual/learning disability and specific learning difficulties
  • epilepsy
  • anxiety and depression
  • OCD
  • sleep disorders
  • feeding problems
  • tics/Tourette's
  • motor coordination difficulties (dyspraxia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How is ASD diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Clinically and multidisciplinarily (a specialist 'autism team') — detailed developmental history + observation across settings (home + school), against DSM-5 criteria; there is no single diagnostic blood test or scan.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What structured tools support ASD diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: ADOS (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule) and ADI-R (Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised) — they support but don't replace clinical judgement.Assess for comorbidities and check hearing and vision; consider genetic testing where indicated.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is the core/first-line management of ASD (NICE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
There is no cure — management is support-based, individualised and MDT-led. Psychosocial/behavioural interventions are the foundation:
  • a play-based intervention with parents/carers/teachers to increase joint attention, engagement and reciprocal communication
  • SALT
  • occupational therapy (incl. sensory strategies)
  • educational support/EHCP
  • structured/predictable environments
  • parent/carer training and family support.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Does any medication treat the core features of ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: No — no medication treats the core social-communication/RRB features; medication is only for comorbidities/challenging behaviour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: When are antipsychotics used in ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: First exclude a treatable trigger — pain, constipation, dental disease, otitis media, reflux, an unmet communication need or a change of routine; a child who cannot report symptoms may show them only as aggression or self-injury (NICE). If psychosocial interventions are insufficient, an antipsychotic (risperidone/aripiprazole) is started and monitored by a paediatrician or psychiatrist for behaviour that challenges — time-limited, reviewed at 3–4 weeks and stopped by 6 weeks if no clinically important response. Monitor weight, height, BMI, pulse, BP, glucose, lipids and prolactin, and watch for extrapyramidal effects.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: When are SSRIs and methylphenidate used in ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back:
• SSRIs — for comorbid anxiety, depression or OCD/repetitive behaviours (specialist, cautiously)
  • Methylphenidate — for comorbid ADHD
  • Also treat epilepsy
  • For sleep disturbance, sleep-hygiene measures come first; if insufficient, prolonged-release melatonin is licensed for insomnia in autistic children aged 2–18 — 2 mg at bedtime, increased if needed to a maximum of 10 mg (BNFC).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How do inherited neuromuscular disorders impair movement?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: By affecting the muscle itself (the muscular dystrophies) or the motor neuron/lower motor unit (spinal muscular atrophy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Which four inherited neuromuscular disorders are needed for finals?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• The two dystrophinopathies (Duchenne, Becker),
  • myotonic dystrophy, and
  • spinal muscular atrophy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Give the genetics and hallmark of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: X-linked recessive; no dystrophin (Xp21). Boy ~2–5 yrs, proximal weakness, Gower's sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, huge CK.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Give the genetics and hallmark of Becker muscular dystrophy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: X-linked recessive; partial dystrophin (in-frame). Same picture as DMD but milder + later; prominent cardiomyopathy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Give the genetics and hallmark of myotonic dystrophy (DM1).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Autosomal dominant; CTG repeat (DMPK); anticipation. Myotonia (can't release grip) + distal weakness, frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction block.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Give the genetics and hallmark of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Autosomal recessive; SMN1 deletion (a motor-neuron disease, NOT a dystrophy). Floppy baby, areflexia, tongue fasciculations, preserved intellect.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the key framing distinguishing these disorders?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Dystrophies are primary muscle diseases (proximal weakness, high CK) — except myotonic dystrophy which is distal + multisystem. SMA is a lower-motor-neuron disease (anterior horn cell) → floppy, areflexic, with fasciculations.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: A severe, progressive, X-linked recessive muscle-wasting disease caused by a near-total absence of dystrophin — a structural protein anchoring the muscle-cell membrane to the internal cytoskeleton.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Why does DMD matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: It is the commonest and most severe inherited muscular dystrophy of childhood (~1 in 3500–5000 male births), following a relentless course (walking → wheelchair by ~teens → death from cardiorespiratory failure in the 20s–30s); early recognition enables surveillance + steroid treatment that alter the course.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the core mechanism of DMD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: The dystrophin gene (Xp21) is the largest human gene. DMD = a frameshift/nonsense mutation → NO functional dystrophin → muscle-membrane fragility → repeated damage → necrosis → replacement by fat and fibrous tissue.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How does the mutation type differ between Duchenne and Becker?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Duchenne: frameshift → NO dystrophin (severe).
  • Becker: in-frame mutation → some partial dystrophin (milder, later).
The amount of residual dystrophin determines severity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the inheritance of DMD and who is affected?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: X-linked recessive → affects boys; mothers are usually carriers (may have raised CK and can develop dilated cardiomyopathy — carriers need cardiac surveillance too). ~1/3 are new (de novo) mutations with no family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the presentation of DMD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
Progressive proximal muscle weakness from ~2–5 years —
  • delayed walking,
  • frequent falls,
  • difficulty climbing stairs/running,
  • waddling gait,
  • difficulty getting up off the floor.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is Gower's sign?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: The child 'walks his hands up his legs' to stand from squatting/the floor — due to proximal hip/thigh weakness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is calf pseudohypertrophy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Enlarged calves from fat/fibrous replacement of muscle — looks bulky but is weak.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What proportion of DMD boys have intellectual impairment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: ~30% have intellectual impairment/learning difficulty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What are the later musculoskeletal features of DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Loss of ambulation,
  • contractures,
  • scoliosis,
  • respiratory muscle weakness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the leading cardiac complication of DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Dilated cardiomyopathy → heart failure, arrhythmias (the most common association).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the commonest cause of death in DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Cardiorespiratory failure. Progressive respiratory-muscle weakness causes nocturnal hypoventilation and recurrent chest infections, but since non-invasive ventilation became routine, cardiac causes (heart failure and sudden cardiac death) have overtaken respiratory failure as the leading cause of death.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the key screening investigation in a boy with weakness suggesting DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Markedly raised creatine kinase (CK) — often 10–100x normal, and raised from birth. Check a CK in any boy not walking by 18 months, or with unexplained global/speech delay or incidentally raised transaminases; diagnosis is otherwise typically delayed to around age 5. A normal CK effectively excludes DMD.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the definitive diagnostic test for DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Genetic testing (dystrophin gene deletion/duplication/point mutation — MLPA + sequencing), replacing muscle biopsy in most cases. Biopsy (if genetics inconclusive) shows absent dystrophin on immunostaining (vs reduced in Becker).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What surveillance investigations are used in DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• ECG and echocardiography (or cardiac MRI) from diagnosis, at least 2-yearly until age 10 and annually thereafter, for cardiomyopathy;
  • plus lung function/spirometry (FVC), with sleep studies once ambulation is lost.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the disease-modifying mainstay of DMD management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Corticosteroids (prednisolone/deflazacort) — slow the decline and prolong ambulation, started once the boy plateaus at around 4–6 years. Typically prednisolone 0.75 mg/kg daily, or an intermittent 10-days-on/10-days-off schedule; deflazacort ~0.9 mg/kg daily is an alternative. Monitor weight, growth, BP, glucose, bone health and cataracts. Never stop abruptly — every boy needs a steroid emergency card and a sick-day plan, because adrenal crisis is a preventable cause of death. Vamorolone is a newer steroid with a better side-effect profile.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What mutation-specific therapies exist for DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
Specialist and mutation-dependent.
  • Ataluren for nonsense mutations — still available in the UK although its European authorisation was not renewed (MHRA).
  • Exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides for skippable mutations — not licensed in the UK or Europe, so access is through managed-access schemes only.
  • Micro-dystrophin gene therapy — not licensed in the UK or Europe, and carries a warning for acute liver failure including fatal cases.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What organ-protection and support are used in DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Cardiac: ACE inhibitors ± beta-blockers for the dilated cardiomyopathy — started by age 10 at the latest, even with a normal ejection fraction, because the damage precedes symptoms.
  • Respiratory: monitoring, non-invasive ventilation, cough assist, chest physio, vaccinations.
  • MDT: physiotherapy, OT, orthotics, scoliosis surgery, bone health, nutrition, psychology, education.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: A milder, later-onset X-linked muscle-wasting disease caused by a partial deficiency of dystrophin — the same protein and gene as Duchenne, but with some partially-functional dystrophin preserved.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the relationship between Becker and Duchenne?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: They are allelic (same-gene) counterparts on a severity spectrum set by how much functional dystrophin remains.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the 'reading-frame rule'.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• In-frame mutations keep the reading frame → shortened but partially functional dystrophin → milder Becker;
  • frameshift/out-of-frame mutations → no functional dystrophin → severe Duchenne.
Residual dystrophin sets the severity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How do onset and progression differ between Becker and Duchenne?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Becker: later onset (~5–15 yrs, up to adulthood), slower progression, often walking into 40s+.
  • Duchenne: onset ~2–5 yrs, rapid progression, wheelchair by early teens.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How does cognition and survival differ between Becker and Duchenne?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Becker: cognition usually normal, near-normal/later adulthood survival.
  • Duchenne: ~30% cognitive impairment, survival 20s–30s.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is a useful clinical rule of thumb distinguishing Becker from Duchenne?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• A boy still walking after age 16 = Becker;
  • wheelchair-bound before 13 = Duchenne.
Between those, genetic testing settles it.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the clinical features of Becker muscular dystrophy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
Progressive proximal weakness (legs/pelvic girdle first, like DMD but later + milder) —
  • difficulty running, climbing stairs, getting up;
  • later trunk/upper limbs;
  • calf pseudohypertrophy;
  • Gower's sign may be present;
  • muscle cramps on exertion are relatively characteristic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What can be the first/presenting sign of Becker muscular dystrophy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Cardiac involvement — dilated cardiomyopathy may appear (and be severe) even when skeletal weakness is mild.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is often the leading cause of death in Becker muscular dystrophy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Dilated cardiomyopathy — as the skeletal disease is milder, the heart becomes the limiting problem; also arrhythmias/conduction defects.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Why do female carriers of Becker need cardiac screening?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: They can develop dilated cardiomyopathy (and have mildly raised CK).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How is Becker muscular dystrophy investigated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Raised CK (high, though generally less extreme than DMD);
  • definitive = genetic testing (identifies the in-frame mutation);
  • biopsy shows reduced/patchy dystrophin (vs absent in DMD).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is central to Becker muscular dystrophy management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Cardiac surveillance (echocardiography/cardiac MRI + ECG) and cardiac protection with ACE inhibitors ± beta-blockers, given the cardiac burden;
  • supportive MDT (physiotherapy, OT, orthotics);
  • steroids used more selectively than in DMD;
  • genetic counselling + cardiac screening of female carriers.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: The commonest adult-onset muscular dystrophy — an autosomal dominant, multisystem disorder caused by a CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the DMPK gene.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What three exam-defining features set DM1 apart from the other dystrophies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• It is autosomal dominant (not X-linked)
  • it causes myotonia (delayed relaxation) with DISTAL rather than proximal weakness
  • and it is multisystem — so cardiac and respiratory complications (not the weakness) are what kill.
It is the classic example of genetic anticipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the core mechanism of DM1.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: An unstable CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the 3′-untranslated region of DMPK (chromosome 19) produces a toxic RNA that disrupts RNA splicing across many tissues → the multisystem picture. The repeat expands in successive generations → earlier onset + more severe disease = anticipation (normal <~34 repeats; disease >~50; congenital >~1000–2000).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is myotonia, the hallmark of DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Delayed muscle relaxation after contraction — e.g. can't quickly let go of a handshake/grip ('grip myotonia'), or a percussion dimple slow to relax; it warms up (improves) with repeated use.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the muscle (distal) pattern of DM1.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Distal weakness first (hand grip, foot drop)
  • facial weakness → long, thin 'hatchet'/myopathic face, ptosis, wasted temples/masseters, weak neck flexors
  • dysphagia, dysarthria (bulbar involvement).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What are the multisystem features of DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Cataracts (early, posterior subcapsular)
  • cardiac conduction defects & arrhythmias (heart block, AF; risk of sudden death)
  • frontal balding (esp. men)
  • insulin resistance/diabetes
  • testicular atrophy/hypogonadism
  • excessive daytime sleepiness
  • mild cognitive impairment
  • respiratory-muscle weakness
  • constipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe congenital DM1.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Almost always inherited from an affected MOTHER (very large repeat expansions); presents at birth with severe hypotonia ('floppy infant'), facial diplegia, feeding/respiratory difficulty, talipes, and later intellectual disability; high neonatal mortality — a key example of anticipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the definitive diagnostic test for DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Genetic testing — detects the DMPK CTG-repeat expansion (length roughly correlates with severity/onset).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the CK level in DM1, and why is this useful?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Normal or mildly raised — unlike the very high CK of DMD/BMD, a useful distinguishing point.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What EMG finding is characteristic of DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: 'Dive-bomber'/myotonic discharges (waxing-waning).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What other investigations are used in DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: ECG (essential — conduction defects; regular surveillance), echocardiography; slit-lamp (cataracts), glucose/HbA1c, sleep/respiratory assessment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the most important intervention in DM1 management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Cardiac surveillance — annual ECG (± Holter/echo); pacemaker/ICD for significant conduction disease/arrhythmia (reduces sudden death).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Why is anaesthetic caution vital in DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: DM1 patients are highly sensitive to anaesthetic agents + opioids (respiratory depression, prolonged apnoea, arrhythmia) → specialist anaesthetic care; flag before surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How is troublesome myotonia and other DM1 problems managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
Myotonia → mexiletine (sodium-channel blocker) — specialist use only and unlicensed in myotonic dystrophy; as a class Ib antiarrhythmic it needs an ECG and echocardiogram first and is contraindicated with significant conduction disease.
  • Physiotherapy/OT, orthotics (foot drop)
  • modafinil for hypersomnia — avoid in pregnancy, ensure effective contraception during and for 2 months after, and note it reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraception (MHRA)
  • treat diabetes
  • cataract surgery
  • respiratory support (NIV)
  • dysphagia/aspiration management
  • genetic counselling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How does DM2 differ from DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: DM2 is a milder, purely adult, proximal variant — a CCTG repeat in CNBP/ZNF9 (chromosome 3); no congenital form, no clear anticipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: An autosomal recessive motor neuron disease in which the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord degenerate → progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness and wasting. It is NOT a muscular dystrophy — the lesion is in the NERVE (anterior horn cell), not the muscle.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the core mechanism of SMA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Homozygous loss of the SMN1 gene (survival motor neuron 1, chromosome 5) → deficient SMN protein → degeneration of anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) → the muscle loses its nerve supply → denervation atrophy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the role of the SMN2 gene in SMA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: A near-identical back-up gene makes ~10–15% functional protein — so MORE SMN2 copies → MILDER disease (explains the type 0–4 spectrum and is the target of every modern therapy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How does SMA differ from muscular dystrophy in lesion, reflexes and CK?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• SMA: lesion in the anterior horn cell (motor neuron), neurogenic, areflexia, tongue fasciculations, normal/mildly raised CK, no pseudohypertrophy, normal cognition.
  • Dystrophy: lesion in the muscle fibre, myopathic, reflexes reduced late, very high CK (DMD), calf pseudohypertrophy, ~30% cognitive impairment (DMD).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the 'floppy infant' clinical features of SMA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Symmetrical, proximal muscle weakness + hypotonia (legs > arms)
  • areflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes — key sign of the lower motor neuron lesion)
  • tongue fasciculations (hallmark of anterior horn cell disease)
  • weak cry, poor feeding/swallow
  • 'bell-shaped chest' with paradoxical (abdominal) breathing in severe forms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is preserved in SMA despite the weakness?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Normal cognition + a bright, alert, expressive face (the child is mentally normal, 'trapped' in a weak body)
  • no pseudohypertrophy
  • sensation and sphincters intact.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe SMA type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Onset <6 months
  • NEVER SITS
  • commonest
  • historically death <2 yrs (respiratory).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe SMA type 2 (intermediate).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Onset 6–18 months
  • SITS but never walks
  • survival into adulthood.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe SMA type 3 (Kugelberg-Welander).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Onset >18 months
  • WALKS (may lose it)
  • near-normal lifespan.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe SMA types 0 and 4.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Type 0: prenatal onset; never sits; very severe, death in days–weeks.
  • Type 4: adulthood onset; walks; mildest, slow progression.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the memory aid for the SMA subtypes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Type 1 never Sits
  • Type 2 Sits
  • Type 3 Stands/walks
  • Type 4 adult.
More SMN2 copies → higher type number → milder.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the definitive diagnostic test for SMA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Genetic testing — homozygous SMN1 deletion/mutation; SMN2 copy number is prognostic (guides severity/treatment).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the CK in SMA and what other tests are used?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: CK normal or mildly raised (helps distinguish from the very high CK of DMD); EMG/nerve conduction show a neurogenic pattern (largely replaced by genetics). Newborn screening detects SMA presymptomatically, but it is NOT yet part of the routine UK newborn blood spot programme — it is being introduced through evaluation programmes, so most UK cases still present clinically as a floppy infant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What disease-modifying therapies exist for SMA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
All raise SMN protein:
  • nusinersen (intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide modifying SMN2 splicing)
  • onasemnogene abeparvovec (one-off IV gene therapy delivering a working SMN1 gene via AAV9)
  • risdiplam (oral SMN2-splicing modifier).
Earlier treatment = better outcome (before motor neurons are lost).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What supportive/MDT care is essential in SMA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back:
• Respiratory (main threat): NIV, cough assist, chest physio, secretion management, vaccination (respiratory failure = leading cause of death in severe types)
  • nutrition (feeding support/gastrostomy, aspiration prevention)
  • physiotherapy/OT, orthotics, wheelchairs
  • scoliosis surgery
  • contracture prevention
  • genetic counselling (autosomal recessive — carrier testing; 1-in-4 recurrence risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What are the commonest childhood malignancies covered in this topic?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Leukaemia (commonest overall) plus the classic solid tumours neuroblastoma, Wilms' and retinoblastoma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the organising principle for paediatric cancers?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
Presentation by tumour:
  • ALL = marrow failure (pallor, bruising, infection) ± bone pain
  • abdominal mass in a young child → Wilms' (renal) or neuroblastoma (adrenal/sympathetic chain)
  • white pupillary reflex → retinoblastoma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Give the origin and clue for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bone marrow; pallor, bruising/petechiae, infections, bone pain; the commonest childhood cancer.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Give the origin and clue for neuroblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Neural crest (adrenal/sympathetic); abdominal mass crossing the midline, <5yr; raised catecholamines.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Give the origin and clue for Wilms' tumour.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Kidney; unilateral mass (doesn't cross the midline), haematuria; don't repeatedly palpate — vigorous palpation risks rupturing the tumour into the peritoneum and upstaging the disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Give the origin and clue for retinoblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Retina; leukocoria (white reflex), squint; hereditary (RB1).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What findings should prompt urgent action for possible childhood cancer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly → immediate (same-day) specialist assessment for leukaemia; unexplained pallor, bruising or persistent bone pain → very urgent FBC within 48 hours + blood film (NICE). A new-onset squint TOGETHER WITH loss of the red reflex → refer immediately, seen within hours; a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) or absent fundal red reflex on its own → refer on a suspected cancer pathway, seen within 2 weeks, to exclude retinoblastoma (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A malignant proliferation of immature lymphoid precursor cells (lymphoblasts) in the bone marrow.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why does ALL matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: It is the commonest childhood cancer (~80% of childhood leukaemias); its presentation is a bone-marrow-failure picture; and it is one of oncology's great success stories, with cure rates now ~90%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe the core mechanism of ALL.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A lymphoid precursor acquires mutations → clonal proliferation of lymphoblasts that crowd out normal haematopoiesis → failure of the three cell lines (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) plus infiltration of other tissues (bone, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, CNS, testes).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the commonest lineage of childhood ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: B-cell precursor (B-ALL); a minority is T-cell (T-ALL).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the peak age and key association of ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Peak incidence 2–5 years; markedly increased risk in Down syndrome (also Fanconi anaemia, ataxia-telangiectasia, Li-Fraumeni; ionising radiation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the marrow-failure triad of ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Anaemia → lethargy, pallor (± breathlessness)
  • neutropenia → frequent/severe infections
  • thrombocytopenia → easy bruising, petechiae (± bleeding).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What infiltration/systemic features occur in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Bone pain (a child who won't weight-bear/limps)
  • hepatosplenomegaly
  • lymphadenopathy
  • fever (up to 50%)
  • testicular enlargement
  • CNS involvement (headache, cranial nerve palsies)
  • mediastinal mass (especially T-ALL → SVC obstruction/respiratory distress).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the red-flag rule for ALL referral?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
Two different urgencies.
  • Unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly → IMMEDIATE (same-day) specialist assessment for leukaemia.
  • Unexplained pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, persistent or unexplained infection, generalised lymphadenopathy, persistent unexplained bone pain or unexplained bruising → very urgent FBC within 48 hours + blood film (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What FBC and blood film findings occur in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• FBC — anaemia, thrombocytopenia; WCC may be low, normal or very high; often pancytopenia with circulating blasts.
  • Blood film — lymphoblasts (the key finding).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the diagnostic test for ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bone marrow aspirate & trephine biopsy — >20% blasts confirms acute leukaemia; sent for immunophenotyping (flow cytometry) and cytogenetics/molecular studies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Which cytogenetic findings carry a good vs poor prognosis in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Good: hyperdiploidy and ETV6-RUNX1 t(12;21).
  • Poor: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) BCR-ABL, KMT2A (MLL) rearrangement, hypodiploidy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why is a lumbar puncture done in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: To assess central-nervous-system involvement (blasts in CSF).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What baseline blood chemistry is checked in ALL and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Urate, potassium, phosphate, calcium, renal function (baseline for tumour lysis); LDH; coagulation; LFTs. Plus CXR for a mediastinal mass (T-ALL).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What two emergencies must be stabilised first in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Neutropenic sepsis (neutrophils ≤0.5 × 10⁹/L with temperature >38°C, or other signs of significant sepsis) → broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour — piperacillin with tazobactam 90 mg/kg (max 4.5 g) every 6–8 hours; take cultures but do NOT wait for the neutrophil count or cultures.
  • Tumour lysis syndrome → hyperhydration plus allopurinol 10 mg/kg/day (max 400 mg), or rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV if high-risk — rasburicase is CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD deficiency; monitor/correct ↑potassium, ↑phosphate, ↑urate, ↓calcium.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the mainstay of ALL treatment and its phases?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Chemotherapy over ~2–3 years: induction (achieve remission) → consolidation/intensification → CNS-directed therapy (intrathecal chemotherapy — CNS/testes are sanctuary sites; cranial irradiation is no longer used routinely in UK childhood protocols) → maintenance (prolonged, lower-intensity).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: How is Philadelphia-positive ALL treated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Add a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib/dasatinib).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What newer therapies exist for relapsed/refractory ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Immunotherapy — blinatumomab (bispecific), inotuzumab, and CAR-T cell therapy (tisagenlecleucel)
  • allogeneic stem cell transplant for high-risk/relapsed disease
  • minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring guides risk and treatment intensity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the cure rate and the good prognostic factors in childhood ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
Cure rate ~90%. Good:
  • age 2–10 years
  • low WCC at diagnosis
  • B-cell precursor
  • favourable cytogenetics (hyperdiploidy, ETV6-RUNX1)
  • rapid response/low MRD
  • no CNS disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What are the poor prognostic factors in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Age <1 or >10
  • high WCC (>50)
  • T-cell
  • Philadelphia chromosome/hypodiploidy/KMT2A
  • CNS involvement at diagnosis
  • slow response/high MRD
  • male sex.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A malignant embryonal tumour of the sympathetic nervous system, arising from primitive neural crest cells.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why does neuroblastoma matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: It is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood and the commonest cancer in infancy; a classic exam contrast with Wilms tumour; and it has an extraordinary biological spectrum from spontaneous regression in infants to aggressive disease in older children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Where does neuroblastoma arise?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Anywhere sympathetic tissue exists — most commonly the adrenal medulla (~50%), but also the paravertebral sympathetic chain (neck→pelvis). Because these cells produce catecholamines, the tumour often secretes them → raised urinary VMA/HVA.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: How does neuroblastoma contrast with Wilms tumour in origin, age and the child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Neuroblastoma: sympathetic chain/adrenal medulla (neural crest), <5yr median ~18 months, often systemically unwell (metastatic at diagnosis ~50%).
  • Wilms: kidney (metanephric blastema), peak 3–4 yr, often a well child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: How does the abdominal mass differ between neuroblastoma and Wilms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Neuroblastoma: irregular, hard, CROSSES the midline.
  • Wilms: smooth, confined to one side, rarely crosses midline.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What tumour markers and key genetics distinguish neuroblastoma from Wilms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Neuroblastoma: raised urinary catecholamines (VMA/HVA); MYCN amplification (poor prognosis).
  • Wilms: usually no markers; WT1/WT2, WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the exam one-liner for neuroblastoma vs Wilms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: An unwell young child with a hard abdominal mass crossing the midline + bone pain + raised urinary VMA → neuroblastoma; a well child with a smooth flank mass not crossing the midline → Wilms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the commonest presentation of neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: An abdominal mass — firm, irregular, non-tender, may cross the midline; plus systemic features (weight loss, malaise, fever, pallor — often looks unwell).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What features come from bone-marrow metastases in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bone pain, limp, pancytopenia — can mimic leukaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is a classic sign of orbital/skull metastases in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes') and proptosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What site-specific features can neuroblastoma cause?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Thoracic tumour → respiratory symptoms
  • paraspinal tumour → cord compression (dumbbell extension through the intervertebral foramen)
  • cervical tumour → Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What catecholamine and paraneoplastic effects occur in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Catecholamine effects: hypertension, sweating, flushing, secretory diarrhoea (VIP).
  • Paraneoplastic: opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia ('dancing eyes, dancing feet' — immune-mediated, paradoxically good prognosis); VIP secretion → intractable watery diarrhoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the key biochemical test for neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Urinary catecholamine metabolites — VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) and HVA (homovanillic acid) raised in ~90%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What imaging is used in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Ultrasound (initial abdominal mass) → CT/MRI (extent, staging); MIBG scan (taken up by sympathetic/catecholaminergic tissue) for the tumour and metastases.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What does neuroblastoma biopsy show, and what molecular testing is done?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Histology: small round blue cells, ± Homer-Wright rosettes; molecular testing including MYCN amplification, ALK, and chromosomal changes (1p/11q loss). Also bone marrow aspirate/trephine (marrow involvement common); FBC, LDH, ferritin (raised = adverse).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: How is neuroblastoma treatment risk-stratified?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
INRG: age, stage, histology, MYCN, ploidy.
  • Low-risk/infant → observation (may spontaneously regress, especially stage 4S infants) or surgery alone
  • intermediate-risk → surgery + moderate chemotherapy
  • high-risk → intensive multimodal therapy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the high-risk neuroblastoma treatment sequence?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Induction chemotherapy → surgery → high-dose chemo + autologous stem cell rescue → radiotherapy → maintenance with immunotherapy (anti-GD2 monoclonal antibody, e.g. dinutuximab) + retinoic acid.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What are the good and poor prognostic factors in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Good: infants <18 months, localised disease, favourable histology, hyperdiploidy, no MYCN amplification, opsoclonus-myoclonus.
  • Poor: MYCN amplification, age >18 months, metastatic (high-risk) disease, 1p/11q loss (high-risk survival only ~50%).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What unique feature can occur in some infant neuroblastomas?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Some infant tumours (stage 4S) regress spontaneously without treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A malignant embryonal tumour of the kidney, arising from primitive metanephric blastema (the embryonic tissue that forms the kidney).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why does Wilms tumour matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: It is the commonest renal malignancy of childhood (and commonest paediatric abdominal cancer), the classic exam contrast with neuroblastoma, and a modern oncology success story with cure rates >85–90%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe the core mechanism of Wilms tumour.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Metanephric blastema fails to differentiate and proliferates, producing a triphasic tumour (blastemal + epithelial + stromal elements). Mutations in WT1/WT2 (chromosome 11) underlie the syndromic forms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the age and laterality of Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Typically <5 years, peak 3–4 years (slightly older than neuroblastoma); usually unilateral, bilateral in ~5–10%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is WAGR syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Wilms
  • Aniridia
  • Genitourinary malformations
  • Retardation (intellectual disability)
associated with WT1 deletion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and its link to Wilms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: An overgrowth syndrome — macrosomia, macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycaemia — associated with Wilms tumour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is Denys-Drash syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Nephropathy + genitourinary malformation + Wilms (~90% develop Wilms). (Also isolated hemihypertrophy is associated.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the classic clinical stem for Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: An asymptomatic abdominal mass discovered incidentally (by a parent bathing the child, or on routine exam).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe the abdominal mass of Wilms tumour.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Large, smooth, firm, unilateral, does not cross the midline.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What other clinical features occur in Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Painless haematuria
  • flank/abdominal pain
  • anorexia, fever, malaise
  • hypertension (from renin secretion/renal artery compression — a classic feature)
  • rarely rapid enlargement/pain after minor trauma (haemorrhage into tumour).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the referral rule for an unexplained abdominal mass in a child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Paediatric review within 48 hours (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the initial investigation for Wilms tumour, and what follows?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Abdominal ultrasound (confirms a renal-origin mass) → CT/MRI abdomen & chest for staging (local extent, contralateral kidney, lung metastases — the commonest site).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What does Wilms tumour histology show?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Triphasic: epithelial tubules, immature glomerular structures, stroma with spindle cells, and small-cell blastematous tissue resembling metanephric blastema, ± necrosis. (In the European/SIOP approach, chemotherapy is often given before biopsy/surgery based on imaging.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the mainstay of Wilms tumour treatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Nephrectomy — surgical removal of the tumour and affected kidney.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the role of chemotherapy and radiotherapy in Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Chemotherapy — often neoadjuvant (before surgery, standard in the European/SIOP protocol) and/or adjuvant after surgery.
  • Radiotherapy — for advanced/higher-stage or unfavourable-histology disease.
  • Bilateral disease → nephron-sparing surgery where possible.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the prognosis of Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Excellent — overall survival >85–90% (favourable histology, localised); worse with anaplastic (unfavourable) histology, higher stage, or metastatic disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A malignant tumour of the developing retina — the commonest intraocular/ocular malignancy of childhood.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why does retinoblastoma matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• It is the classic paradigm of the 'two-hit hypothesis' of tumour-suppressor genes
  • its hallmark sign leukocoria is detectable on the routine red-reflex check (so early detection saves sight and life)
  • and the hereditary form predisposes to bilateral disease and second cancers.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe the core mechanism of retinoblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: RB1 (chromosome 13q14) is a tumour-suppressor gene whose protein (pRb) restrains the cell cycle; retinoblastoma requires inactivation of BOTH copies of RB1 (Knudson's two-hit hypothesis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe hereditary retinoblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: ~40% — a germline RB1 mutation is inherited (the 'first hit' is in every cell) → only one further somatic hit is needed → tumours arise early, bilaterally and multifocally, with lifelong risk of second malignancies (especially osteosarcoma).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe sporadic retinoblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: ~60% — both hits are somatic in a single retinal cell → usually unilateral, unifocal, later onset.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the age at diagnosis of retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Average ~18 months; nearly all <5 years (bilateral present earlier, ~1 yr; unilateral ~2 yr).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the inheritance of hereditary retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Autosomal dominant (germline mutation, high penetrance) — all bilateral (and multifocal) cases are hereditary. Tumour formation is 'recessive at the cellular level' (needing both alleles hit).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is leukocoria and its significance in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A white pupillary reflex / absent (or white) red reflex — the commonest and most important sign; often first noticed as a white pupil in flash photographs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the second commonest presentation of retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Strabismus (squint) — the tumour impairs vision so the eye deviates. Any child with a new squint needs fundoscopy to exclude retinoblastoma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What other/advanced features occur in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Deteriorating/loss of vision
  • a red or painful eye
  • a change in eye appearance
  • advanced: proptosis, orbital inflammation, buphthalmos (enlarged eye).
May be picked up on routine red-reflex screening (newborn & 6-week checks) or family screening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the key diagnostic assessment for retinoblastoma, and what is avoided?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Examination under anaesthesia (EUA) with dilated fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist. Biopsy is AVOIDED (risk of seeding tumour outside the eye) — diagnosis is clinical/imaging-based when confined to the eye.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What imaging is used in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Ocular ultrasound (often shows calcification) and MRI (extent, optic nerve/CNS involvement — avoid CT to limit radiation, especially in hereditary cases).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why is RB1 genetic testing essential in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: To identify hereditary disease → screen the child's siblings/relatives and future offspring, and guide surveillance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the order of treatment priorities in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Save life → save the eye → preserve vision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What treatments are used for retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back:
• Focal/local therapies for small tumours (laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, thermotherapy, plaque brachytherapy)
  • chemotherapy — systemic (carboplatin, vincristine, etoposide) or intra-arterial/intravitreal to salvage the eye
  • enucleation for advanced/large tumours with no useful vision (a prosthesis is fitted)
  • external-beam radiotherapy reserved and avoided where possible in hereditary disease (raises second-cancer/osteosarcoma risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the prognosis and follow-up of retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Excellent — UK 5-year survival is close to 100%, the highest of any childhood cancer; worse with extraocular/optic nerve/CNS spread or metastasis. Long-term survival into adulthood is lower in hereditary disease, and hereditary survivors need lifelong surveillance for second malignancies (especially osteosarcoma, also soft-tissue sarcomas and melanoma), heightened by radiotherapy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is 'trilateral retinoblastoma'?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bilateral retinoblastoma + an intracranial (pineal) tumour — a rare, serious hereditary association.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the organising principle for the painful/limping child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
Age is the key discriminator for the painful/limping hip:
  • DDH (neonatal screen)
  • Perthes (4–8yr, avascular necrosis)
  • SUFE (adolescent, often overweight)
  • Osgood-Schlatter (adolescent knee, overuse)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Give the age and clue for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Neonate; Barlow/Ortolani, ultrasound; harness or surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Give the age and clue for Perthes disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: 4–8yr (boys); avascular necrosis of femoral head; painless limp; X-ray.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Give the age and clue for SUFE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: 10–16yr, overweight; hip/knee pain, externally rotated leg; surgical pinning.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Give the age and clue for Osgood-Schlatter disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Adolescent; anterior knee pain/tibial tuberosity swelling, overuse; self-limiting.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What should you always do in a child presenting with knee pain, and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Always examine the hip — an adolescent with hip or referred knee pain and an externally rotated leg → think SUFE (urgent fixation; avoid weight-bearing).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A spectrum of abnormal development of the hip joint — from a shallow/dysplastic acetabulum, through a subluxatable/dislocatable hip, to a frankly dislocated hip.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Why does DDH matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: It is common (~1–3% of newborns have some instability); early detection and simple treatment (a harness) give excellent outcomes, whereas late diagnosis means surgery and lifelong consequences (limp, pain, early osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis) — hence UK newborn screening (NIPE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the core concept of hip development in DDH.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: The hip must develop congruently — a well-seated femoral head stimulates the acetabulum to deepen. If the head sits abnormally, the acetabulum stays shallow, worsening the problem (a vicious cycle). Early reduction and holding the hip flexed/abducted (Pavlik harness) allows normal development.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the strongest risk factor for DDH?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Breech presentation (especially breech at/after 36 weeks, or breech at delivery).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: List the risk factors for DDH.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Breech (strongest)
  • female sex (~6:1)
  • family history (first-degree relative)
  • firstborn
  • oligohydramnios
  • macrosomia
  • multiple pregnancy
left hip most commonly affected; associated packaging disorders (talipes, torticollis, plagiocephaly) and laxity syndromes (Down, Ehlers-Danlos).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is DDH screened in the UK?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: NIPE — a newborn hip exam (<72 h) and a repeat at the 6–8-week check; ultrasound at ~4–6 weeks for breech (at/after 36 weeks or at delivery), first-degree family history, or an abnormal/uncertain clinical exam.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the Ortolani test.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Relocates a dislocated hip: with hips/knees flexed, abduct and lift the femur → a palpable 'clunk' as the head reduces into the acetabulum ('Ortolani = Open out, back In').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the Barlow test.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Dislocates a dislocatable hip: adduct the flexed hip and apply gentle posterior pressure → the head slips out posteriorly ('Barlow = pushes Back').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the significance of a 'clunk' vs a 'click' in DDH examination?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A 'clunk' (relocation/dislocation) is significant; a 'click' is usually benign.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the other/later signs of DDH?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Limited/asymmetrical hip abduction (a key sign, especially after the neonatal period)
  • asymmetrical skin/thigh/gluteal creases
  • leg-length discrepancy — Galeazzi sign (knees at different heights when hips/knees flexed, feet flat)
  • later (walking age): painless limp, waddling/Trendelenburg gait (if bilateral), toe-walking

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the imaging of choice for DDH and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Ultrasound under ~4.5–6 months (the femoral head is not yet ossified, so X-ray is unreliable) — assesses acetabular morphology and head position; Graf classification grades severity. X-ray (pelvis) from ~4.5–6 months onward once the femoral head ossifies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the timing pitfall in DDH ultrasound?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Ultrasound too early (first few weeks) over-detects transient laxity — hence screening ultrasound at ~4–6 weeks; many mild cases/neonatal instability resolve spontaneously.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is first-line management for DDH in infants <6 months?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Pavlik harness — a dynamic splint holding the hips flexed and abducted, allowing normal acetabular development; worn continuously for several weeks (~6–12), with regular ultrasound monitoring. Avoid forced/full abduction (risk of avascular necrosis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is DDH managed in older infants (>6 months) or after failed harness?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Surgery — closed reduction (± adductor tenotomy) and hip spica cast, or open reduction ± acetabular/femoral osteotomy for late/severe cases; follow-up to ensure normal development.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the complications of DDH?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (from untreated DDH or over-aggressive splinting)
  • persistent dysplasia/subluxation, leg-length discrepancy, gait abnormality
  • early (premature) osteoarthritis of the hip (the major long-term consequence of missed/late DDH)
  • redislocation, need for repeat surgery

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Idiopathic avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head in a child — the blood supply to the developing femoral epiphysis is temporarily disrupted, the bone dies, collapses, then slowly revascularises and remodels.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Why does Perthes disease matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: It is a key cause of the limping child, the classic 'painless limp in a young school-age boy'; although self-healing, the shape the femoral head heals into determines lifelong hip function (a flattened, deformed head → early osteoarthritis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the core mechanism of Perthes disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: The femoral head's blood supply in this age group is precarious (largely via the lateral epiphyseal vessels, little collateral). An interruption → osteonecrosis of the epiphysis; the dead bone is weak → collapses/fragments under weight-bearing, then is resorbed and replaced (revascularisation/remodelling) over months–years. Treatment aims to keep the softened head well-seated ('contained') so it remodels round.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the classic age and sex of Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Age 4–8 years (range ~2–12); boys ~4–5:1; usually unilateral, bilateral ~10–15%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What does bilateral Perthes disease warrant?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Investigation for multiple epiphyseal dysplasia / hypothyroidism / sickle cell — it shouldn't be symmetrical Perthes. Perthes is a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out sickle cell, leukaemia, steroids, Gaucher's).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How does Perthes differ from SUFE and transient synovitis by age/habitus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Perthes: 4–8yr, small/active, insidious painless limp
  • SUFE: 10–15yr, overweight, hip/knee pain
  • Transient synovitis: 3–10yr, any habitus, acute after viral illness
All are systemically well — an unwell/febrile child needs septic arthritis excluded first (Kocher criteria).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the clinical features of Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Painless or mildly painful limp, insidious over weeks–months
  • hip, groin, thigh or referred KNEE pain
  • worse with activity, better with rest
  • no systemic upset (afebrile, well)
  • restricted hip movement (especially abduction and internal rotation)
  • antalgic gait, later Trendelenburg gait, thigh/gluteal wasting from disuse

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the first-line investigation for Perthes disease and its evolving findings?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: X-ray of both hips (AP + frog-leg lateral). Findings evolve: early widened joint space → increased density/sclerosis and a smaller epiphysis → subchondral fracture/'crescent sign' → fragmentation → flattening/collapse → remodelling (Waldenström stages).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the role of MRI and bloods in Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: MRI — more sensitive for early disease (before X-ray changes) and to assess necrosis extent. Bloods (FBC, CRP/ESR) — normal in Perthes; used to exclude septic arthritis/infection/malignancy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the guiding principle of Perthes management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Containment — keep the femoral head deep in the acetabulum so it remodels spherically.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is Perthes managed in younger children (<6 years) with limited involvement?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Conservative: observation, activity restriction, physiotherapy (maintain range of movement, especially abduction), analgesia, and monitoring — most remodel well (years of growth left); restricted weight-bearing/abduction bracing/casting in selected cases.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is Perthes managed in older children (>6–8 years) or severe involvement?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Surgery — femoral or pelvic (Salter) osteotomy to re-contain and re-orient the head; long-term follow-up; total hip replacement may eventually be needed if the head heals poorly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the good and poor prognostic factors in Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Good: younger age at onset (more remodelling potential; children <6 often do very well)
  • Poor: older age (>8), female sex, more of the head involved (lateral pillar/Herring classification), greater deformity at healing
Main long-term risk: premature osteoarthritis (from a non-spherical head).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE/SCFE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis relative to the metaphysis through the growth plate (physis) — the femoral neck slips anteriorly and rotates externally, while the femoral head stays seated in the acetabulum.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Why does SUFE matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: It is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence, is frequently missed (up to ~50% at first presentation — classically because it presents with knee pain, not hip pain), and delayed diagnosis dramatically raises the risk of avascular necrosis and lifelong hip disability.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the core mechanism of SUFE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: During the adolescent growth spurt the physis is at its weakest and under high shear; excess load (obesity) and/or hormonal factors overwhelm it → the epiphysis 'slips' — essentially a Salter-Harris type I fracture through the growth plate occurring atraumatically.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the classic patient and age for SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Age 10–15 years (boys ~13, girls ~12, around the growth spurt); boys ~2–3:1; the classic 'overweight adolescent male'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Obesity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What endocrine associations should prompt screening in SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Hypothyroidism
  • hypogonadism
  • growth hormone deficiency/treatment
  • panhypopituitarism
  • also renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D deficiency.
Screen for endocrine disease if the child is young (<10), underweight, or has bilateral slips.Bilateral in ~20–40% (often sequential).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the clinical features of SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Hip, groin, thigh or classically KNEE pain (referred; ~25–50% present with knee/thigh pain, hip pain may be absent in up to half)
  • limp (antalgic), reduced weight-bearing
  • sub-acute/chronic onset over weeks, sometimes acute-on-chronic after minor trauma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the most reliable examination sign in SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: The affected leg is held in EXTERNAL rotation, with loss of internal rotation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is Drehmann's sign?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Obligatory external rotation of the hip as it is passively flexed — highly characteristic of SUFE.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What X-ray views are used for SUFE, and which is most sensitive?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: X-ray of BOTH hips — AP AND frog-leg lateral views; the frog-leg lateral is the most sensitive (a subtle slip may be invisible on AP).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is Trethowan's sign / Klein's line?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A line along the superior border of the femoral neck should normally intersect part of the epiphysis; in SUFE it doesn't (epiphysis slips below it) — the 'melting ice-cream cone/scoop' appearance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is SUFE classified, and why does it matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Stable (can weight-bear, ± crutches) vs unstable (cannot weight-bear even with crutches) — unstable slips carry a much higher risk of avascular necrosis (the key prognostic split).Also graded by chronicity and magnitude.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the immediate management of SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Make the child NON-WEIGHT-BEARING and refer to orthopaedics urgently (further slipping worsens outcome).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the surgical mainstay of SUFE treatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: 'Pinning in situ' with a single cannulated screw across the physis to stabilise the epiphysis and prevent further slip; severe/unstable slips → open reduction/realignment osteotomy in specialist hands (higher AVN risk with manipulation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: When is prophylactic pinning of the contralateral hip considered in SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Especially with an underlying endocrine disorder or young age (high bilateral risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the complications of SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (the major complication — much higher with unstable slips and forced reduction)
  • chondrolysis (cartilage loss → stiffness)
  • leg-length discrepancy, deformity, altered gait
  • premature osteoarthritis of the hip.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity — inflammation and micro-injury at the growth-plate/apophysis where the patellar tendon inserts into the top of the shin; one of the commonest causes of anterior knee pain in adolescents, especially active/sporty boys.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Why does Osgood-Schlatter disease matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: It is a benign, self-limiting overuse condition with a clinical diagnosis and conservative management; recognising it avoids unnecessary imaging and allows confident reassurance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the core mechanism of Osgood-Schlatter disease.
