conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: The patellar (quadriceps) tendon inserts into the tibial tuberosity, which in adolescence is still a growth plate (apophysis) — the weak link. During a growth spurt, repetitive forceful quadriceps pull (running, jumping, kicking) causes repeated micro-avulsions → inflammation and new bone growth → a visible/palpable lump; initially tender, then hard, non-tender and permanent as it heals.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the epidemiology of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Adolescents during the growth spurt — girls ~8–12, boys ~10–15 (slightly younger in girls); more common in boys and physically active children (jumping/sprinting sports); usually unilateral but can be bilateral (~20–30%).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the clinical features of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Gradual (insidious, atraumatic) onset
  • a visible/palpable, tender, hard lump over the tibial tuberosity (the classic sign)
  • anterior knee pain
  • pain exacerbated by activity, kneeling and knee extension (resisted extension/squatting/stairs/running/jumping); relieved by rest
  • no systemic symptoms, no true joint effusion, knee otherwise normal (full range of movement).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Where is tenderness localised in Osgood-Schlatter disease, and why does this matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: To the tibial tuberosity (not the joint line) — this helps distinguish it from intra-articular pathology.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is Osgood-Schlatter disease diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Clinically — the history and localised tuberosity tenderness are usually sufficient; no imaging needed in a typical case.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: When is X-ray used in Osgood-Schlatter disease, and what may it show?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Only if the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude other pathology; a lateral knee X-ray may show fragmentation/irregularity or a separate ossicle at the tuberosity (changes overlap with normal, so confirmatory not required).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What red flags should prompt considering alternatives to Osgood-Schlatter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Night pain, rest pain, systemic symptoms, effusion, or non-tuberosity pain → exclude infection, malignancy (osteosarcoma around the knee), juvenile idiopathic arthritis, patellar tendinopathy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the key management message for Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Reassurance — it is self-limiting and settles as the growth plate fuses (skeletal maturity).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the initial management of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back:
• Reduction/modification of physical activity (relative rest from aggravating sports — not complete inactivity)
  • ice after activity
  • NSAIDs/simple analgesia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What management follows once Osgood-Schlatter symptoms settle?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Stretching and physiotherapy — quadriceps/hamstring stretching and strengthening to offload the tuberosity; protective knee pads for kneeling; occasionally a short period of reduced loading.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the outcome of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Symptoms fully resolve over time (months–up to ~2 years), typically leaving a painless hard bony lump at the tuberosity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the rare complications of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Complete avulsion fracture (the tuberosity separates from the tibia) → needs surgery; rarely a persistent painful ossicle in skeletally mature patients may warrant excision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What two childhood-specific seizure disorders are covered in this topic?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Infantile spasms (a serious epileptic encephalopathy) and febrile convulsions (common, usually benign).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the organising principle for paediatric seizures?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Age + context: infantile spasms (~4–8 mo; clusters of flexion spasms, developmental regression, hypsarrhythmia on EEG) is serious; febrile convulsion (6mo–5yr; brief generalised seizure with fever, normal neurology) is common and benign.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Give the clue and management for infantile spasms (West syndrome).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Clusters of flexion 'salaam' spasms, regression; hypsarrhythmia → vigabatrin/ACTH; poor prognosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Give the clue and management for febrile convulsion.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: 6mo–5yr with fever; simple (brief, generalised) vs complex → reassure and safety-net, and treat the underlying infection. Antipyretics are for comfort only and do NOT prevent recurrence. Small increased epilepsy risk if complex.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What makes a febrile convulsion 'complex', and what does it prompt?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Focal, prolonged (>15 min) or recurrent within 24h → further assessment; always exclude meningitis/encephalitis if unwell.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is West syndrome (infantile spasms)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A severe, age-specific epileptic encephalopathy of infancy (now also called infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, IESS).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Why does West syndrome matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: It is a paediatric neurological emergency in disguise — the spasms are easily mistaken for colic, reflux or startle, yet delayed treatment worsens the already-serious developmental outcome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the classic triad defining West syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
• (1) Epileptic (infantile) spasms — the 'salaam attacks'
  • (2) hypsarrhythmia on EEG — chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised interictal pattern
  • (3) developmental stagnation or regression — loss/plateau of skills.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the typical onset age of infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Typically 3–12 months, peaking around 4–7 months (almost always under 2 years); slight male predominance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What proportion of infantile spasms have an identifiable cause, and why does it matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: ~70–75% have an identifiable underlying cause ('symptomatic') — the brain insult matters for prognosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Which classic condition causes infantile spasms and changes treatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Tuberous sclerosis complex — vigabatrin is especially effective here.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: List causes of infantile spasms.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
• Tuberous sclerosis complex
  • structural/malformations (cortical dysplasia, lissencephaly)
  • hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
  • congenital infection
  • Down syndrome
  • metabolic disorders
  • genetic (ARX, CDKL5)
  • 'cryptogenic/idiopathic' (no cause found — better prognosis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Describe 'salaam attacks'.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A sudden flexion of the head, trunk and arms, then extension of the arms (like the 'salaam' greeting; also 'jack-knife' spasms). Each spasm is brief (1–2 seconds) but occurs in CLUSTERS — repeated up to ~50 times, typically on waking/drifting off to sleep.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How do you distinguish infantile spasms from infantile colic?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: In colic the baby is distressed DURING the episodes; in infantile spasms the baby is often distressed/unsettled BETWEEN the spasms (and may cry after a cluster). If in doubt, do an EEG.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the key EEG finding in West syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Hypsarrhythmia — chaotic, high-voltage, disorganised slow waves and multifocal spikes. An urgent/sleep EEG is needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What imaging and cause work-up are done in infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
• MRI brain (structural cause — malformation, tuberous sclerosis tubers, HIE)
  • examine skin for tuberous sclerosis signs (ash-leaf macules under Wood's lamp, shagreen patch)
  • metabolic/genetic work-up
  • TORCH screen.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is first-line drug treatment for infantile spasms, and its key caveat?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Vigabatrin — a GABAergic anticonvulsant, started at 50 mg/kg/day and escalated (typically to 100 then 150 mg/kg/day) if spasms continue (BNFC); the drug of choice especially in tuberous sclerosis. Caveat: risk of irreversible peripheral visual field loss (retinal toxicity) — needs baseline and about 6-monthly visual assessment (MHRA).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the role of corticosteroids in infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: High-dose oral prednisolone — 10 mg four times daily for 14 days, increased to 20 mg three times daily if spasms persist at day 7 or recur (or tetracosactide/ACTH). For spasms NOT due to tuberous sclerosis, prednisolone PLUS vigabatrin is the first-line combination (vigabatrin alone if the infant is at high risk of steroid side effects). Monitor blood pressure and urinary glucose weekly on the steroid. Hormonal therapy gives faster short-term spasm control; long-term outcomes are similar.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Why avoid steroids as first-line in tuberous sclerosis-related infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Because vigabatrin is especially effective in tuberous sclerosis — a classic distinction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How are refractory infantile spasms managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
• Other anticonvulsants
  • ketogenic diet
  • or epilepsy surgery (for a focal structural cause).
Refer urgently to paediatric neurology.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the prognosis of infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Generally poor — most children have long-term intellectual disability and ongoing epilepsy (may evolve into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome). Depends on cause: cryptogenic/idiopathic + prompt treatment = better; symptomatic (structural/tuberous sclerosis) = worse. Early recognition and treatment improve outcomes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is a febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A seizure triggered by a fever in a young child, WITHOUT any central-nervous-system infection or other identifiable neurological cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Why do febrile convulsions matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: They are the commonest seizure disorder of childhood (~3%); usually benign and self-limiting (so the skill is reassurance and safety-netting), but the fever means you must exclude a serious cause — especially meningitis/encephalitis — before attributing the seizure to a simple febrile convulsion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Describe the core concept of febrile convulsions.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: The immature brain has a low seizure threshold, and a rapidly rising temperature (during an intercurrent viral illness) tips it over → a seizure. It requires the fever to be from outside the CNS (e.g. viral URTI, tonsillitis, otitis media) — a seizure with fever from meningitis is NOT a febrile convulsion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the definition/epidemiology of a febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A seizure provoked by fever in an otherwise normal/neurologically healthy child, age 6 months–5 years (peak ~18 months), with no CNS infection, no metabolic cause and no history of afebrile seizures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How is a simple febrile convulsion defined?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
• Duration <15 min
  • generalised (tonic-clonic)
  • no recurrence within 24h/same illness
  • complete recovery within <1 hour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How is a complex febrile convulsion defined?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
Any one of:
  • >15 min (no upper limit)
  • focal features
  • recurring within 24h/the same febrile illness
  • or incomplete recovery within 1 hour.
Febrile status epilepticus (>30 min) is a prolonged COMPLEX seizure, not a separate third category.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is febrile status epilepticus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A febrile seizure lasting >30 minutes (prolonged/continuous).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What are the typical clinical features of a febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
• Occurs early in a viral illness as the temperature rapidly rises
  • usually brief (<5 minutes)
  • mostly generalised tonic-clonic
  • a post-ictal period of drowsiness then complete recovery (in simple febrile convulsion)
  • often a family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the priority in assessing a child with a febrile seizure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Find the source of the fever and EXCLUDE serious infection — especially meningitis/encephalitis (and pneumonia, UTI, etc.); use the NICE traffic-light system to risk-stratify.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: When should you have a low threshold for lumbar puncture in a febrile seizure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: In the very young (<18 months, especially <12 months) — meningeal signs are hard to elicit and a febrile seizure can be the presenting feature of meningitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Are routine investigations needed for a typical simple febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: No routine investigations in a well child with an obvious infection source; investigate as directed by the illness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: When should a child with a febrile convulsion be admitted/referred to paediatrics?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
• First febrile convulsion
  • complex features (>15 min, focal, or recurrent in the same illness)
  • child <18 months
  • diagnostic uncertainty
  • suspected serious infection (e.g. meningitis)
  • no identified focus for the fever
  • currently or recently on antibiotics (these can mask the signs of meningitis)
  • or the child appears unwell/incomplete recovery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How is a prolonged febrile seizure (>5 minutes) managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A rescue benzodiazepine. Buccal midazolam is the UK first choice and is AGE-banded, not weight-banded — 2.5 mg (3–11 months), 5 mg (1–4 years), 7.5 mg (5–9 years), 10 mg (10–17 years) (BNFC). Rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg (max 10 mg) only if buccal midazolam is unsuitable or unavailable. Call 999; repeat ONCE after 10 minutes if the seizure continues — two benzodiazepine doses in total, counting any given before arrival — then escalate to the hospital status epilepticus pathway (IV levetiracetam 40 mg/kg, max 2.5 g).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Who initiates home rescue benzodiazepines for febrile convulsions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Only a specialist — for children with prolonged seizures/high recurrence risk/poor access to care.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Do antipyretics prevent febrile convulsions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: No — antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) are for comfort only; they do NOT prevent febrile convulsions. No routine prophylactic anti-epileptic drugs (benign condition; adverse effects outweigh benefit).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the recurrence rate of febrile convulsions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
~1 in 3 (30%) will have another; recurrence risk factors:
  • younger age at onset (<18 months)
  • lower fever/shorter fever before seizure
  • family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the epilepsy risk after a febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Very low — after a simple febrile convulsion the risk is only slightly above the general population (~0.5–1% baseline → ~1–2%); higher after a complex febrile convulsion (~6–8%), and higher still with a family history of epilepsy, a neurodevelopmental abnormality, or multiple complex features.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What seizure first aid should be taught to parents?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back:
• Protect from injury
  • recovery position
  • time the seizure
  • don't restrain or put anything in the mouth
  • and call an ambulance if the seizure lasts >5 minutes, if it is the first seizure, or there are repeated seizures, breathing difficulty, a non-blanching rash, drowsiness/difficulty waking, or the child doesn't recover.
Reassure explicitly that simple febrile convulsions do not cause brain damage and do not affect development or intelligence.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What does the paediatric surgical GI topic cover?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The paediatric surgical abdomen — causes of obstruction, bilious vomiting and acute abdominal pain needing prompt surgical assessment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the organising principle for the paediatric surgical abdomen?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
Age + vomiting character + stool:
  • bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate = malrotation/volvulus until proven otherwise
  • non-bilious projectile at 4–6 wks = pyloric stenosis
  • colicky pain + redcurrant-jelly stool 6mo–2yr = intussusception.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the age and clue for intussusception.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: 6mo–2yr; colicky pain, redcurrant-jelly stool, sausage mass; air/contrast enema ± surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the age and clue for pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: 2–8 wks (peak 3–6); non-bilious projectile vomiting, olive mass, hypochloraemic alkalosis; pyloromyotomy after fluid and electrolyte correction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the age and clue for malrotation/volvulus.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Neonate/infant; bilious vomiting; upper-GI contrast; emergency Ladd's procedure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the age and clue for Hirschsprung's disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Neonate; delayed meconium (>48h), distension; rectal biopsy (absent ganglia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the clue for Meckel's diverticulum and mesenteric adenitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Meckel's: 'rule of 2s', painless PR bleeding, technetium scan.
  • Mesenteric adenitis: post-viral, mimics appendicitis, self-limiting (exclusion).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The telescoping ('invagination') of one segment of bowel into the adjacent distal segment — the proximal bowel (intussusceptum) slides into the lumen ahead of it (intussuscipiens).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does intussusception matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: It is the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction in infants/young children (6 months–2 years) and a surgical emergency — untreated, the trapped bowel's blood supply is cut off → ischaemia, necrosis, perforation and peritonitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core mechanism of intussusception.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The bowel telescopes → the mesentery is dragged in → venous compression → oedema and congestion → the bowel weeps blood and mucus (redcurrant jelly stool) → if unrelieved, arterial supply is compromised → ischaemia/gangrene/perforation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the commonest anatomical type of intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Ileocolic (~90%) — the ileum invaginates through the ileocaecal valve into the colon.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the usual cause of intussusception in infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Mostly idiopathic — often follows a viral illness → hypertrophied Peyer's patches/lymphoid hyperplasia in the terminal ileum act as the lead point (rotavirus/adenovirus links).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: When should you suspect a pathological lead point in intussusception, and what are the causes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
With older age (>2–3 yr) or recurrence. Causes:
  • Meckel's diverticulum (classic)
  • intestinal polyp
  • duplication cyst
  • Henoch-Schönlein purpura (intramural haematoma)
  • lymphoma (e.g. Burkitt's)
  • cystic fibrosis (inspissated stool)
  • post-op
  • tumours.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the classic pain pattern of intussusception.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Sudden, severe, paroxysmal colicky abdominal pain — episodes every ~15–20 min; the child draws the knees/legs up, screams, goes pale, then appears well/settled between episodes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How does vomiting evolve in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Initially non-bilious/reflex; becomes bilious as obstruction develops (bilious vomiting in a child = surgical until proven otherwise).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is 'redcurrant jelly' stool and its timing?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Blood + mucus — a LATE sign of intussusception; don't wait for it.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What abdominal signs occur in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A palpable 'sausage-shaped' mass (typically right upper quadrant/along the colon) with emptiness in the right iliac fossa (Dance's sign).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the atypical/apathetic presentation of intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Lethargy — may be the sole or dominant feature (a lethargic, pale infant 'as if drugged'; ~15% present without the colic phase).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How often is the classic triad of intussusception present?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: In <25% of cases (colicky pain + redcurrant jelly stool + sausage mass) — so a high index of suspicion is needed; don't wait for all three.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the investigation of choice for intussusception and its findings?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Ultrasound — shows the 'target'/'doughnut' sign (concentric rings on transverse view) or 'pseudokidney' sign (longitudinal).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What may abdominal X-ray show in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Not diagnostic, but may show signs of obstruction (distended loops, paucity of gas in right iliac fossa), a soft-tissue mass, or free air (perforation → contraindicates enema).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the initial management of intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
Resuscitate first — 'drip and suck':
  • IV fluids (often dehydrated/shocked)
  • NG tube for decompression
  • analgesia
  • and involve paediatric surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the first-line non-operative treatment for intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Air (pneumatic) enema (or contrast enema) under radiological guidance — both diagnostic AND therapeutic (~80–90% success) in a stable child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: When is an enema contraindicated in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Peritonitis, perforation, or haemodynamic instability/shock → straight to surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: When is surgery indicated in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: If the enema fails, there's perforation/peritonitis/shock, or a pathological lead point is found → operative reduction ± bowel resection (if gangrenous); antibiotics if perforation/peritonitis suspected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the recurrence rate after enema reduction of intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: ~5–10% (usually within 24–48h); recurrent episodes raise suspicion of a lead point.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter muscle → gastric outlet obstruction in an infant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why is pyloric stenosis a classic exam scenario?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A firstborn baby boy with projectile NON-bilious vomiting at a few weeks old, and a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (the most-examined paediatric biochemistry); and it is NOT a surgical emergency — correct fluids/electrolytes first, then operate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core mechanism of pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The pyloric muscle progressively hypertrophies → narrows/obstructs the gastric outlet → the stomach can't empty → forceful (projectile) vomiting of gastric contents only (non-bilious — the obstruction is proximal to the bile duct). Persistent vomiting of HCl drives the biochemical picture.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the age and demographics of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Presents at ~2–8 weeks (peak 3–6 weeks) — well at birth, then progressive vomiting; boys ~4:1, especially firstborn males; positive family history (especially maternal); associated with maternal smoking.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the hallmark clinical feature of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Projectile, NON-bilious vomiting — forceful, shortly after feeds.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What behaviour of the infant helps distinguish pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The baby remains HUNGRY and eager to feed again ('hungry vomiter') — unlike an unwell/septic infant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is found on examination during a 'test feed' in pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A palpable, firm, non-tender 'OLIVE'-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant/epigastrium (the hypertrophied pylorus) + visible peristalsis (left-to-right waves after a feed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the biochemical picture of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — with paradoxical aciduria (↓Cl⁻, ↓potassium, ↑bicarbonate, alkalotic pH, acidic urine).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Explain how vomiting causes the metabolic alkalosis in pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Vomiting loses HCl → loss of H⁺ and Cl⁻ → ↓Cl⁻ (hypochloraemia) + ↑bicarbonate → metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Explain the hypokalaemia in pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Volume depletion → the kidney activates RAAS/aldosterone → retains sodium and water but excretes potassium → ↓potassium (hypokalaemia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Explain 'paradoxical aciduria' in pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Despite systemic alkalosis, once potassium is depleted the kidney is forced to excrete H⁺ (instead of potassium) to reabsorb sodium → the urine becomes acidic despite the blood being alkaline.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the investigation of choice for pyloric stenosis and its criteria?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Ultrasound — shows pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm and pyloric channel length >15–17 mm. Venous/capillary blood gas + U&Es identify and quantify the alkalosis and guide fluid correction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why is pyloric stenosis NOT an immediate surgical emergency?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Operating on an alkalotic, hypokalaemic baby risks post-op apnoea/arrhythmia and anaesthetic danger — resuscitate and correct fluids/electrolytes first.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the initial management of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Stop oral feeds
  • pass an NG tube (decompress/aspirate)
  • IV fluid resuscitation + correct electrolytes — a 10–20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride if shocked, then 0.45% sodium chloride with 5% glucose and added potassium at about 1.5x maintenance.
Theatre only once chloride >100 mmol/L, bicarbonate <30 mmol/L and potassium are normal — pyloromyotomy is never an emergency operation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the definitive treatment of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy — surgical division of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle (down to but not through the mucosa), open or laparoscopic; excellent prognosis, feeds restart within hours–a day post-op.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is intestinal malrotation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A congenital abnormality of the position and fixation of the gut, from failure of the normal rotation of the midgut during fetal development.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does malrotation matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: It leaves the bowel anchored on a dangerously narrow mesenteric base, predisposing to midgut volvulus — the whole midgut twisting around the superior mesenteric artery → a surgical emergency: the twist strangles the artery → rapid ischaemia and necrosis of the entire small bowel within hours (short-bowel syndrome or death).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the embryology behind malrotation.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Normally the midgut undergoes a 270° anticlockwise rotation around the SMA and fixes the duodenojejunal (DJ) flexure to the left of midline and the caecum in the right iliac fossa (a broad, stable mesenteric base). In malrotation this is incomplete → the caecum ends up high/midline, the DJ flexure is malpositioned, and the mesentery has a narrow pedicle → the bowel can twist, and Ladd's bands stretch across and obstruct the duodenum.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What conditions are associated with malrotation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Exomphalos (omphalocele)
  • congenital diaphragmatic hernia
  • intrinsic duodenal atresia
also gastroschisis, heterotaxy/situs abnormalities & congenital heart disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the cardinal red flag of malrotation/volvulus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Bilious (green) vomiting — from duodenal obstruction (Ladd's bands or the volvulus twist), which is distal to the ampulla → bile-stained.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What are the late/ischaemic signs of volvulus with strangulation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Abdominal tenderness/peritonism
  • PR bleeding (haematochezia)
  • a distended tense abdomen
  • and shock
— indicating bowel ischaemia → emergency.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How can malrotation present in older children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Chronic intermittent bilious vomiting, recurrent abdominal pain, or failure to thrive (intermittent volvulus/Ladd's band obstruction).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is THE rule about bilious vomiting in a neonate?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Bilious vomiting in a neonate = malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. (Contrast pyloric stenosis = non-bilious projectile vomiting.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for malrotation and its findings?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Upper GI contrast study — shows the DJ flexure malpositioned (not left of midline) and, in volvulus, the pathognomonic 'corkscrew' appearance of the twisted duodenum/proximal jejunum.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What ultrasound sign indicates volvulus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The 'whirlpool sign' — the superior mesenteric vein and mesentery wrapping clockwise around the SMA; may show the artery/vein relationship inverted.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What might abdominal X-ray show in malrotation, and what is the caveat?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Often non-specific; may show a 'double bubble' ± distal gas (duodenal obstruction) or a gasless abdomen (concerning). Not diagnostic. Do NOT delay surgery for imaging in an unstable/ill child with suspected volvulus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the initial management of midgut volvulus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Resuscitate (IV fluids, NG decompression, correct electrolytes, broad-spectrum antibiotics) and urgent paediatric surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What are the steps of Ladd's procedure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Detorse the volvulus (untwist, usually anticlockwise)
  • divide Ladd's bands (relieve duodenal obstruction)
  • broaden the mesenteric base (prevent re-twisting)
  • place small bowel on the right, caecum/colon on the left (non-rotated position)
  • appendicectomy
  • resect any necrotic/gangrenous bowel (± second-look laparotomy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why is appendicectomy done during Ladd's procedure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The repositioned caecum would make future appendicitis present atypically.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How is asymptomatic (incidental) malrotation managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Usually elective Ladd's procedure (~15–20% lifetime volvulus risk), individualised.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the feared complication of malrotation with volvulus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Bowel ischaemia/necrosis → short-bowel syndrome (if extensive resection needed); also perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, death (untreated volvulus).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A congenital absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the distal bowel — the nerves that drive peristalsis fail to develop, so the affected segment can't relax or propel stool → functional bowel obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does Hirschsprung's disease matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: It is a key cause of failure to pass meconium/neonatal bowel obstruction, the classic delayed meconium (>48 h) + distension + bilious vomiting scenario, strongly associated with Down syndrome, and its complication HAEC can be life-threatening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core mechanism of Hirschsprung's disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: During embryogenesis, neural crest cells migrate craniocaudally down the gut to form the enteric nervous system (Meissner submucosal and Auerbach myenteric plexuses). In Hirschsprung's this migration stops short → the distal bowel has NO ganglion cells → the aganglionic segment is tonically contracted/unable to relax → functional obstruction → the proximal bowel dilates (megacolon), with a transition zone between them.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the extent and commonest form of aganglionosis in Hirschsprung's?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Always distal and continuous from the anus proximally — ~75% is short-segment (rectosigmoid); rarely total colonic. Boys ~4:1.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What conditions and genes are associated with Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Strongly associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — also Waardenburg syndrome, MEN2, congenital central hypoventilation. The RET proto-oncogene (chromosome 10) is the strongest genetic association; can be familial.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the classic red flag of Hirschsprung's disease in the neonate?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life (normally passed within 24–48 h).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the classic neonatal triad of Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Abdominal distension
  • bilious vomiting
  • and delayed meconium
(neonatal distal bowel obstruction).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How does Hirschsprung's present in older infants/children (short-segment)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Chronic severe constipation
  • abdominal distension
  • failure to thrive.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the 'squirt/blast sign' on PR examination in Hirschsprung's?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A tight/empty rectum, then explosive passage of stool and gas when the finger is withdrawn (decompression of the obstructed proximal bowel).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How does Hirschsprung's contrast with functional constipation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Hirschsprung's: from birth/delayed meconium, empty rectum on PR.
  • Functional constipation: later onset, stool in the rectum, responds to laxatives.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A life-threatening complication — inflammation/infection of the obstructed bowel: fever, explosive/foul diarrhoea, abdominal distension, sepsis; can → toxic megacolon and perforation. Can be the presenting feature; needs urgent resuscitation, IV antibiotics including anaerobic cover (metronidazole) per local protocol, and gentle rectal washouts with warm 0.9% sodium chloride to decompress the bowel.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Rectal (suction) biopsy — shows ABSENCE of ganglion cells in the submucosal/myenteric plexuses, with hypertrophied/thickened nerve fibres and increased acetylcholinesterase staining.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What do contrast enema and anorectal manometry show in Hirschsprung's?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Contrast (barium) enema — may show the transition zone (narrow aganglionic distal segment → dilated proximal colon); helps plan surgery but is not diagnostic alone.
  • Anorectal manometry — absent recto-anal inhibitory reflex (the internal sphincter fails to relax); a screening adjunct.
Abdominal X-ray shows distal obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the initial management of Hirschsprung's disease (obstructed/HAEC)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Resuscitate
  • NG decompression
  • bowel/rectal washouts (to decompress and bridge to surgery)
  • IV antibiotics if enterocolitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the definitive treatment of Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Surgical 'pull-through' procedure — resect the aganglionic segment and anastomose normally innervated bowel to the anus (e.g. Soave, Swenson, Duhamel), often single-stage (± an initial defunctioning colostomy in sick/late cases). There are no effective medical cures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is Meckel's diverticulum?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The commonest congenital anomaly of the GI tract — a true diverticulum of the distal ileum that is a remnant of the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does Meckel's diverticulum matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Although most are asymptomatic, it is the number-one cause of painless, massive lower-GI bleeding in young children, and it can mimic appendicitis or cause bowel obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core mechanism of Meckel's diverticulum.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct connects the developing gut to the yolk sac and normally obliterates by ~week 7. Incomplete obliteration leaves a blind-ending pouch on the antimesenteric border of the ileum — a true diverticulum (all bowel-wall layers). It often contains ectopic gastric (± pancreatic) mucosa: the ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid → ulcerates adjacent ileal mucosa → painless bleeding.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: State the 'rule of 2s' for Meckel's diverticulum.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Occurs in ~2% of the population
  • 2 feet (~60 cm) proximal to the ileocaecal valve
  • ~2 inches (~5 cm) long
  • 2:1 male predominance
  • usually symptomatic before age 2
  • 2 common ectopic tissue types (gastric + pancreatic)
  • ~2% become symptomatic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What are the three classic presentations of symptomatic Meckel's diverticulum?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Painless rectal bleeding
  • abdominal pain mimicking appendicitis ('Meckel's diverticulitis')
  • and intestinal obstruction (via an omphalomesenteric band, volvulus, or as a lead point for intussusception).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the bleeding presentation of Meckel's diverticulum.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: It is the No.1 cause of painless, massive lower-GI bleeding in children aged 1–2 years requiring transfusion — bright red/maroon PR bleed from acid-induced ileal ulceration. (The other classic paediatric painless-PR-bleed cause is a juvenile polyp.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the investigation of choice for Meckel's diverticulum?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan ('Meckel's scan') — the radiotracer is taken up by gastric mucosa (including ectopic gastric mucosa in the diverticulum), highlighting it; high sensitivity/specificity when ectopic gastric mucosa is present (won't detect a non-gastric-lined Meckel's).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What other investigations are used in Meckel's diverticulum?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Bloods (FBC — anaemia from bleeding; group & save/crossmatch), resuscitation for significant bleeds; CT/angiography or laparoscopy if the scan is negative but suspicion remains (obstruction/diverticulitis often diagnosed at surgery); plain films/ultrasound have limited value.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How is symptomatic Meckel's diverticulum managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Surgical resection (diverticulectomy or small-bowel segmental resection), open or laparoscopic; resuscitate/transfuse first if bleeding. Excellent prognosis after resection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How is an incidentally found Meckel's diverticulum managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Debated — resect if features suggest higher complication risk (young patient, long/narrow-necked diverticulum, palpable ectopic tissue, band); often left alone if truly incidental in an older adult.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is mesenteric adenitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Inflammation/enlargement of the mesenteric lymph nodes (usually those in the right iliac fossa), typically following a viral illness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does mesenteric adenitis matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: It is the commonest mimic of acute appendicitis in children — a child with right-sided abdominal pain who does NOT need an operation — so the skill is recognising the benign, self-limiting picture and distinguishing it from appendicitis (which must not be missed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core concept of mesenteric adenitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Enteric/respiratory pathogens are ingested or reach the gut → drain to the mesenteric lymph nodes → the nodes react and enlarge (reactive lymphadenopathy). Because the ileocaecal mesenteric nodes sit in the right iliac fossa, the pain overlaps with appendicitis. It is benign and self-limiting.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What causes mesenteric adenitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Usually post-viral (often after a URTI or gastroenteritis) — viruses: adenovirus, coxsackievirus, EBV, measles. Bacteria — classically Yersinia enterocolitica (also Streptococcus, E. coli, Campylobacter, Salmonella). Commonest in children/adolescents <16.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What are the clinical features of mesenteric adenitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Abdominal pain (often central or right iliac fossa) without the guarding/rigidity of appendicitis
  • preceded by/concurrent with a viral illness (recent cold or sore throat)
  • higher/spiking fever may be present
  • associated URTI features (cough, coryza, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy)
  • nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea may occur but the child is often less 'toxic'
  • self-limiting — the pain often fluctuates/moves and settles over days.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the classic vignette for mesenteric adenitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: 'A child had a cold a week ago, now has abdominal pain, normal stools, and is tender on palpation.'

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How does mesenteric adenitis differ from appendicitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
• Mesenteric adenitis: recent viral URTI/sore throat, central/RIF pain often fluctuating/less localised, absent/mild guarding, often higher/spiking fever, cough/coryza/cervical nodes, self-limiting.
  • Appendicitis: usually no preceding illness, pain migrates periumbilical → RIF then localises/worsens, present guarding/peritonism, low-grade fever, anorexia/focal signs, progressive course.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why must you never anchor on mesenteric adenitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Because it is hard to be certain — appendicitis must always be excluded. Active observation with serial examination is used only in a child with a SHORT history and equivocal findings; a child under about 6 years with symptoms for more than 48 hours is likely already perforated and needs urgent senior surgical review, not observation. If doubt remains, imaging or diagnostic laparoscopy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How is mesenteric adenitis investigated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back:
Largely a clinical/exclusion diagnosis to rule out appendicitis.
  • Bloods (FBC, CRP) — limited discriminatory value.
  • Ultrasound — the mainstay: enlarged mesenteric nodes (≥3 nodes, short-axis ≥8 mm) with a NORMAL appendix and no other pathology.
  • Urinalysis, throat swab as appropriate
  • diagnostic laparoscopy if appendicitis can't be excluded.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How is mesenteric adenitis managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Supportive and self-limiting — reassurance, analgesia/antipyretics, hydration; resolves in ~2–4 weeks (usually sooner). Safety-net: return if pain worsens, localises, becomes constant, or fever persists. No antibiotics for typical (viral) cases; treat a specific bacterial cause (e.g. Yersinia) if identified/severe.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What common paediatric renal-tract problems does this topic cover?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Urinary tract infection
  • the reflux that predisposes to it (vesicoureteric reflux, VUR)
  • and nocturnal enuresis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is the organising principle for the paediatric urinary tract?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• A childhood UTI needs a clean-catch sample and prompt treatment
  • atypical/recurrent UTI prompts imaging for underlying VUR (retrograde reflux → renal scarring)
  • enuresis is common and usually resolves.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: Give the clue and management for paediatric UTI.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Fever, dysuria; vomiting/irritability in infants → clean-catch culture; antibiotics; image if atypical/recurrent.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: Give the clue and management for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Recurrent UTI, renal scarring → diagnosed and graded on MCUG (not done routinely); management is conservative in most cases — treat UTIs and constipation, with antibiotic prophylaxis or surgery reserved for selected children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: Give the clue and management for nocturnal enuresis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Bedwetting ≥5yr → exclude UTI/constipation/diabetes; enuresis alarm, desmopressin.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What should atypical or recurrent childhood UTI prompt, and what else to consider in enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Investigate (USS ± DMSA/MCUG) for underlying VUR and renal scarring; consider constipation (and safeguarding) in enuresis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is a paediatric UTI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: A bacterial infection of the urinary tract (lower = cystitis; upper = pyelonephritis) in a child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: Why do paediatric UTIs matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: They are common (~1 in 10 girls, ~1 in 30 boys by 16); in infants/young children the presentation is non-specific (can hide behind an unexplained fever); and upper UTIs (pyelonephritis) can cause renal scarring → future hypertension and chronic kidney disease — so UTI flags underlying structural/functional abnormalities (e.g. VUR).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is the commonest organism and mechanism of paediatric UTI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: E. coli (~80%), ascending from the bowel/perineum; others include Klebsiella, Proteus (associated with stones), Enterococcus. Anything impairing urine flow/drainage (reflux, obstruction, constipation, incomplete voiding) predisposes. A non-E. coli organism is a feature of 'atypical' UTI.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How does the sex distribution of paediatric UTI change with age?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: More common in boys until ~3 months (male neonates, often with structural anomalies; uncircumcised infant boys higher risk), then much more common in girls (short urethra).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What are the non-specific features of UTI in infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Poor feeding
  • vomiting
  • irritability
  • fever
  • lethargy
  • poor weight gain
  • jaundice (neonate).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What are the features of UTI in younger and older children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Younger children: abdominal pain, fever, dysuria, vomiting, poor feeding
  • Older children: dysuria, frequency, urgency, haematuria, suprapubic pain, incontinence/enuresis, offensive/cloudy urine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What features suggest an upper UTI (pyelonephritis)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Temperature ≥38°C and/or loin pain/tenderness (± rigors, systemically unwell).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: When should you test the urine for UTI (NICE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• If symptoms/signs suggestive of UTI
  • OR an unexplained fever ≥38°C
  • OR an alternative site of infection but the child remains unwell.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How should urine be sampled and tested in a child (NICE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Clean-catch urine is preferred
  • if not possible → another non-invasive method (a urine collection pad) — never cotton wool balls, gauze or sanitary towels
  • only if non-invasive methods fail → catheter sample or suprapubic aspiration (under ultrasound guidance)
Under 3 months: send urine for urgent microscopy & culture and refer — do not rely on dipstick. From 3 months upwards, dipstick (leucocyte esterase + nitrite) guides management — treat if either is positive. Refrigerate/boric acid if not cultured within 4 hours.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How are infants <3 months with suspected UTI managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Refer IMMEDIATELY to paediatrics (treat as per serious infection/sepsis pathway; IV antibiotics).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How is an upper UTI/pyelonephritis managed in a child ≥3 months?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Consider referral/hospital admission; if not admitted → oral antibiotics for 7–10 days. First choice cefalexin 12.5 mg/kg twice daily; co-amoxiclav ONLY if culture results are available and the organism is susceptible (NICE). Nitrofurantoin must NOT be used — it does not achieve tissue levels in upper-tract infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How is a lower UTI managed in a child ≥3 months?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Oral antibiotics for 3 days (NICE), per local sensitivities; review if not improving. First choice trimethoprim 4 mg/kg twice daily (max 200 mg per dose) if resistance risk is low, or nitrofurantoin 750 micrograms/kg four times daily — nitrofurantoin only if eGFR ≥45 mL/min/1.73m² and only for LOWER UTI. Second choice cefalexin 12.5 mg/kg twice daily; amoxicillin only if culture confirms susceptibility (BNFC).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What predisposing factors should be addressed in paediatric UTI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Constipation (a big one), incomplete/dysfunctional voiding, adequate fluid intake/toileting; antibiotic prophylaxis for recurrent UTIs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What defines an 'atypical' UTI (NICE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Seriously ill/septic
  • poor urine flow
  • abdominal/bladder mass
  • raised creatinine
  • non-E. coli organism
  • or failure to respond within 48h.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What defines a 'recurrent' UTI (NICE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• ≥2 upper UTIs
  • or 1 upper + ≥1 lower
  • or ≥3 lower UTIs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What does ultrasound assess in paediatric UTI, and when?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Structural abnormalities/obstruction — during the acute illness if atypical (any age); within 6 weeks if under 6 months with a first UTI that responded, or if recurrent.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What do DMSA and MCUG scans detect in paediatric UTI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: DMSA — renal parenchymal defects/scarring (done 4–6 months after infection, for atypical/recurrent, especially <3 years). MCUG (micturating cystourethrogram) — detects vesicoureteric reflux and posterior urethral valves; not done routinely, and considered mainly in young infants with atypical/recurrent UTI (especially <6 months). Give oral prophylactic antibiotics for 3 days, with the MCUG on the second day (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is the NICE imaging simplification for a first childhood UTI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: A child >6 months with a first, E. coli, treatment-responsive UTI needs NO routine imaging — imaging is for the young (<6 months), atypical, or recurrent.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is vesicoureteric reflux (VUR)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: The abnormal backflow (retrograde flow) of urine from the bladder up the ureter towards the kidney.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: Why does VUR matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• It is the commonest urological abnormality found after a childhood UTI
  • it predisposes to recurrent UTIs and to pyelonephritis reaching the kidney
  • and repeated infected reflux → renal scarring ('reflux nephropathy') → hypertension and chronic kidney disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: Describe the core mechanism of VUR.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Normally the ureters enter the bladder at an oblique angle through the bladder wall, so bladder contraction compresses the intramural ureter shut (a one-way flap valve). In VUR the ureters are displaced laterally and enter more perpendicularly (short/abnormal intramural tunnel) → the valve fails → urine refluxes back up during voiding.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: Why is VUR harmful?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Refluxed urine that isn't cleared is a bacterial reservoir (predisposes to UTI); it carries infection up to the kidney → pyelonephritis → renal scarring (reflux nephropathy) → hypertension, proteinuria and chronic kidney disease/renal failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is the difference between primary and secondary VUR?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Primary VUR = congenital abnormal vesicoureteric junction (the usual paediatric type)
  • Secondary VUR = from raised bladder pressure/obstruction (e.g. posterior urethral valves, neuropathic bladder).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How is VUR graded (International Reflux Study I–V)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
On MCUG by how far up urine refluxes and how dilated the system becomes:
  • I — ureter only (no dilatation)
  • II — up to renal pelvis/calyces, no dilatation
  • III — mild dilatation of ureter/pelvis/calyces
  • IV — moderate dilatation + tortuous ureter, blunted calyces
  • V — gross dilatation & tortuosity, ureteric kinking, loss of calyceal/papillary impressions.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How does VUR grade relate to prognosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Low-grade (I–II) usually resolves spontaneously (>80%) with growth; high-grade (IV–V) less likely to resolve and carries the highest scarring/CKD risk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How is VUR most commonly detected?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• During investigation of a childhood UTI (especially atypical or recurrent — the NICE trigger)
  • antenatally detected hydronephrosis can be the first clue
  • also via recurrent febrile UTIs/pyelonephritis or family screening (familial tendency).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for VUR?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) — contrast instilled into the bladder via a catheter with X-rays during voiding to see reflux; it also grades VUR. It is not performed routinely. Give oral prophylactic antibiotics for 3 days, with the MCUG on the second day (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What do DMSA and ultrasound show in VUR?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• DMSA — looks for renal scarring/parenchymal defects (typically 4–6 months after an infection so acute change isn't mistaken for a scar)
  • Ultrasound — structural assessment (hydronephrosis, duplex systems), often first-line imaging.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What monitoring is done for reflux nephropathy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Blood pressure, renal function, urinalysis (proteinuria) — long-term.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is the general principle of VUR management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Protect the kidneys from infected reflux until the child grows out of it or it's corrected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How is low-grade VUR managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Conservative/observation — it often resolves spontaneously as the child grows (the intramural ureter lengthens); treat/prevent UTIs and address bladder-bowel dysfunction (constipation, dysfunctional voiding).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: When is antibiotic prophylaxis used in VUR?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis — trimethoprim 2 mg/kg (max 100 mg) at night or nitrofurantoin 1 mg/kg at night (BNFC). UK practice is narrower than often taught: it is not routine after a first UTI and is not given for reflux grade alone — consider it for recurrent UTI, and never for asymptomatic bacteriuria (NICE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: When and how is VUR corrected surgically?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
For high-grade/persistent VUR, breakthrough febrile UTIs on prophylaxis, or progressive scarring:
  • endoscopic injection of a bulking agent beneath the ureteric orifice (the 'STING' procedure, minimally invasive)
  • or open ureteric reimplantation (ureteroneocystostomy — creates a longer oblique tunnel, highest success rate).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is nocturnal enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Involuntary wetting during sleep (bedwetting) in a child aged ≥5 years — the age at which night-time bladder control is normally expected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: Why does nocturnal enuresis matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: It is very common (~15–20% of 5-year-olds, resolving spontaneously ~15%/year), causes distress/embarrassment and impacts self-esteem (so handle sympathetically — it is NOT the child's fault), and occasionally signals an underlying medical problem to exclude.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What are the contributory causes of primary bedwetting?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• (1) A 'deep sleeper' who doesn't wake to a full bladder (arousal problem)
  • (2) nocturnal polyuria (reduced overnight ADH → too much urine at night)
  • (3) a small/overactive bladder (reduced functional capacity/detrusor overactivity)
— often with a strong genetic/familial tendency.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is primary vs secondary enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Primary — the child has NEVER been reliably dry at night (>6 months); the commonest, usually delayed maturation
  • Secondary — the child was previously dry for ≥6 months then started wetting again → think of an acquired cause: UTI, constipation, diabetes, or a psychological/emotional stressor (bullying, family upheaval, abuse).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is monosymptomatic vs non-monosymptomatic enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Monosymptomatic — bedwetting only
  • Non-monosymptomatic — bedwetting + daytime symptoms (urgency, frequency, daytime wetting) → points to bladder dysfunction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How is bedwetting in a child under 5 managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Reassure and give advice — bedwetting is normal at that age, no treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What underlying causes/triggers should be looked for in enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Constipation, diabetes mellitus and UTI — plus daytime symptoms (bladder dysfunction), sleep-disordered breathing (obstructive sleep apnoea), and psychosocial stressors (especially in secondary enuresis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: When is urinalysis indicated in enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: NOT routine; only if recent-onset (?diabetes/UTI), daytime symptoms, unwell, or signs of ill health.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What general advice/modifiable factors apply to all children with enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back:
• Reassure (not the child's fault, avoid punishment/blame)
  • adequate daily fluid intake spread through the day — fluid restriction is NOT a treatment — while avoiding caffeine-based and fizzy drinks
  • regular daytime toileting and just before sleep
  • treat constipation and any UTI first
  • reward systems (star charts) for agreed behaviours — NOT for 'dry nights' (which the child can't fully control).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is the first-line active treatment for nocturnal enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: An enuresis alarm — a sensor pad/alarm that detects wetness and wakes the child, conditioning them to wake to a full bladder/hold on; best long-term/sustained success but takes weeks and needs commitment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: What is the role of desmopressin in enuresis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: A synthetic ADH analogue that reduces overnight urine production. Offer over 7 years; consider at 5–7 years if treatment is needed (NICE). Dose 200 micrograms at bedtime, increased to 400 micrograms if not dry after 1–2 weeks (sublingual 120 → 240 micrograms). Used for short-term/rapid results (sleepovers, school trips) or when an alarm is unsuitable, declined or has failed. Sips of fluid only from 1 hour BEFORE the dose until 8 hours AFTER (hyponatraemia/water intoxication risk); stop during vomiting or diarrhoea until fluid balance is normal; the nasal route must not be used for bedwetting (NICE, MHRA).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.front: How is refractory enuresis managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Urin.back: Refer to specialist; options include anticholinergics — oxybutynin (licensed from 5 years) for overactive bladder, and rarely tricyclics (imipramine — specialist initiation only; cardiac risk and dangerous in overdose).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What are the two childhood vasculitides covered in this topic?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Kawasaki disease (medium-vessel) and Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA small-vessel).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the organising principle for paediatric vasculitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Kawasaki = prolonged fever ≥5 days + mucocutaneous features → risk of coronary aneurysms; HSP = palpable purpura (buttocks/legs) + arthralgia + abdominal pain + nephritis, often post-URTI.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Give the features and management of Kawasaki disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Fever ≥5d + conjunctivitis, rash, cervical node, red cracked lips/strawberry tongue, extremity changes → IVIG + aspirin; echo for coronary aneurysms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Give the features and management of HSP/IgA vasculitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Palpable purpura (extensor/buttocks), arthralgia, abdominal pain, IgA nephritis → usually self-limiting; monitor BP + urine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the key time-critical action in Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Give IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days to cut coronary-artery aneurysms from roughly 20–25% to under 5% (with echo follow-up); it is one of the few paediatric indications for aspirin.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: A medium-vessel vasculitis of early childhood — the second most common childhood vasculitis after HSP, but the one that threatens the heart.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Why does Kawasaki disease matter above all?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: It causes coronary artery aneurysms; untreated it is a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in the developed world. The urgency is recognising it and giving IVIG within 10 days to protect the coronaries.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the epidemiology of Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Typically children <5 years (peak 6 months–4 years), more common in boys and in children of East Asian (Japanese) ancestry. Cause unknown — likely an abnormal immune response to an infectious trigger in a genetically susceptible child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the difference between complete and incomplete Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
• Complete: fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of 5 principal features.
  • Incomplete (atypical): fever + fewer features + supportive labs/echo — especially infants <1 year, who present atypically and have the highest aneurysm risk.
Both get the same urgent treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What are the diagnostic criteria of Kawasaki disease (CRASH mnemonic)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
Fever ≥5 days PLUS ≥4 of 5:
  • C — Conjunctivitis (bilateral, non-purulent, limbal sparing)
  • R — Rash (polymorphous, non-vesicular)
  • A — Adenopathy (cervical, often unilateral, ≥1.5 cm, the least common feature)
  • S — Strawberry tongue (+ cracked red lips, oral mucositis)
  • H — Hands/feet (erythema/oedema acutely → peeling/desquamation of fingertips/toes in convalescence).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What are two timing pearls in Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Desquamation of the extremities is a later (week 2+) sign, often after the acute illness; and there is a classic association with redness/induration at the site of a previous BCG scar.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: How is the 5-day fever rule applied flexibly?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Comprehensive clinical assessment over rigidly waiting 5 days — treatment can start on day 4 if all features are present, and incomplete Kawasaki is treated promptly rather than observed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Describe the acute phase of Kawasaki disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: 1–2 weeks: fever, the principal features, irritability (very characteristic — a miserable child), myocarditis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Describe the subacute phase of Kawasaki disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: 2–4 weeks: fever settles, desquamation, thrombocytosis (platelets rise strikingly), and the period of highest coronary aneurysm and thrombosis risk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Is there a single diagnostic test for Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: No — it is clinical, supported by bloods and echo.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What blood findings support Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: ↑↑ inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), neutrophilia, normocytic anaemia, ↑ ALT/bilirubin; thrombocytosis (platelets often >450, classically rising in the second week — an important supportive clue).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the role of echocardiography in Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: At diagnosis, repeated at 1–2 weeks and again at 6–8 weeks — looks for coronary artery dilatation/aneurysm (Z-score ≥2.5 defines abnormality), myocarditis, valve regurgitation, pericardial effusion. If the 6–8 week echo is normal, aspirin can stop; if abnormal, echoes are more frequent and antiplatelet therapy continues. A normal early echo does NOT exclude Kawasaki and must not delay treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What are the key differentials/mimics of Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
• Measles
  • scarlet fever
  • staphylococcal/streptococcal toxic shock
  • Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  • systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
  • and — since 2020 — MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, post-COVID).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the coronary-protecting treatment for Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion, given within 10 days of illness onset (as soon as possible after diagnosis); it reduces coronary artery aneurysms from roughly 20–25% untreated to under 5%. Still give it after day 10 if there is ongoing fever/inflammation or coronary abnormalities.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: How is aspirin used in Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: High-dose aspirin 7.5–12.5 mg/kg four times daily (30–50 mg/kg daily, anti-inflammatory) until afebrile, then low-dose aspirin 3–5 mg/kg once daily (antiplatelet) for 6–8 weeks until a follow-up echo confirms no coronary changes (BNFC). Kawasaki is the key exception to the rule that aspirin is contraindicated in children (Reye's syndrome risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is IVIG resistance in Kawasaki disease, and how is it managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Fever recurring/persisting ≥36 hours after the first IVIG infusion → a second IVIG dose, steroids, or infliximab. Corticosteroids are also used for high-risk patients.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What follow-up and vaccine caution apply after Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Cardiology surveillance with serial echocardiography; avoid live vaccines for a period after IVIG (passive antibodies blunt the response) — defer MMR and varicella vaccination and check the recommended interval (UKHSA).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What are the complications of Kawasaki disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
• Coronary artery aneurysms (the defining complication → thrombosis, stenosis, MI, sudden death; highest risk in infants <6–12 months, delayed/missed treatment, IVIG resistance)
  • myocarditis, pericarditis, arrhythmia, valve regurgitation acutely
  • Kawasaki disease shock syndrome and macrophage activation syndrome (rare, severe).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is HSP (IgA vasculitis)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: The commonest vasculitis of childhood — an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis driven by IgA immune-complex deposition in small vessels.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Why does HSP matter, and what dictates its follow-up?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: It is common, usually benign and self-limiting, but renal involvement (IgA vasculitis nephritis) is the source of essentially all its long-term morbidity — the skin, joints and gut settle on their own; the kidney is the reason for follow-up.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the epidemiology and trigger of HSP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Peak age 3–10 years (usually <10), slight male predominance, often 1–3 weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection (classically group A strep); more common in winter.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the decisive fork in HSP prognosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
Whether the kidney is involved.
  • No renal involvement: purpura + joints + gut, normal urine/BP → self-limiting, excellent prognosis.
  • IgA vasculitis nephritis: haematuria/proteinuria ± hypertension → the source of long-term morbidity (rarely → chronic/end-stage kidney disease), needing nephrology referral.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Why does normal early urinalysis not exclude HSP nephritis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Nephritis can appear weeks later even after a normal initial urine — which is why HSP has a prolonged monitoring schedule.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the classic tetrad of HSP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
• Palpable purpura (buttocks/extensor lower limbs)
  • arthralgia/arthritis
  • abdominal pain
  • renal involvement (IgA nephritis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Describe the purpura of HSP and its key distinction.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Symmetrical, non-blanching, palpable purpura over the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the lower limbs; NOT due to low platelets (platelets are normal/raised — the key distinction from ITP).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Describe the joint involvement in HSP.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Arthralgia/arthritis of large joints (knees, ankles), transient and non-destructive.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Describe the abdominal involvement in HSP and its key complication.
