conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Colicky abdominal pain from bowel-wall vasculitis; can cause GI bleeding and — importantly — intussusception (classically ileoileal), the key acute abdominal complication.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Describe the renal involvement in HSP.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: IgA vasculitis nephritis: haematuria (micro/macroscopic) ± proteinuria; ranges from trivial to nephritic/nephrotic; rarely progresses to chronic kidney disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What other feature can HSP cause in boys?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Scrotal involvement — a differential for testicular torsion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What are the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES diagnostic criteria for HSP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
Mandatory: palpable purpura (or petechiae) with lower-limb predominance, without thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy — PLUS at least one of:
  • (1) diffuse abdominal pain
  • (2) arthritis or arthralgia
  • (3) renal involvement (proteinuria or haematuria)
  • (4) histopathology — leukocytoclastic vasculitis with predominant IgA deposition.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the core renal screen in HSP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Urinalysis (haematuria/proteinuria) + urine protein:creatinine ratio + blood pressure — repeated over follow-up.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: Why is FBC & film done in HSP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Platelets are normal/raised with no coagulopathy — this excludes ITP and other thrombocytopenic causes of purpura (the essential differential). U&Es, albumin if renal involvement; skin/renal biopsy only in atypical/severe cases → IgA deposition on immunofluorescence.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the mainstay of HSP management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Supportive — most cases self-limiting: rest, hydration, analgesia; simple analgesia/NSAIDs for joint pain (use NSAIDs cautiously/avoid if renal involvement). Most skin/joint symptoms resolve within ~4 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the role of corticosteroids in HSP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: NOT routine — they do not prevent nephritis and aren't used for the rash. Considered for severe abdominal pain/GI involvement once intussusception has been excluded — oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg once daily for 1–2 weeks, then weaned — and in significant nephritis under specialist care.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: How is HSP nephritis managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
• Refer to paediatric nephrology for significant proteinuria, hypertension, or impaired renal function
  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs for persistent proteinuria
  • immunosuppression for severe biopsy-proven nephritis (renal biopsy guides treatment).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: What is the most examinable follow-up point in HSP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back: Blood pressure + early-morning urine dipstick, densely at first (about weekly for the first month, then less often) and continuing to at least 6 months, because nephritis can appear late even after a normal initial urine — most renal involvement declares within the first month. Discharge only with normal urine and blood pressure at 6 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.front: How does HSP differ from ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Vasc.back:
• HSP: palpable (vasculitic) purpura, normal/raised platelets, IgA immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis, systemic (joints, gut, kidney).
  • ITP: non-palpable petechiae/purpura and bruising, low platelets (isolated thrombocytopenia), anti-platelet antibodies, usually isolated bleeding/bruising.
The palpable rash + normal platelets is the discriminator.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Defective mineralisation of growing bone at the epiphyseal growth plates, producing soft, weak, deformable bones in children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: Why does rickets matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: It is largely preventable and treatable, a marker of underlying vitamin D or calcium deficiency (with public-health and safeguarding dimensions), and a favourite exam topic for its classic deformities and biochemical fingerprint.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is the adult equivalent of rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Osteomalacia — the same process after the growth plates fuse, without bowing deformities.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is the core biochemical logic of calcipenic rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Low vitamin D → low calcium → secondary hyperparathyroidism → PTH drags calcium back toward normal but wastes phosphate in the urine. Hallmark: low phosphate + high ALP with calcium often near-normal.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is the decisive fork in classifying rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Calcipenic (calcium/vitamin D pathway) vs phosphopenic (phosphate-wasting) — which is what the biochemistry is for.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: Describe the cause and biochemistry of calcipenic rickets.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Cause: vitamin D deficiency (commonest) or dietary calcium deficiency. Mechanism: ↓ vit D → ↓ Ca → ↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) → phosphate wasting. Calcium low/low-normal, PTH high, phosphate low, ALP high.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: Describe the cause and biochemistry of phosphopenic rickets.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Cause: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (commonest inherited); also Fanconi, renal disease. Mechanism: renal phosphate wasting via ↑ FGF-23. Calcium normal, PTH normal (or slightly ↑), phosphate low, ALP high.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What are the nutritional causes/risk factors for rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back:
• Vitamin D deficiency (usual cause)
  • dietary calcium deficiency
  • prolonged/exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation
  • unsupplemented formula/cow's milk
  • lack of sunlight (darker skin, covering clothing, northern latitudes, institutionalised children).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What are the secondary and inherited causes of rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back:
• Malabsorption (coeliac, CF, cholestatic liver disease)
  • chronic kidney disease (renal rickets — failure of 1-α-hydroxylation)
  • anticonvulsants (induce vitamin D catabolism)
  • X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (PHEX mutation → ↑FGF-23 → renal phosphate wasting)
  • vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 (1-α-hydroxylase defect)/type 2 (receptor defect).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What are the general/early clinical features of rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back:
• Aching bones and joints
  • general misery
  • delayed motor milestones
  • hypotonia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: Describe the lower-limb deformity of rickets and its age-dependent switch.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Genu varum (bow legs) in toddlers → genu valgum (knock knees) in older children — the age-dependent switch is a classic exam point.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is a rachitic rosary?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Expansion of the costochondral junctions → beading along the chest.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is craniotabes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: A soft skull with delayed suture/fontanelle closure and frontal bossing.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is Harrison's sulcus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: A horizontal groove along the lower ribcage (diaphragmatic pull on soft ribs).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: List other clinical features of rickets.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back:
• Kyphoscoliosis
  • wide/swollen wrists and ankles (metaphyseal flaring)
  • delayed dentition with enamel hypoplasia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What hypocalcaemic features can occur if calcium falls far enough in rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Tetany, carpopedal spasm, seizures, and (in infants) stridor — occasionally the presenting problem.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is the biochemical fingerprint of nutritional rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back:
• ↓ 25-hydroxyvitamin D
  • ↓/low-normal calcium
  • ↓ phosphate
  • ↑↑ ALP
  • ↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: Why is ALP a key marker in rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: It is raised in all forms of rickets — a sensitive marker of osteoblast activity/healing.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What biochemical pattern points to X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Low phosphate with normal calcium and normal PTH.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What are the X-ray findings of rickets (classically at the wrist)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Cupping, fraying and splaying of the metaphyses, widened growth plate, osteopenia — the radiological hallmark.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: How is nutritional rickets treated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back:
• Oral vitamin D (colecalciferol) with adequate dietary calcium — high healing doses for weeks-to-months, then a maintenance dose
  • correct the underlying cause (treat malabsorption, adjust diet, sunlight advice)
  • monitor ALP and biochemistry to confirm healing.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: How is renal rickets / vitamin D-dependent rickets treated, and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol), because the failing step is 1-α-hydroxylation — plain colecalciferol will not work.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: How is X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back: Historically oral phosphate + activated vitamin D (calcitriol), but this risks nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism. Burosumab (an anti-FGF-23 monoclonal antibody) is now recommended (NICE) for children ≥1 year with radiographic bone disease and outperforms conventional therapy for skeletal outcomes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.front: What is the UK public-health prevention advice for rickets?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Rickets.back:
• All breastfed infants and at-risk groups receive vitamin D supplementation (~400 IU/10 µg daily)
  • pregnant and breastfeeding women should supplement too (10 µg daily).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What does the safeguarding & child protection topic cover?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Recognising and acting on child maltreatment, and the legal/ethical frameworks underpinning children's care.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the organising principle for safeguarding?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Maintain a professional suspicion — injuries inconsistent with the history or developmental stage, delayed presentation, or inconsistent accounts; and know the frameworks for consent and protection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Give the key points for non-accidental injury (NAI).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Injuries inconsistent with history/development (e.g. bruising in a non-mobile infant, certain fractures), delayed presentation → document + escalate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Give the key points for SUDI.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Sudden unexpected death in infancy; risk reduction (back to sleep, smoke-free); multi-agency investigation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Name the key safeguarding frameworks.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Gillick competence (capacity to consent)
  • Fraser guidelines (contraception)
  • Children Act (welfare paramount)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What findings mandate a safeguarding assessment and escalation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Bruising or a fracture in a non-mobile infant, or injuries inconsistent with the mechanism given. The child's welfare is paramount.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is non-accidental injury (NAI)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Physical harm to a child inflicted or knowingly not prevented by a carer — one form of child maltreatment (alongside neglect, emotional abuse, sexual abuse, and fabricated/induced illness).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Why does recognising NAI matter so much?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Missing it can be fatal; every doctor has a statutory safeguarding duty; and the presentation is deliberately obscured — recognition depends on a pattern of red flags, not any single injury.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the doctor's role in suspected NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Not to prove abuse or confront the family, but to recognise the possibility, keep the child safe, document meticulously, and refer — the safeguarding system (social care, police, named/designated professionals) does the investigating. A child's safety overrides confidentiality.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the NICE distinction between 'consider' and 'suspect' maltreatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• 'Consider' maltreatment = one possible explanation
  • 'suspect' maltreatment = a serious level of concern → must act/refer

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the core decisive question in suspected NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Does the injury, in this child, with this explanation, fit the story and the child's developmental stage?

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: List the red flags that raise concern about NAI.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Injury inconsistent with the explanation
  • injury inconsistent with developmental stage
  • changing/vague/absent history
  • delay in presentation
  • inappropriate carer-child interaction/affect
  • multiple injuries of different ages
  • repeated attendances

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the single most important red flag for NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Bruising in a non-independently-mobile infant ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise') — accidental bruising is rare (0–1.3%), so it is a sentinel injury mandating safeguarding action.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What bruising sites and patterns are suggestive of NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Sites unusual for accidents — ears, neck, cheeks, trunk, buttocks, genitalia, inner thighs (accidental bruises are over bony prominences: shins, forehead, knees)
  • patterned bruises — hand/slap marks, grip marks, ligature marks, implement outlines, bite marks

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Can you age a bruise by its colour with the naked eye?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: No — this is a common exam misconception; you cannot accurately age a bruise by its colour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Which fractures are suggestive of NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Any fracture in a non-mobile infant without a clear major-trauma explanation
  • multiple fractures, especially of different ages (different healing stages)
  • posterior rib fractures (from squeezing/compression — highly specific)
  • metaphyseal corner ('bucket-handle') fractures (from shaking/pulling/twisting — highly specific)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the triad of abusive head trauma (Shaken Baby)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Encephalopathy + subdural haemorrhage(s) + retinal haemorrhages, typically in a child under 3 years. It is highly suggestive of abusive head trauma but not diagnostic of mechanism on its own — medical mimics must be excluded.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What does NICE say about abusive head trauma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Suspect maltreatment with multiple subdural haemorrhages ± subarachnoid/hypoxic-ischaemic damage, or retinal haemorrhages, without major confirmed accidental trauma or medical cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Which head-injury CT triggers are safeguarding triggers?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Suspicion of non-accidental head injury, and <1 yr with bruise/swelling/laceration >5 cm on the head.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What burn/scald patterns suggest NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Glove-and-stocking/immersion scalds with sharp margins
  • cigarette burns (well-demarcated circular)
  • burns to unusual sites
  • patterns matching an implement

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Which internal injuries can occur in NAI without external marks?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Intracranial, intra-abdominal, or intrathoracic injury without confirmed major accidental trauma; also oral injuries (torn frenulum in a non-mobile infant) and anogenital signs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What are the four categories of child maltreatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
Four statutory categories:
  • physical abuse
  • emotional abuse
  • sexual abuse (including child sexual exploitation)
  • and neglect (the commonest)
Fabricated or induced illness is a further form of abuse, categorised under physical and/or emotional — not a fifth category. Also on the radar: FGM, trafficking, criminal exploitation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What does assessment of suspected NAI involve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Full history (mechanism, timeline, who was present — taken non-judgementally, documented verbatim)
  • full examination (growth plotting, whole-skin body map with size/site/description, developmental assessment, demeanour/interaction)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What investigations are used in suspected NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Skeletal survey — indicated in all children under 2 years with suspected physical abuse (selective at 2–5 years, not routine above 5), with a repeat film at 11–14 days for occult/healing fractures
  • CT/MRI head for suspected abusive head trauma
  • ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhages
  • coagulation screen/FBC and bone profile to exclude bleeding disorders and osteogenesis imperfecta/rickets as mimics

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Which mimics of NAI must be considered/excluded?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Meningococcal septicaemia
  • coagulopathy (ITP, haemophilia, leukaemia)
  • congenital dermal melanocytosis
  • osteogenesis imperfecta
  • birth-related retinal haemorrhage

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What are the management steps a doctor takes in suspected NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Ensure the child is safe now (admit if necessary) — but you cannot lawfully detain a child, so if the family try to leave, contact children's social care and the police immediately (police protection powers under s46 Children Act 1989 can prevent removal for up to 72 hours; the local authority can seek an emergency protection order under s44)
  • Escalate to the senior paediatrician/safeguarding lead
  • refer to children's social care (± police) on reasonable suspicion, not proof
  • document meticulously with body maps and verbatim quotes
  • consider siblings

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: How does confidentiality apply in suspected NAI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Child safety overrides confidentiality — you may share information without consent if a child is at risk of significant harm (GMC). Refer on suspicion, not proof; the threshold to seek senior advice is low.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is SUDI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: The sudden, unexpected death of an infant (or child) where the cause is not immediately obvious at presentation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Why does SUDI matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• It is the leading category of postneonatal infant death in the UK (~200 deaths/year in England and Wales)
  • much is preventable through safe-sleep advice
  • and every such death triggers a statutory multi-agency investigation with a safeguarding dimension.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Distinguish SUDI, SIDS and SUDC.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• SUDI = the umbrella term used at presentation (sudden, unexpected, before investigation)
  • SIDS ('cot death') = the diagnosis of exclusion used only after a full investigation (including post-mortem) finds no cause
  • SUDC = the equivalent term when the child is >12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: How is SUDI sorted after investigation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Into explained SUDI (infection, inborn error of metabolism, congenital cardiac/arrhythmia, trauma — accidental or inflicted) or unexplained → SIDS (no cause after full work-up + post-mortem).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Why is every SUDI investigated with a safeguarding lens?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: A proportion of SUDI is inflicted injury/neglect — so investigation is a duty, not an accusation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the epidemiology of SUDI/SIDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Peak age 1–2 months
  • ~87% occur before 6 months
  • rare after 6 months
  • strong socioeconomic gradient (highest in young parents and deprivation, up to ~4x the general rate).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the triple-risk model of SIDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
SIDS occurs when three things coincide:
  • a vulnerable infant (e.g. prematurity, low birth weight)
  • a critical developmental period (the first months, immature cardiorespiratory/arousal control)
  • and an exogenous stressor (e.g. prone sleeping, overheating, smoke exposure).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What are the non-modifiable infant risk factors for SIDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Prematurity
  • low birth weight (<2.5 kg)
  • male sex
  • multiple birth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the single most strongly linked modifiable risk factor for SIDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Smoking (in pregnancy and household exposure).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: How does sleeping position affect SIDS risk?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Prone or side sleeping increases risk; prone increases risk up to ~6-fold.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: When is co-sleeping hazardous for SIDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Especially on a sofa/armchair (never safe)
  • or bed-sharing when a parent smokes/drinks alcohol/takes drugs
  • or the baby was premature/low birth weight.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What environmental factors increase SIDS risk?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Overheating/head covering
  • soft/cluttered sleep surface (pillows, duvets, bumpers, soft toys, sleep pods)
  • maternal young age, high parity, late/no antenatal care, drug/alcohol use.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What factors are protective against SIDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Breastfeeding
  • room-sharing (without bed-sharing) for the first 6 months
  • immunisation
  • and dummy/pacifier use (once breastfeeding established).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the core safe-sleep advice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Back to sleep (supine for every sleep — the campaign cut UK SIDS by >80%)
  • clear, flat cot (firm flat mattress, no pillows/duvets/bumpers/soft toys/positioners)
  • 'feet to foot' (baby's feet at the foot of the cot)
  • room-share, don't bed-share for the first 6 months
  • smoke-free pregnancy and household
  • never sleep with baby on a sofa/armchair
  • avoid overheating (room 16–20°C, no hat indoors)
  • breastfeed where possible
  • keep immunisations up to date.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What happens after a SUDI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Full resuscitation unless clearly inappropriate
  • a Joint Agency Response (JAR) is triggered — a coordinated multi-agency investigation (paediatrics, police, coroner, social care).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What investigations follow a SUDI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
Detailed history/examination, body map, and a structured set of investigations to find a cause and exclude inflicted injury/metabolic disease:
  • bloods
  • cultures/septic screen
  • metabolic samples
  • toxicology
  • imaging/skeletal survey
  • and (via the coroner) a post-mortem.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What formal processes are mandatory after a SUDI?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Coroner referral (sudden unexplained death)
  • a home visit/death-scene assessment documenting the sleep environment
  • Child Death Review processes
  • and bereavement support throughout (non-negotiable — investigation is explained as routine, not accusatory).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What are the three commonly confused safeguarding frameworks, and how do they differ?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Gillick competence = can this under-16 consent to this treatment? (capacity)
  • Fraser guidelines = the specific criteria for giving contraception/sexual-health advice to an under-16 without parental knowledge
  • Children Acts 1989/2004 = the statutory framework for welfare, parental responsibility, and state intervention.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the consent status of a 16–17-year-old?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Presumed to have capacity to consent to treatment, like an adult (Family Law Reform Act 1969). Their refusal of life-saving treatment may be overridden by a person with parental responsibility or the court — but seek urgent legal advice and, where time allows, a court decision; in Scotland a competent young person's refusal cannot be overridden by a parent.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the consent status of an under-16?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: No automatic right; may consent IF Gillick competent for that specific decision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the rule for under-13s and sexual activity?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Cannot legally consent to any sexual activity — any disclosure of sexual activity is an automatic safeguarding referral, regardless of competence.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the key consent asymmetry for minors?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: A competent minor can consent to beneficial treatment, but their refusal of life-saving treatment can be overridden (by a parental-responsibility holder or the court) — this is not true for a competent adult. Justified only where refusal would likely lead to death or grave, irreversible harm.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is Gillick competence?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: A child under 16 can consent to their own medical treatment if they have sufficient understanding and intelligence to fully understand what is proposed — its purpose, nature, benefits, risks, alternatives and consequences. There is no lower age limit.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What did the Gillick ruling establish about parental rights?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: That parental rights are not absolute and diminish as the child matures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Is Gillick competence a fixed status?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: No — it is decision-specific (a child may be competent for a simple decision but not a complex one; assess each time) and consent must be voluntary (not coerced).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What are the five Fraser criteria (all must be satisfied)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• (1) The young person understands the advice
  • (2) they cannot be persuaded to inform their parents (or let the professional inform them)
  • (3) they are likely to begin or continue having sexual intercourse with or without contraception
  • (4) without treatment their physical or mental health is likely to suffer
  • (5) their best interests require the advice/treatment without parental consent.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the exam distinction between Gillick and Fraser?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Gillick = the general test of a child's capacity to consent (Lord Scarman)
  • Fraser = the specific checklist for contraception/sexual health (Lord Fraser)
Not interchangeable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is parental responsibility (Children Act 1989)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: The legal rights, duties and authority a parent has for a child; consent from one holder is usually sufficient.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: Who has parental responsibility?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• The mother automatically
  • the father if married to the mother or named on the birth certificate (from Dec 2003)
  • others via court orders/agreements (step-parents, guardians, local authority under a care order)
It is exercised for the child's benefit and yields to the child's own competent decisions as they mature.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What is the paramountcy principle of the Children Act 1989?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: 'The child's welfare is the paramount consideration' — the single most quotable line.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What do sections 17 and 47 of the Children Act 1989 cover?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• Section 17 — a duty on the local authority to safeguard and promote the welfare of 'children in need' (support, not child protection)
  • Section 47 — a duty on the local authority to make enquiries (not to 'investigate') where there is reasonable cause to suspect a child is suffering, or likely to suffer, significant harm, triggered after a strategy discussion between social care, police and health.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What did the Children Act 2004 introduce?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back:
• It strengthened multi-agency working after the Victoria Climbié inquiry
  • created the Children's Commissioner
  • and embedded 'Every Child Matters'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What does the statutory multi-agency safeguarding guidance require?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: 'Safeguarding is everyone's responsibility' — the multi-agency duty across health, education, police and social care; it replaced the old structure with multi-agency safeguarding partnerships (local authority, integrated care board, police).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: How does confidentiality apply to young people?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: They are owed the same duty of confidentiality as adults, but it is NOT absolute — it is overridden where a child is at risk of significant harm; you may share information without consent when necessary to protect a child. Tell the young person what you're sharing and why, unless doing so would increase risk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.front: What must you assess even when an under-16 appears 'competent' for sexual-health advice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Safeguarding &.back: Consider the Sexual Offences Act 2003 context — assess for exploitation, grooming, or a significant age gap; an under-13 disclosing sexual activity always triggers referral (cannot consent in law).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What does the stridor & upper airway topic cover?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Causes of upper-airway obstruction in children, presenting with stridor — the skill is separating the emergency (epiglottitis) from common, benign causes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the organising principle for paediatric stridor?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Acute barking cough = croup (viral)
  • toxic child, drooling, tripod, no cough = epiglottitis (emergency — don't examine the throat)
  • chronic stridor appearing in the first days to weeks of life, worse supine/feeding = laryngomalacia (usually benign).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: Give the age/cause and management of croup.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: 6mo–3yr, parainfluenza; barking cough, stridor, worse at night → oral dexamethasone (nebulised adrenaline if severe).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: Give the cause and management of epiglottitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Hib; toxic, drooling, tripod, muffled voice, NO cough → secure airway + IV antibiotics.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: Give the features and course of laryngomalacia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Inspiratory stridor appearing in the first days to two weeks of life (not usually at the moment of birth), worse supine, when feeding, crying or with an URTI; it typically worsens to a peak around 6–8 months, then settles, resolving in most by 18–24 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the golden rule in suspected epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: It is a life-threatening emergency — keep the child calm, do not examine the throat or lie them flat; call senior anaesthetics/ENT to secure the airway. Now rare thanks to the Hib vaccine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: An acute viral upper-airway infection causing subglottic inflammation → the classic barking cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor in a young child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: Why does croup matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: It is extremely common (~2–3% of children/year); although usually mild and self-limiting, it sits at the top of the paediatric stridor differential — the job is to recognise it, treat with a single steroid dose, and confidently exclude dangerous mimics.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the reassuring pattern of croup vs its mimics?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
Croup is the common, viral, gradual-onset, barking-cough, well-ish child. Mimics:
  • epiglottitis (toxic, drooling, no cough)
  • inhaled foreign body (sudden, choking)
  • bacterial tracheitis (toxic, high fever).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the golden rule across all paediatric stridor conditions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Keep the child calm and do NOT distress them (no throat exam, no cannulas, keep on parent's lap) — agitation worsens airway obstruction and can precipitate complete obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the age, season and cause of croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Age 6 months–3 years (peak ~2 years; rare <6 months)
  • autumn/early winter
  • parainfluenza virus (types 1 & 3) is commonest (also RSV, adenovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: Which children are at higher risk of severe croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Children with pre-existing airway narrowing (subglottic stenosis, laryngomalacia) and Down syndrome — admit even if symptoms look mild.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What are the clinical features of croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Barking ('seal-like') cough (the hallmark)
  • inspiratory stridor (worse when upset)
  • hoarse voice/cry
  • preceding coryza and low-grade fever
  • symptoms worse at night
  • in severe cases suprasternal/intercostal recession, tracheal tug, tachypnoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What are the late/danger signs of croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Fatigue, drowsiness, cyanosis, silent chest → impending obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What tool grades croup severity, and what defines mild croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
The Westley croup score (stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, conscious level). Mild:
  • barking cough
  • stridor only when upset
  • no/mild recession
  • happy
  • eating/drinking.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What defines moderate and severe croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Moderate: stridor at rest, recession at rest, but not distressed/agitated.
  • Severe: stridor at rest + marked recession, agitation or lethargy, tachycardia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What are the features of impending respiratory failure in croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Fatigue, ↓ consciousness, cyanosis, silent chest, bradycardia — peri-arrest.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How is croup diagnosed and what investigations are avoided?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Clinically — do NOT perform investigations that distress the child (no bloods, no cannula, no throat exam); imaging is not routine (the 'steeple sign' subglottic narrowing on X-ray is not needed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the standard treatment for ALL children with croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: A single dose of oral corticosteroid regardless of severity — oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (alternatives: oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg, nebulised budesonide 2 mg, or IM dexamethasone); steroids reduce symptoms within ~2 hours.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How is mild croup managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Single steroid dose → manage at home; safety-net advice (return if stridor at rest, distress, drooling, colour change). No antibiotics (viral).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How is severe croup / impending obstruction managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Nebulised adrenaline (1:1000) 0.4 mL/kg — 400 micrograms/kg — to a maximum of 5 mL, repeatable after 30 minutes; rapid but temporary relief (wears off ~2 hours → observe ≥3–4 hours for rebound) + oxygen (minimal handling) + steroid + senior/anaesthetic + ENT airway support; keep the child calm on the parent's lap.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: When should a child with croup be admitted?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Moderate–severe croup
  • stridor at rest not settling
  • respiratory distress
  • hypoxia
  • needing repeated adrenaline
  • poor intake
  • age <6 months
  • high-risk group (Down syndrome, pre-existing airway narrowing)
  • or diagnostic uncertainty.
Discharge once stridor-free at rest.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What are the complications of croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
Usually none (self-limiting over ~48 hours). Rarely:
  • secondary bacterial tracheitis
  • dehydration from poor intake
  • and very rarely airway obstruction requiring intubation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Rapidly progressive inflammation and swelling of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures that can cause complete upper-airway obstruction within hours — the 'can't-miss' paediatric airway emergency and dangerous mimic of croup.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the single most important management principle of epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Do NOTHING that might upset the child until the airway is secured (no throat exam, no cannula, no lying flat) — the wrong move (e.g. a tongue depressor) can precipitate fatal obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How does epiglottitis contrast with croup in appearance?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Epiglottitis is the acutely toxic, drooling, still, silent child with a rapid onset and no cough; croup is common, viral, gradual, well-ish with a barking cough.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the vaccine story of epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Classically children aged 2–6, caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Since the Hib vaccine it has become rare in children; epidemiology shifted toward unvaccinated children and adults — now often Streptococcus pneumoniae, Strep pyogenes, and Staph aureus. Consider it in an incompletely immunised child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How does epiglottitis differ from croup in onset, cough and voice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Epiglottitis: rapid onset (hours), absent/minimal cough, muffled ('hot potato') voice. Croup: gradual onset (days after coryza), barking cough, hoarse voice.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How does epiglottitis differ from croup in drooling, posture and toxicity?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Epiglottitis: drooling (can't swallow), tripod/sitting forward and still, high fever and toxic. Croup: no drooling, variable posture, low-grade fever and looks well-ish.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the significance of stridor in epiglottitis vs croup?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: In epiglottitis stridor is soft and late (ominous — quiet stridor means near-obstruction); in croup it is harsh and prominent.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What are the '4 D's' of epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Dysphagia (can't swallow)
  • Drooling (saliva pools as swallowing is too painful)
  • Dysphonia (muffled, 'hot potato' voice — not hoarse)
  • Dyspnoea (respiratory distress).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What additional features occur in epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Rapid onset high fever, toxic/septic appearance, severe sore throat, the tripod position (leaning forward on hands, mouth open, tongue out), minimal/absent cough, and soft inspiratory stridor (a late, ominous sign); the child is anxious, still and quiet.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How is epiglottitis diagnosed, and what is forbidden?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Clinically, and securing the airway comes BEFORE any investigation. No throat examination, no venepuncture, no X-ray in a distressed child until the airway is safe. Definitive diagnosis is direct visualisation of a cherry-red, swollen epiglottis — but only in a controlled setting (theatre) by the airway team during intubation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the 'thumbprint sign'?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: A swollen epiglottis resembling a thumb on lateral neck X-ray — only obtained if stable, low suspicion, with airway support present; must not delay airway management. (Croup = steeple sign.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the first step in managing suspected epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Do NOT distress the child (keep them calm on the parent's lap, sitting upright, in their position of comfort; oxygen only if tolerated). Summon the airway team immediately — a 'call everyone' emergency: senior anaesthetist/ENT/paediatrician + ICU.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How is the airway secured in epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Controlled intubation in theatre (gas induction, ENT ready for emergency tracheostomy if intubation fails).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What antibiotics are given in epiglottitis, and when?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: AFTER the airway is secured: an IV third-generation cephalosporin covering Hib and Streptococcus — ceftriaxone 50–80 mg/kg once daily or cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6–8 hours — for a 7–10 day course, stepping down to oral (e.g. co-amoxiclav) once improving. Supportive: IV fluids, ICU monitoring; dexamethasone is often given to reduce oedema, though the evidence is limited.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How is epiglottitis prevented, and what prophylaxis is given to contacts?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Hib vaccination is why it is now rare. For a confirmed Hib case, rifampicin 20 mg/kg once daily (maximum 600 mg) for 4 days is given to household contacts — but only where the household includes a vulnerable contact: a child under 10 who is unimmunised or partially immunised, or an immunosuppressed person of any age (UKHSA).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What are the complications of epiglottitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Complete airway obstruction and death (the feared outcome)
  • epiglottic abscess
  • sepsis/bacteraemia
  • and rarely aspiration or secondary pneumonia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is laryngomalacia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Congenital softening/immaturity of the supraglottic cartilage so that the tissues above the vocal cords collapse inward during inspiration, producing chronic inspiratory stridor in an infant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: Why does laryngomalacia matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: It is the single commonest cause of stridor in infants (~60–75% of congenital stridor); it is the benign, chronic, 'well baby' end of the stridor differential; the key skill is recognising the reassuring pattern and knowing the small minority of red flags.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the framing of laryngomalacia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: 'Noisy but thriving' — an otherwise well baby, feeding and growing, just noisy on breathing in, which self-resolves; recognise the reassuring picture, don't mistake it for something dangerous, and spot the ~10–20% with severe features.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: Distinguish mild from severe laryngomalacia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Mild (majority): otherwise well, feeding and growing, inspiratory stridor with no distress → reassure + watchful waiting, resolves by ~18–24 months.
  • Severe (~10–20%): failure to thrive, feeding difficulty, respiratory distress/recession/cyanosis/apnoea → ENT referral → supraglottoplasty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What are the clinical features of laryngomalacia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: High-pitched inspiratory stridor from softened laryngeal cartilage collapsing on inspiration; positional/situational — worse when supine, feeding, crying/agitated, or with intercurrent URTI, and better prone; onset typically in the first 2 weeks of life, peaks ~6 months, then improves; otherwise well infant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What feeding-related symptoms occur in more significant laryngomalacia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Regurgitation, choking/coughing with feeds, slow feeds, difficulty coordinating suck-swallow-breathe → in severe cases poor weight gain/failure to thrive. Strong association with GORD (reflux and laryngomalacia coexist and aggravate each other).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What is the anatomical mechanism of laryngomalacia ('omega-shaped')?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Floppy/immature supraglottic structures — an omega-shaped (curled) epiglottis, short (tight) aryepiglottic folds, and redundant arytenoid mucosa that prolapse into the airway on inspiration.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How is laryngomalacia diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Often clinically in a well, thriving infant with classic positional stridor. Gold standard = flexible (awake) nasolaryngoscopy — visualises the dynamic supraglottic collapse and omega epiglottis; indicated if diagnosis unclear, severe or atypical. Consider a synchronous airway lesion (bronchoscopy) if severe/atypical. Airway fluoroscopy is not recommended.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: How is mild/most laryngomalacia managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Conservatively — reassure parents, watchful waiting; self-resolves before ~2 years; feeding support and upright/positional feeding help; treat coexisting GORD (positioning, feed thickening, anti-reflux medication).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What surgery is used for severe laryngomalacia, and when?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back: Supraglottoplasty (division of tight aryepiglottic folds ± trimming redundant mucosa) — for the ~10–20% with severe stridor + respiratory distress, failure to thrive from poor feeding, significant apnoea/hypoxia, or pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale from chronic obstruction; high success rate (~90%+). Tracheostomy rarely, for severe cases not suitable for/failing supraglottoplasty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What red flags suggest noisy breathing is NOT simple laryngomalacia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Failure to thrive/poor feeding, cyanosis or apnoeic episodes, severe recession/distress
  • biphasic stridor (inspiratory + expiratory — suggests a glottic/subglottic lesion like vocal cord palsy or subglottic stenosis)
  • stridor from birth that is severe/worsening or not improving after age 2
  • a weak/abnormal cry (think vocal cord pathology).
Any of these warrants ENT referral and nasolaryngoscopy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.front: What are the complications of severe untreated laryngomalacia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Stridor & Upper.back:
• Failure to thrive
  • feeding aspiration
  • obstructive sleep apnoea
  • and — from chronic hypoxia — pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What is supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: A narrow-complex tachyarrhythmia originating at or above the atrioventricular node — the commonest significant arrhythmia in children and the commonest cause of pathological tachycardia in infancy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: Why does SVT matter in infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: They can't report palpitations — they present with poor feeding, irritability, or, if prolonged, heart failure and shock; and the acute management is a clean, algorithmic emergency (vagal → adenosine → shock) gated by stability.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What is the single organising question in SVT management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Is the child stable or unstable? Everything downstream (vagal manoeuvres and adenosine vs immediate synchronised DC cardioversion) hangs on that assessment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What is the first diagnostic step in a child with a fast heart rate?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Distinguishing SVT from sinus tachycardia — they look superficially similar but mean completely different things.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: How is stable SVT managed (steps)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back:
• Step 1: vagal manoeuvres.
  • Step 2: IV adenosine.
Principle: try to convert non-invasively.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: How is unstable SVT (shock/decompensation) managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Step 1: immediate synchronised DC cardioversion. Adenosine only if it doesn't delay cardioversion (or while preparing). Principle: electricity first — don't waste time.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What signs indicate unstable SVT?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back:
• Hypotension,
  • poor perfusion,
  • altered consciousness,
  • heart failure/shock.
Stable SVT: alert, perfusing, no heart failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: How does the rate distinguish SVT from sinus tachycardia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: SVT is very fast: infants often >220, children >180. Sinus tachycardia is usually <220 infant / <180 child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: How do onset and rate variability distinguish SVT from sinus tachycardia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: SVT: abrupt onset/offset ('switch on/off'), fixed monotonous rate that doesn't vary with stimulation. Sinus tachycardia: gradual, varies with activity, beat-to-beat variability, settles with fluids/rest.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: How do P waves and history distinguish SVT from sinus tachycardia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: SVT: P waves absent/abnormal, hidden in QRS/T; no cause (or known SVT). Sinus tachycardia: normal P waves and axis; a reason present (fever, dehydration, pain, sepsis, blood loss). Both usually narrow QRS.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What should you do if there is an obvious cause and the rate varies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Treat the cause (it's sinus tachycardia), don't give adenosine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What is the commonest mechanism of paediatric SVT?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT) using an accessory pathway — the classic being Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW: delta wave + short PR on the resting/post-conversion ECG). AVNRT (re-entry within the AV node) is commoner in older children/adolescents. Both are AV-node-dependent, which is why node-blocking manoeuvres work.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: How does SVT present in infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Non-specific — poor feeding, irritability, pallor, tachypnoea, sweating; and if prolonged (hours) → heart failure/cardiogenic shock (SVT can be present a long time before it's noticed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: How does SVT present in older children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back:
• Palpitations,
  • chest discomfort,
  • dizziness,
  • 'racing heart',
  • sometimes syncope.
ECG: narrow-complex tachycardia, fixed rate, absent/abnormal P waves.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What investigations are used in SVT?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back:
• 12-lead ECG (confirm SVT, distinguish from sinus tachy, look for WPW);
  • continuous cardiac monitoring throughout treatment (record a rhythm strip during adenosine — diagnostic as the rhythm transiently blocks);
  • assess for heart failure/perfusion and reversible contributors (electrolytes, fever, drugs);
  • echocardiography for ventricular function/structural disease (especially if recurrent or in heart failure).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What are the universal first steps in acute SVT management (APLS)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back:
• ABC,
  • oxygen if hypoxaemic or shocked (titrated to saturations),
  • cardiac monitoring,
  • IV/intraosseous access.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What vagal manoeuvres are used in stable SVT?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back:
• Infants — the 'diving reflex' (a bag of iced water/ice pack applied briefly to the face, without obstructing the airway);
  • older children — Valsalva (blow through a syringe / modified Valsalva with leg-raise).
Do NOT use eyeball pressure (risks eye injury) or carotid sinus massage in children. Do them on the monitor with a rhythm strip running.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What is the adenosine regimen for stable SVT (APLS)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: If vagal fails → IV/intraosseous adenosine (rapid bolus into a large proximal vein + immediate saline flush): first dose 0.1 mg/kg (max 6 mg) → 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg) → a further 0.3 mg/kg (max 12 mg).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What should you warn about with adenosine, and what is its half-life?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Warn of brief flushing/chest tightness/'sense of doom'; very short half-life (<10 s). Ask about asthma first — use adenosine with caution in severe asthma, and consider cardioversion or an alternative such as amiodarone in severe asthma, sinus node disease, pre-excited atrial arrhythmias or a heart transplant (Resuscitation Council UK).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What if adenosine fails or SVT recurs?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Senior + paediatric cardiology; consider amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV (max 300 mg) — in a child with a pulse this must be given slowly with continuous ECG and BP monitoring, because a rapid bolus causes hypotension (BNFC).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: How is unstable SVT managed in detail?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back:
• Synchronised DC cardioversion without delay: 1 J/kg → 2 J/kg, considering up to 4 J/kg with expert help if unsuccessful, reassessing the pulse and signs of life after each shock, with sedation/analgesia unless the child is already unconscious (Resuscitation Council UK);
  • adenosine only if it doesn't delay cardioversion (e.g. while the defibrillator charges and IV access is in);
  • consider amiodarone 5 mg/kg before a third shock;
  • involve seniors/cardiology/PICU.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.front: What is the long-term management of paediatric SVT?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__SVT (paediatric.back: Many infants grow out of it; recurrent episodes may need prophylaxis (e.g. beta-blockers, or other antiarrhythmics under paediatric cardiology — in known WPW/pre-excitation avoid digoxin and verapamil, which can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway if atrial fibrillation develops). NEVER give IV verapamil to an infant — it has caused fatal cardiovascular collapse. Radiofrequency catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is curative for recurrent/refractory SVT in older children; teach parents age-appropriate vagal manoeuvres and when to seek help.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: When is the newborn blood-spot (Guthrie) test performed?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: On day 5 of life (acceptable range day 5–8), by a midwife via heel prick, once feeding is established.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Name the 10 conditions screened by the UK newborn blood spot.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism, and 7 inherited metabolic diseases: PKU, MCADD, maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), isovaleric acidaemia (IVA), glutaric aciduria type 1 (GA1), homocystinuria and tyrosinaemia type 1. Tyrosinaemia type 1 is the most recent addition and is not yet offered in all UK nations — Wales and Northern Ireland currently screen for 9.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Why must PKU be detected early, and what is the treatment?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Untreated PKU causes severe, irreversible intellectual disability. Early detection allows a low-phenylalanine diet, which prevents the neurological damage.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: An abnormal newborn blood-spot result — what does it mean and what happens next?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: It is only a positive SCREEN, not a diagnosis. It requires urgent confirmatory diagnostic testing and specialist referral before the condition is confirmed and treated.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Why is congenital hypothyroidism on the screening panel?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Untreated it causes irreversible neurodevelopmental delay ('cretinism'); early levothyroxine started after screen-detection prevents this harm.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: When must a transcutaneous bilirubinometer (TcB) reading be confirmed with a serum bilirubin (SBR)?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: When the baby is <24 hours old, <35 weeks gestation, unwell, or the TcB reads at/above the treatment threshold. TcB is also unreliable after phototherapy has started and at high bilirubin levels — use SBR in these situations.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: How is the serum bilirubin used to guide management of neonatal jaundice?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Plot the TOTAL SBR against the baby's postnatal age in HOURS on the NICE age- and gestation-specific threshold graph. It has a lower phototherapy line and a higher exchange-transfusion line; management depends on which line the value crosses, not the raw number.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Why is jaundice in the first 24 hours of life always significant?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: It is always pathological and a medical emergency → urgent SBR. Causes are haemolytic (rhesus/ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis) or sepsis. Never rely on TcB alone in this window.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: What is the key investigation in prolonged neonatal jaundice, and what serious diagnosis must be excluded?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Measure the conjugated (direct) bilirubin fraction ('split bilirubin'). A raised conjugated bilirubin with pale stools and dark urine suggests biliary atresia — refer urgently for Kasai portoenterostomy, ideally before ~8 weeks of age. Also consider congenital hypothyroidism, UTI and breast-milk jaundice.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: How does high unconjugated bilirubin harm the neonatal brain?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble, crosses the blood–brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia, causing kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy) → cerebral palsy and sensorineural deafness. Phototherapy and exchange transfusion prevent this.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: What is a skeletal survey and when is it performed?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: A standardised series of dedicated radiographs of the whole skeleton (multiple optimised views, NOT a single "babygram"), performed when physical abuse/NAI is suspected — typically in a child under 2 years — and reported by a paediatric radiologist.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Name three fracture patterns highly specific for non-accidental injury.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Metaphyseal corner/"bucket-handle" fractures (classic metaphyseal lesions, from twisting/pulling); posterior rib fractures (from chest squeezing/AP compression); and multiple fractures of different ages with no medical explanation. Any fracture in a non-mobile infant is also high concern.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Which combination of findings suggests abusive head trauma ("shaken baby")?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Retinal haemorrhages plus subdural haematoma. Arrange CT/MRI head and an ophthalmology assessment.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: What medical mimics of NAI should be excluded, and how?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Osteogenesis imperfecta, rickets/osteopenia of prematurity, and copper deficiency. Investigate with bone profile (Ca, PO₄, ALP), vitamin D, and expert radiology review — but a mimic does not exclude coexisting abuse.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Why and when is a follow-up skeletal survey performed?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: A repeat survey at ~11–14 days increases fracture detection — healing changes (callus, periosteal reaction) make initially subtle or occult fractures visible.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: What are the four NIPE screens and the referral each triggers?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Eyes: absent/white red reflex → urgent ophthalmology (cataract/retinoblastoma). Heart: murmur/absent femoral pulses/cyanosis → echo + cardiology. Hips: Barlow/Ortolani → hip USS + orthopaedics. Testes: undescended → refer (orchidopexy by ~6 months). Done <72h and at 6–8 weeks.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Which babies get a hip ultrasound even with a normal examination?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: Those with DDH risk factors: breech ≥36 weeks, a first-degree family history (± first-born girl) → selective hip USS at ~6 weeks. USS is used <4.5–6 months (before ossification); X-ray thereafter.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.front: Outline the newborn hearing screening pathway.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Sc.back: OAE first → if no clear response, AABR → a fail goes to audiology for diagnostic ABR. High-risk infants (NICU >48h, family history, congenital infection) go straight to AABR.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is the diagnostic investigation of choice for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and the key ultrasound criteria?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Ultrasound. Diagnostic thresholds: pyloric muscle wall thickness >3-4 mm and pyloric canal length >15-17 mm, with a non-relaxing pylorus and the 'target'/donut sign in cross-section (and 'cervix' sign longitudinally).

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is the classic biochemical derangement in pyloric stenosis and why?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, caused by loss of gastric HCl in the vomit (with renal K+ loss); late there may be a paradoxical aciduria as kidneys retain H+ to conserve Na+/K+.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: Describe the classic demographic and clinical presentation of pyloric stenosis.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Typically a firstborn male, 2-8 weeks old (peak 4-6 weeks), often with a family history. Non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds; the baby stays hungry ('hungry vomiter'). Signs: visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis and a palpable 'olive' mass in the RUQ/epigastrium (best felt during a test feed), plus weight loss/dehydration.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: Outline the management sequence for pyloric stenosis.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: It is NOT an immediate surgical emergency. First resuscitate and correct fluid and electrolyte/acid-base derangement (IV fluids, correct hypochloraemia, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis). Then definitive surgery: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: A vomiting infant has BILIOUS (green) vomit. Is this pyloric stenosis?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: No. Pyloric stenosis causes NON-bilious vomiting. Bilious/green vomiting signals intestinal obstruction, particularly malrotation with volvulus, which is a true surgical emergency requiring urgent assessment and upper GI contrast study.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is the first-line investigation for suspected intussusception, and what two classic signs does it show?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Ultrasound. It shows the 'target'/donut sign (concentric rings) in transverse section and the 'pseudokidney' sign longitudinally.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: Why is the air/contrast enema described as 'both diagnostic and therapeutic'?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: It confirms the diagnosis on fluoroscopy AND reduces the intussusception by pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic (contrast) pressure. Success ~75-90%; air enema is preferred (higher success, lower perforation risk).

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: Name the classic clinical triad of intussusception and state which feature is a late sign.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Colicky abdominal pain (infant draws up legs, screams, settles between episodes), a sausage-shaped RUQ mass, and redcurrant-jelly (blood + mucus) stool. The redcurrant-jelly stool is the LATE sign.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What are the contraindications to enema reduction in intussusception?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Peritonitis, perforation (free air), or a shocked/unstable child. These require resuscitation and surgery, not an enema. A failed enema also proceeds to surgery.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: In an older child or with recurrent intussusception, what should you actively look for?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: A pathological lead point, e.g. Meckel's diverticulum (classic), a polyp, Henoch-Schonlein purpura (bowel-wall haematoma), or lymphoma.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for Hirschsprung's disease, and what are the classic histological findings?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Rectal suction biopsy. Histology shows absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses, hypertrophied/thickened nerve fibres, and increased acetylcholinesterase (AChE) staining.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is the underlying pathophysiology of Hirschsprung's disease?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Congenital absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) due to failed craniocaudal neural-crest cell migration. The aganglionic segment (most often rectosigmoid) cannot relax, causing a functional obstruction.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: Give the classic neonatal presentation of Hirschsprung's disease and its key associations.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting and neonatal bowel obstruction (or later chronic constipation/failure to thrive). Associations: Down syndrome, male sex (~4:1), family history.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What do the contrast enema and anorectal manometry show in Hirschsprung's disease?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Contrast enema: narrowed distal aganglionic segment with a transition zone to dilated proximal ganglionic bowel. Anorectal manometry: absent recto-anal inhibitory reflex (internal anal sphincter fails to relax).

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) and why does it matter?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: A life-threatening emergency: fever, abdominal distension, explosive/bloody diarrhoea and sepsis. Needs urgent resuscitation, IV antibiotics and rectal decompression. It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in Hirschsprung's.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is a Meckel's diverticulum, and from what embryological structure does it arise?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: The commonest congenital anomaly of the GI tract; a TRUE diverticulum (all bowel wall layers) on the ANTIMESENTERIC border of the ileum, arising from the persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: State the "Rule of 2s" for Meckel's diverticulum.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: ~2% of population; ~2 feet proximal to the ileocaecal valve; ~2 inches long; ~2% become symptomatic; often presents before age 2; male:female ~2:1; may contain 2 ectopic tissues (gastric and pancreatic).

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: Why does Tc-99m pertechnetate localise a bleeding Meckel's diverticulum?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Tc-99m pertechnetate is taken up by gastric mucosa, including the ECTOPIC gastric mucosa within the diverticulum. This produces a focal hot spot (classically RLQ) appearing simultaneously with the stomach. The same ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid, causing ileal ulceration and bleeding.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: How can the sensitivity of a Meckel's scan be improved?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Pre-medication that enhances pertechnetate uptake/retention by gastric mucosa — an H2-receptor antagonist (e.g. ranitidine) or pentagastrin.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is the definitive management of a symptomatic Meckel's diverticulum?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Surgical resection — diverticulectomy or segmental small-bowel resection (segmental resection preferred if broad-based or with adjacent ileal ulceration), after adequate resuscitation.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for malrotation with suspected midgut volvulus?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: An upper GI contrast study. It shows the position of the duodenojejunal (DJ) flexure — normally left of the midline at the level of the duodenal bulb/pylorus; abnormally placed (right of midline/low) in malrotation; with a 'corkscrew'/Z-shaped spiralling duodenum or duodenal 'beak' in volvulus.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: A 3-week-old presents with sudden bilious (green) vomiting. What is the diagnosis until proven otherwise, and why is it urgent?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Malrotation with midgut volvulus. It is a time-critical surgical emergency — the midgut twists around the narrow SMA-based mesentery, causing closed-loop obstruction and ischaemia. Delay leads to bowel necrosis and short-gut syndrome. Never dismiss bilious vomiting as reflux.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What ultrasound findings support a diagnosis of midgut volvulus?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: An inverted SMA/SMV relationship (SMV lying to the left of the SMA) and the 'whirlpool sign' — swirling of the mesentery and SMV around the SMA. Ultrasound is supportive but the upper GI contrast study is definitive.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What are the key steps of Ladd's procedure?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Untwist the volvulus (anti-clockwise), divide Ladd's bands, broaden/widen the mesenteric base, and perform an appendicectomy. Preceded by fluid resuscitation, NG decompression and cross-match.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: Anatomically, why does malrotation predispose to volvulus?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Failure of normal 270-degree midgut rotation and fixation leaves a short, narrow mesenteric pedicle. This narrow base lets the whole midgut twist around the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) axis, producing volvulus. Ladd's bands can additionally cause duodenal obstruction.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What are the AXR findings in NEC and the management?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: AXR: pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, dilated fixed loops; perforation = free air/Rigler’s/football sign. Manage: NBM, NG decompression, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluids/TPN, serial AXR; laparotomy if perforation or deterioration.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: A baby is jaundiced beyond 2 weeks with pale stools — what test and what surgery, by when?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Split the bilirubin: a conjugated rise suggests biliary atresia (USS triangular cord sign; HIDA shows uptake but no bowel excretion). Treat with Kasai portoenterostomy by ~8 weeks — outcomes fall after 60–90 days.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.front: What does a "double bubble" on AXR indicate, and its key association?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric.back: Duodenal atresia (gas in stomach + proximal duodenum, gasless distal abdomen), strongly associated with Down syndrome. Manage with NG decompression, fluids and duodenoduodenostomy.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Which imaging modality is the investigation of choice for suspected DDH in an infant under ~6 months, and why?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Ultrasound using the Graf technique. Under ~4.5–6 months the femoral head is still largely cartilaginous and not yet ossified, so it is poorly seen on X-ray but well visualised on USS (with no ionising radiation).

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What do the Graf alpha and beta angles measure, and what is the normal alpha angle?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: The alpha angle measures the depth of the bony acetabular roof (normal ≥60°; a low/shallow angle indicates dysplasia). The beta angle measures the cartilaginous roof/labrum and increases as the hip subluxes.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Name the four line/index constructions assessed on an AP pelvis X-ray for DDH.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: 1) Hilgenreiner's line (horizontal through triradiate cartilages); 2) Perkin's line (vertical at lateral acetabular edge — nucleus should sit in the lower-inner quadrant); 3) Shenton's line (arc from obturator foramen to medial femoral neck — disrupted in dislocation); 4) Acetabular index (increased in dysplasia).

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Differentiate the Barlow and Ortolani tests.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Barlow: adduct the hip with posterior pressure to dislocate a dislocatable hip. Ortolani: abduct the hip with anterior lift to relocate an already-dislocated hip. (Barlow dislocates, Ortolani relocates.)

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What is the first-line treatment for DDH diagnosed under ~6 months, and what does it do?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: A Pavlik harness, which holds the hips flexed and abducted to keep the femoral head reduced and deepen the acetabulum. Failed harness or older/late presentation requires closed/open reduction with a spica cast, and delayed cases may need pelvic or femoral osteotomy.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Which two urinary metabolites are the biochemical hallmark of neuroblastoma, and what are they derived from?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) — from noradrenaline/adrenaline — and HVA (homovanillic acid) — from dopamine. Both are raised catecholamine metabolites, typically measured as a spot urine catecholamine:creatinine ratio.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What is neuroblastoma, in terms of tissue origin and epidemiology?
