investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: A malignancy of neural crest (sympathetic nervous system) origin, usually arising in the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain. It is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood and the commonest cancer of infancy, typically in children under 5 years.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Name three imaging/staging investigations used in neuroblastoma beyond urinary catecholamines.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: USS/CT/MRI abdomen (calcified suprarenal mass, midline crossing, vascular encasement); mIBG scan (uptake by tumour and metastases); and bone marrow biopsy for staging. Tissue biopsy (small round blue cells, rosettes) confirms the diagnosis.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Which genetic marker is a key adverse prognostic factor in neuroblastoma?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: MYCN amplification — it indicates high-risk disease and guides more intensive treatment.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Why should periorbital bruising in a young child not be automatically attributed to trauma?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Periorbital bruising and proptosis ('raccoon eyes') can result from orbital/skull metastases of neuroblastoma. A child with an abdominal mass, bone pain/limp or periorbital bruising needs urgent paediatric oncology referral, urinary VMA/HVA and imaging.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Which 5 parameters make up the Westley croup score?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Level of consciousness, cyanosis, stridor, air entry, and retractions (chest wall recession). Total maxes at 17.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: How is the Westley score interpreted into severity bands?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: ≤2 = mild; 3–7 = moderate; 8–11 = severe; ≥12 = impending respiratory failure.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What is the first-line drug given to essentially all children with croup, and at what dose?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (alternatives: prednisolone or nebulised budesonide) — regardless of severity.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: When is nebulised adrenaline used in croup, and what must you watch for afterwards?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: For moderate/severe croup or poor response to steroids (plus oxygen and admission). Its effect wears off in ~2 hours, so observe for rebound before discharge.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Which clinical picture should make you suspect epiglottitis rather than croup?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: A toxic, drooling child sitting in a tripod position with a soft muffled voice, soft stridor and NO barking cough. It is an airway emergency — keep calm, do not examine the throat, call anaesthetics/ENT.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What is the most common causative organism and typical age for croup?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Parainfluenza virus; peak age 6 months–3 years, typically in autumn. It causes subglottic oedema (laryngotracheobronchitis).

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What are the three components of the West syndrome triad?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: (1) Epileptic/infantile spasms, (2) hypsarrhythmia on EEG, and (3) developmental arrest or regression (loss of previously acquired skills).

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Describe the classic spasms of West syndrome.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Sudden, brief (1–2 second), symmetrical spasms — classically flexor 'salaam'/jack-knife (head and trunk flexion with arm extension/abduction) — occurring in clusters, often on waking. Frequently misdiagnosed as colic, reflux or startle.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What EEG pattern confirms infantile spasms, and how is yield increased?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Hypsarrhythmia — a chaotic, high-amplitude (>200 µV), disorganised pattern of asynchronous slow waves with multifocal spikes/sharp waves. A sleep, prolonged or video EEG increases yield; a spasm often shows an electrodecremental response.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Which condition is classically associated with infantile spasms, and how does it change management?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Tuberous sclerosis (look for ash-leaf macules). It makes vigabatrin the first-line treatment of choice.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What are the first-line UK treatments for infantile spasms and why does timing matter?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: High-dose oral prednisolone or ACTH, and vigabatrin (vigabatrin first-line if tuberous sclerosis). Early treatment improves developmental outcome; prognosis is often guarded and may evolve into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Name the four domains assessed in child developmental review.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: (1) Gross motor; (2) Fine motor & vision; (3) Speech, language & hearing; (4) Social, emotional & behavioural. Global developmental delay = significant delay in ≥2 domains; correct for prematurity up to ~2 years.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Which developmental finding is a red flag at ANY age?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Loss of previously acquired skills (developmental regression) — always warrants urgent referral, regardless of age.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: Which structured tools are central to a NICE ASD assessment?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: ADOS (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule) for structured observation ± ADI-R (Autism Diagnostic Interview – Revised) for developmental history. M-CHAT is a toddler screen. Diagnosis is multidisciplinary and multi-informant — no blood test.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What rating scales inform ADHD assessment, and across how many settings must symptoms be present?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Conners' rating scales and the SDQ (Strengths & Difficulties Questionnaire), completed by parents AND teachers. Symptoms must be present in ≥2 settings (e.g. home AND school), with impairment and onset before age 12.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: List classic red-flag milestone cut-offs in UK developmental surveillance.
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Not smiling by 8 weeks; not sitting unsupported by 9 months; not walking by 18 months; no words by 18 months; persistent hand preference before 18 months; and any loss of skills at any age.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: How does a bone-age X-ray distinguish constitutional delay from pathological short stature?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: Delayed bone age with a NORMAL height velocity (often with a family history of late development) = constitutional delay of growth and puberty → reassure/observe. A low height velocity / crossing centiles down is pathological → investigate (thyroid, GH, coeliac, chronic disease) and refer.

investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.front: What is the management of a Graf IIa (immature) hip in a baby under 3 months?
investigations__PAEDIATRICS__Other Paedi.back: It is often physiological at this age → repeat ultrasound surveillance rather than an immediate Pavlik harness; treat only if it persists or worsens.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 4-year-old collapses with wheeze, stridor and urticaria minutes after eating a peanut. What is the immediate priority?
options: IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh
IM adrenaline into the deltoid once IV access is in
IV chlorphenamine followed by IV hydrocortisone
Nebulised salbutamol for the wheeze, then reassess
High-flow oxygen and an IV crystalloid bolus
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Sudden airway and breathing compromise after a likely allergen makes this anaphylaxis. IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the immediate priority. Oxygen, fluids and bronchodilators are adjuncts that follow it, and the deltoid is not used because absorption there is less reliable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 3-year-old develops stridor, wheeze and hypotension minutes after eating cashew nut. What dose of intramuscular adrenaline should be given?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: A 3-year-old falls in the 6 months to 6 years band: 150 micrograms, which is 0.15 mL of 1:1000, IM into the anterolateral thigh. 100 micrograms is used in infants under 6 months; the larger doses belong to older age bands. 1:10,000 is an intravenous preparation and is not used for IM treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: An 8-year-old with known peanut allergy develops wheeze, a hoarse voice and falling oxygen saturations at a party. What dose of intramuscular adrenaline should be given?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: An 8-year-old falls in the 6 to 12 years band: 300 micrograms, which is 0.30 mL of 1:1000, IM into the anterolateral thigh. The smaller doses belong to younger age bands, and 1:10,000 is an intravenous preparation not used for IM treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 9-year-old weighing 32 kg is being discharged after an episode of food-triggered anaphylaxis. Which adrenaline auto-injector strength should be prescribed?
options: A 1 mg/1 mL adrenaline ampoule with a syringe
A salbutamol inhaler with an oral antihistamine
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Auto-injectors are prescribed by weight rather than age: the 150 microgram device is used from about 7.5 kg to 25 kg and the 300 microgram device above that, so a 32 kg child needs the 300 microgram strength. An ampoule and syringe is not a substitute for a device a carer or school can use under pressure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 4-year-old given IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis still has stridor and hypotension. How soon should the same IM dose be repeated?
options: After 5 minutes, into the other thigh
After 1 minute, into the other thigh
After 15 minutes, if there is still no improvement
After 10 minutes, once IV access is established
Not until a senior clinician has arrived
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: After 5 minutes, into the other thigh
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: If there is no improvement, the same IM dose is repeated after 5 minutes. Waiting longer, or waiting for IV access or for senior help to arrive, delays the one intervention that reverses the airway, breathing and circulation problem.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A child develops symptoms within minutes of eating shellfish. Which finding distinguishes anaphylaxis from a mild or moderate allergic reaction?
options: Lip and eyelid angio-oedema without stridor
Vomiting and abdominal pain after the meal
Symptom onset within minutes of exposure
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Anaphylaxis is defined by a sudden airway, breathing or circulation problem. Skin and mucosal changes usually accompany it but are not required, and rapid onset is common to both mild reactions and anaphylaxis, so neither separates them.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A child has widespread urticaria and itching after a bee sting but normal breathing, a normal voice and stable observations. What is the most appropriate management?
options: IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh now
An IV adrenaline infusion with critical care input
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Skin-only symptoms with no airway, breathing or circulation compromise are a mild to moderate allergic reaction, managed with an antihistamine and a period of observation. Adrenaline by any route is reserved for anaphylaxis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: Under current Resuscitation Council UK guidance, which pair of drugs is NO LONGER given routinely in the acute management of anaphylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Routine chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone have been removed from the acute algorithm because neither treats the airway, breathing or circulation problem. A non-sedating oral antihistamine may still be used afterwards for residual skin symptoms, and bronchodilators are still used for persistent wheeze.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 6-year-old with anaphylaxis is pale, mottled, tachycardic and hypotensive. How should she be positioned while adrenaline is being given?
options: Lie her flat and raise her legs, avoiding sudden posture change
Sit her fully upright in the bed to reduce her work of breathing
Place her in the left lateral position to improve venous return
Sit her forward in the tripod position while oxygen is applied
Nurse her prone with the head of the bed tilted downwards
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: Lie her flat and raise her legs, avoiding sudden posture change
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: With circulatory compromise, lie the child flat and raise the legs to maintain venous return. A sudden change to sitting or standing can precipitate fatal cardiac arrest. Sitting up is reserved for the child whose breathing is the dominant problem.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 20 kg child with anaphylaxis remains hypotensive after IM adrenaline. Which intravenous fluid regimen is appropriate?
options: An isotonic crystalloid bolus of 10 mL/kg
An isotonic crystalloid bolus of 40 mL/kg
A human albumin solution bolus of 20 mL/kg
A 2 mL/kg bolus of 10% glucose intravenously
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: An isotonic crystalloid bolus of 10 mL/kg
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: For circulatory compromise in a child, give an isotonic crystalloid bolus of 10 mL/kg and reassess, repeating and titrating to response. Colloids including albumin are not first line and can themselves trigger a reaction; 10% glucose is the bolus for hypoglycaemia; maintenance-rate fluids will not restore circulating volume.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 7-year-old remains hypotensive with stridor despite two appropriate doses of IM adrenaline. What is this, and what should happen next?
options: Refractory anaphylaxis — start an IV adrenaline infusion with expert help
Refractory anaphylaxis — give a third IM dose and continue observing on the ward
Refractory anaphylaxis — give IV adrenaline 1:10,000 as a single bolus
A biphasic reaction — give IV hydrocortisone and chlorphenamine now
A vasovagal episode — lie her flat and reassure the parents
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: Refractory anaphylaxis — start an IV adrenaline infusion with expert help
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Anaphylaxis not responding to two appropriate IM doses is refractory anaphylaxis. It needs an IV adrenaline INFUSION, given with senior or critical care expertise and continuous monitoring — not an IV bolus, which risks arrhythmia, and not a switch away from adrenaline.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 10-year-old treated successfully for peanut anaphylaxis is being observed on the ward. Which pattern describes a biphasic reaction?
options: Symptoms recur hours later without any further allergen exposure
Symptoms recur within minutes of a second exposure to the allergen
Skin symptoms persist for several days after the reaction settles
A reaction involving both the skin and the gastrointestinal tract
A second, milder reaction occurring on re-exposure weeks later
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: Symptoms recur hours later without any further allergen exposure
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: A biphasic reaction is recurrence of anaphylaxis hours after the initial episode with no further exposure to the allergen. It is the reason a period of observation follows treatment before discharge.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: Which investigation, taken as timed samples around an acute episode, supports a diagnosis of anaphylaxis?
options: Serum tryptase taken 48 hours after the episode
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Timed mast cell tryptase supports the diagnosis by demonstrating mast cell degranulation, but the samples must be taken around the episode, not days later. In children under 16 it is only indicated where the trigger is venom, a drug, or idiopathic — it is often normal in food-triggered paediatric anaphylaxis (NICE). Anaphylaxis remains a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 5-year-old is ready for discharge after treatment for food-triggered anaphylaxis. What should be arranged before she goes home?
options: Two adrenaline auto-injectors with a written allergy action plan
One adrenaline auto-injector with a written allergy action plan
Two adrenaline auto-injectors and a 3-day course of prednisolone
A 4-week course of a non-sedating oral antihistamine and review
Urgent skin-prick testing before any auto-injector is prescribed
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: Two adrenaline auto-injectors with a written allergy action plan
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Discharge with two adrenaline auto-injectors — a spare covers a misfire or a needed second dose — plus device training for child, carers and school, a written allergy action plan, trigger avoidance advice and referral to a paediatric allergy service. Steroid courses are not routinely required, and allergy testing is arranged in clinic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: Which group of triggers accounts for the largest share of anaphylaxis episodes in UK children?
options: Foods such as cow's milk, egg, peanut and tree nuts
Insect venom from wasp and bee stings
Natural rubber latex in gloves and medical devices
Iodinated radiocontrast media used in imaging
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: Foods such as cow's milk, egg, peanut and tree nuts
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Foods are the leading trigger in children — cow's milk, egg, peanut, tree nuts, sesame, fish and shellfish. Venom, drugs, latex and contrast media all cause anaphylaxis but account for far fewer paediatric episodes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A 6-year-old stung by a wasp develops stridor and hypotension with no rash, and responds fully to one dose of IM adrenaline within minutes. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Admit her under a paediatric medical team for observation
Discharge once her observations have been normal for an hour
Discharge with an oral antihistamine and GP review tomorrow
Give a second IM dose of adrenaline before she is discharged
Start an IV adrenaline infusion as a precaution
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: Admit her under a paediatric medical team for observation
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Every child under 16 given emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis is admitted under a paediatric medical team (NICE), because symptoms can return after an apparently complete response. The absence of a rash does not make the episode milder — skin changes are absent in up to about a fifth of cases.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: You are drawing up adrenaline for intramuscular injection in a child with anaphylaxis. Which preparation should you use?
options: Adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) from a 1 mL ampoule
Adrenaline 1:10,000 in a 10 mL prefilled syringe
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: Adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) from a 1 mL ampoule
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis uses 1:1000, that is 1 mg/mL, drawn from a 1 mL ampoule or delivered by auto-injector. More dilute preparations exist for other purposes — 1:10,000 for intravenous use, and 1:200,000 combined with local anaesthetic for infiltration — and none is a substitute for IM 1:1000.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.question: A child develops anaphylaxis part-way through an intravenous antibiotic infusion. What should you do about the trigger?
options: Stop the infusion, but do not let this delay IM adrenaline
Stop the infusion and confirm which drug it was before giving adrenaline
Stop the infusion and flush the line through before giving adrenaline
Stop the infusion and give IV chlorphenamine while adrenaline is drawn up
Continue the infusion so that the antibiotic course is completed
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.answer: Stop the infusion, but do not let this delay IM adrenaline
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Anap.explanation: Remove or stop the trigger where feasible — stop a drug or blood infusion, brush off a stinger — but do not delay IM adrenaline to do it. Adrenaline is the intervention that reverses the airway, breathing and circulation problem.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 13-year-old boy is the shortest in his class and has not started puberty. His father was also a 'late developer'. Examination is normal and his bone age is delayed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Undiagnosed coeliac disease with faltering growth
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.answer: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: A well boy with short stature, delayed puberty and a family history of late development is the classic picture of constitutional delay — a benign variant reaching a normal final adult height. Familial short stature would track on target for the family with normal pubertal timing; the others would usually give abnormal examination or growth findings.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 14-year-old girl is on the 0.4th centile for height and has no breast development. Her LH and FSH are both elevated. Which single investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
options: Karyotype (chromosome analysis on a blood sample)
Serum IGF-1 with a growth hormone stimulation test
MRI of the pituitary and hypothalamus
Pelvic ultrasound to assess the uterus and ovaries
Short Synacthen test for adrenal insufficiency
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.answer: Karyotype (chromosome analysis on a blood sample)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: High LH and FSH mean the pituitary is working but the gonads are not — hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, i.e. primary gonadal failure. In a short girl this should prompt chromosome analysis. A pituitary or growth-hormone cause would give low, not high, gonadotrophins.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A boy's mother is 160 cm tall and his father is 176 cm. What is his mid-parental (target) height?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Mid-parental height for a boy = (mother's + father's height)/2 + 7 cm = (160 + 176)/2 + 7 = 168 + 7 = 175 cm. For a girl you subtract 7 cm instead. 168 cm is the midpoint with the correction forgotten, and 161 cm applies the girls' formula.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 9-year-old girl has had breast development and a growth spurt over 6 months, and her bone age is reported as 12 years. Which other condition characteristically ADVANCES the bone age in the same way?
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Think in two groups: conditions where skeletal maturation lags behind chronological age, and conditions driven by sex-steroid or androgen excess where it runs ahead. Only one of the options offered belongs to the second group.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 6-year-old girl develops breast tissue and pubic hair. Beyond what age would puberty be considered NOT precocious in girls?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Precocious puberty is defined as secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls. The corresponding cut-off in boys is 9 years, and 13 years is the age beyond which absent puberty in a girl is called delayed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 7-year-old boy has developed pubic hair, testicular enlargement and a growth spurt over 6 months. His bone age is 12 years and his basal LH is in the pubertal range. Which investigation is most important next?
options: MRI of the brain with pituitary views
Testicular ultrasound for a Leydig cell tumour
Repeat left-wrist X-ray for bone age
Thyroid function tests and thyroid antibodies
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.answer: MRI of the brain with pituitary views
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Testicular enlargement with a pubertal basal LH indicates gonadotrophin-dependent (central) precocious puberty. In boys this is far more often pathological than in girls, so neuroimaging to look for a CNS lesion is the priority. The other tests address peripheral or secondary causes that this biochemistry has already made unlikely.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: How is central (gonadotrophin-dependent) precocious puberty treated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Central precocious puberty is driven by premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, so continuous GnRH analogue therapy downregulates the axis and halts progression, helping preserve final adult height. The other agents treat peripheral causes or different conditions altogether.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A child has peripheral (gonadotrophin-independent) precocious puberty with café-au-lait patches and bony lesions. What is the likely syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: The triad of peripheral precocious puberty, café-au-lait patches and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is McCune-Albright syndrome. Neurofibromatosis and tuberous sclerosis give skin lesions without this endocrine picture; CAH and an adrenal tumour cause peripheral precocious puberty but not the bone lesions.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: Beyond what age is puberty considered delayed in a boy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Delayed puberty in a boy means no secondary sexual characteristics (testicular volume under 4 mL) by 14 years. The corresponding threshold in girls is 13 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A teenager with delayed puberty is found to have low LH/FSH and anosmia. What is the diagnosis?
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Anorexia nervosa with a low body weight
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Low LH/FSH with anosmia is Kallmann syndrome — isolated GnRH deficiency with failure of olfactory development. The other hypogonadotrophic causes listed do not cause anosmia, and Klinefelter syndrome gives HIGH gonadotrophins from primary testicular failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A boy with delayed puberty has small firm testes, tall stature and gynaecomastia, with high LH/FSH. What is the likely karyotype?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Tall stature, small firm testes, gynaecomastia and high LH/FSH in a boy is Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY — primary testicular failure, so gonadotrophins rise. Note the correct notation for Turner syndrome is 45,X (monosomy X), not 45,XO.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: Which single statement best explains why congenital hypothyroidism is included in the newborn blood-spot screening programme?
options: It is a preventable cause of intellectual disability if treated early
It is the commonest endocrine disorder of childhood in the UK
It causes a life-threatening salt-losing crisis in the first weeks of life
Most cases are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
Untreated disease leads to irreversible cardiomyopathy in infancy
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.answer: It is a preventable cause of intellectual disability if treated early
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Congenital hypothyroidism is usually subtle at birth but causes irreversible neurodevelopmental damage if missed, and early levothyroxine prevents it entirely — the classic case for pre-symptomatic screening. The salt-losing crisis belongs to CAH, which is not on the UK panel; thyroid dysgenesis is usually sporadic rather than inherited.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: What is the commonest cause of congenital hypothyroidism in the UK?
options: Maternal antithyroid drug treatment in pregnancy
Severe maternal and neonatal iodine deficiency
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Thyroid dysgenesis — an absent or ectopic gland — accounts for most UK cases. All the others are genuine causes but are much less common here; iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide but not in an iodine-replete population.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: Which set of features suggests untreated congenital hypothyroidism in an infant?
options: Prolonged jaundice, constipation, hypotonia and a large tongue
Diarrhoea, tachycardia, irritability and poor weight gain
Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and heavy ketonuria
Marked hypotonia, a weak cry and poor feeding requiring tube feeds
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.answer: Prolonged jaundice, constipation, hypotonia and a large tongue
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Untreated congenital hypothyroidism slows everything: prolonged jaundice, constipation, hypotonia, macroglossia, coarse features, an umbilical hernia and a large posterior fontanelle. The second set suggests neonatal thyrotoxicosis, the third a salt-losing adrenal crisis, and the fourth neonatal diabetes; the last shares hypotonia and poor feeding but lacks the jaundice, constipation and macroglossia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A newborn girl has ambiguous genitalia. At 10 days old she becomes shocked with vomiting; bloods show low sodium, high potassium and hypoglycaemia. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Virilisation of a girl plus a salt-losing crisis in the first weeks is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Pyloric stenosis produces the opposite picture (hypochloraemic alkalosis with a LOW potassium), and adrenal haemorrhage could cause the crisis but would not virilise the genitalia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 9-day-old infant with ambiguous genitalia is being investigated. Which biochemical finding would confirm 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the diagnostic marker of 21-hydroxylase deficiency — the enzyme block causes the precursor to accumulate. Aldosterone is low and renin high in salt-losers, and 11-deoxycortisol is the marker of the rarer 11-beta-hydroxylase form.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 12-day-old boy is admitted floppy and mottled with a capillary refill of 4 seconds after three days of vomiting. Sodium is 118 mmol/L, potassium 7.2 mmol/L and glucose 1.9 mmol/L. What is the immediate management?
options: IV hydrocortisone, IV 0.9% saline and glucose
IV 0.9% saline followed by oral hydrocortisone
Oral fludrocortisone and oral salt supplements
IV insulin with dextrose to lower the potassium
IV calcium gluconate and nebulised salbutamol
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.answer: IV hydrocortisone, IV 0.9% saline and glucose
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: This is a salt-losing adrenal crisis. Give IV hydrocortisone (IM if there is no IV access — do not delay while cannulating) with IV 0.9% saline and glucose, and treat on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for results. The oral routes are far too slow in a shocked infant, and treating the potassium alone leaves the underlying cortisol deficiency uncorrected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 3-year-old girl with salt-losing 21-hydroxylase deficiency is well and growing along the 25th centile. What is her long-term maintenance treatment?
options: Prednisolone combined with a GnRH analogue
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Salt-losers need both a glucocorticoid and a mineralocorticoid, with salt supplements in infancy. Hydrocortisone alone is the simple-virilising (non-salt-losing) regimen and would leave her at risk of a crisis; dexamethasone is avoided in growing children because it suppresses growth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 7-year-old boy with late-diagnosed CAH is on the 91st centile for height, but the team warns that his final adult height is likely to be below average. What is the explanation?
options: Excess androgens advance bone age and cause early epiphyseal fusion
Androgens accelerate growth velocity but delay closure of the epiphyses
Chronic hypercortisolaemia blunts the pubertal growth spurt
Oestrogen deficiency prevents the pubertal growth spurt occurring
Persistently raised ACTH directly inhibits long-bone growth
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.answer: Excess androgens advance bone age and cause early epiphyseal fusion
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Excess adrenal androgens drive an early growth spurt but also advance skeletal maturation, so the epiphyses fuse early and growth stops sooner — tall as a child, short as an adult. In untreated CAH cortisol is low, not high.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.question: A 9-year-old boy is on the 2nd centile for height with a BMI on the 91st centile and a height velocity of 3 cm/year. He has taken high-dose oral and inhaled corticosteroids for severe asthma for two years. Which diagnosis does this pattern most suggest?
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Endo.explanation: Short and overweight with a poor height velocity points to an endocrine cause rather than undernutrition — and the steroid history makes iatrogenic Cushing's the answer here. Hypothyroidism gives the same short-and-overweight pattern and is the main differential; malabsorption and constitutional delay would not cause a raised BMI.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: Brachial plexus birth injuries are classified by which factor, which predicts the deformity?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Brachial plexus birth injuries are classified by the NERVE ROOTS involved, and the root level predicts the deformity: upper roots (C5-6) give Erb's palsy ('waiter's tip'), lower roots (C8-T1) give Klumpke's (claw hand).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: What is the general prognosis of brachial plexus birth injuries?
options: Most recover with physiotherapy; refer early, with surgical assessment at ~3 months
Most require immediate surgical nerve grafting
They never recover any useful function
They always cause permanent complete paralysis
They resolve completely within 24 hours of birth
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: Most recover with physiotherapy; refer early, with surgical assessment at ~3 months
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Most brachial plexus birth injuries recover spontaneously with physiotherapy. Refer early to a specialist brachial plexus service and physiotherapy; failure to recover by around 3 months triggers assessment for nerve surgery. They are associated with shoulder dystocia and large babies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: A newborn after a delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia has one arm held adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended and forearm pronated ('waiter's tip'). Which nerve roots are injured?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: The 'waiter's tip' posture is Erb's palsy, from injury to the upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) - the commonest birth plexus injury, classically after shoulder dystocia. C8-T1 injury causes Klumpke's (claw hand).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: Which reflex finding helps distinguish Erb's palsy from Klumpke's palsy?
options: Grasp reflex is absent in Erb's
Both reflexes are lost in Erb's
Grasp is PRESERVED in Erb's (C8-T1 spared) but absent in Klumpke's
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: Grasp is PRESERVED in Erb's (C8-T1 spared) but absent in Klumpke's
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: In Erb's palsy the Moro is absent on the affected side but the GRASP reflex is preserved because C8-T1 (hand) is spared. In Klumpke's (C8-T1), the grasp reflex is lost - this distinguishes them.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: A macrosomic baby of a mother with gestational diabetes develops Erb's palsy. Which additional injuries should be actively excluded?
options: Clavicle/humeral fracture and phrenic nerve (diaphragm) palsy
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: Clavicle/humeral fracture and phrenic nerve (diaphragm) palsy
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Erb's palsy co-occurs with clavicle/humeral fracture (shoulder dystocia) and phrenic nerve palsy (C3-5) causing ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paralysis and respiratory distress - both should be checked for.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: What is the first-line management of Erb's palsy?
options: Immediate nerve grafting in the neonatal period
Amputation of the affected upper limb
Permanent splinting of the arm in adduction
Conservative management with physiotherapy to prevent contractures
A course of high-dose intravenous corticosteroids
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: Conservative management with physiotherapy to prevent contractures
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Erb's palsy is managed conservatively with physiotherapy/OT (gentle passive range-of-movement and positioning to prevent contractures) while the nerve recovers. Surgery is reserved for the minority with no recovery by ~3 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: A baby with a brachial plexus injury also has ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. What does this indicate?
options: T1 involvement (Horner's), meaning a more extensive injury and worse prognosis
A better prognosis, since T1 sparing means a limited upper-trunk injury
An isolated C5 nerve root injury with no involvement of the lower roots
An associated phrenic nerve palsy causing diaphragmatic weakness
A normal newborn variant of no clinical or prognostic significance
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: T1 involvement (Horner's), meaning a more extensive injury and worse prognosis
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis are Horner's syndrome, indicating T1 root involvement/avulsion - a marker of a more extensive, severe injury with a worse prognosis (classically seen with lower-plexus/Klumpke's injury).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: By roughly what age would no recovery in Erb's palsy prompt referral for possible surgery?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Recovery is monitored conservatively; failure to show meaningful recovery by around 3 months suggests rupture/avulsion rather than a stretch, and prompts referral for consideration of nerve reconstruction surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: What is the correct obstetric response to shoulder dystocia that helps prevent Erb's palsy?
options: Strong downward traction on the fetal head
Applying fundal pressure to deliver the shoulder
McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure, avoiding head traction
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure, avoiding head traction
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Erb's palsy is classically caused by excessive traction on the fetal head during shoulder dystocia. The correct response is the McRoberts manoeuvre plus suprapubic pressure (not head traction or fundal pressure).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: A newborn delivered by a difficult breech (arm extended overhead) has a 'claw hand' with hyperextended MCP joints and flexed IP joints, and an absent grasp reflex. Which nerve roots are injured?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: A claw hand with lost grasp reflex after traction on an abducted/overhead arm is Klumpke's palsy, from injury to the lower brachial plexus (C8-T1). C5-C6 injury causes Erb's palsy ('waiter's tip').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: Which additional finding is classically associated with Klumpke's palsy and indicates a poor prognosis?
options: A lower motor neurone facial palsy
Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) from T1 avulsion
Absent Moro with intact hand function
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) from T1 avulsion
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Klumpke's palsy is classically associated with Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) due to T1 root avulsion - a marker of severe injury and poor prognosis. Phrenic nerve palsy is more associated with upper-plexus (Erb's) injury.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: Which feature distinguishes Klumpke's palsy from Erb's palsy on examination?
options: The hand and grasp are affected but shoulder and elbow are preserved
Shoulder abduction is lost in Klumpke's
Klumpke's causes a waiter's tip posture
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: The hand and grasp are affected but shoulder and elbow are preserved
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: In Klumpke's (C8-T1) the intrinsic hand muscles and finger/wrist flexors are paralysed (claw hand, grasp absent) while shoulder and elbow movement are preserved - the reverse of Erb's, where the shoulder/elbow are affected and the hand/grasp are spared.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: Where is sensory loss found in Klumpke's palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Sensory loss in Klumpke's palsy is over the medial (ulnar) aspect of the forearm and hand, corresponding to the C8-T1 dermatomes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: Why does Klumpke's palsy carry a worse prognosis than Erb's palsy?
options: The upper roots are always avulsed in this injury
It is considerably more common than Erb’s palsy
It never requires any surgical intervention
It affects only the shoulder girdle muscles
The lower roots are more often avulsed than stretched, so recovery is less likely
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: The lower roots are more often avulsed than stretched, so recovery is less likely
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Klumpke's has a worse prognosis because the lower roots (particularly T1) are more frequently AVULSED (rather than merely stretched); avulsions do not recover spontaneously, so surgery is more often required.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.question: What is the first-line management of Klumpke's palsy?
options: Immediate surgical amputation of the affected limb to prevent fixed contractures
Conservative care with physiotherapy, splinting and positioning, referring at ~3 months
Permanent casting of the arm in full extension until the palsy resolves
A prolonged course of high-dose oral corticosteroids to reduce nerve swelling
No treatment is needed at any stage, because recovery is always complete
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.answer: Conservative care with physiotherapy, splinting and positioning, referring at ~3 months
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Birth Injuries.explanation: Klumpke's palsy is first managed conservatively with physiotherapy/OT, wrist-hand splinting (given the claw deformity) and positioning to prevent contractures, with referral for nerve reconstruction if there is no recovery by ~3 months (more often needed than in Erb's).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: A 3-year-old with CP begins losing motor skills he had previously acquired. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Expected progression of the brain lesion
That this is NOT cerebral palsy — think neurodegenerative or metabolic
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.answer: That this is NOT cerebral palsy — think neurodegenerative or metabolic
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: CP is non-progressive - the child does not lose acquired skills. Genuine REGRESSION suggests a progressive neurodegenerative or metabolic disorder, not cerebral palsy, and should be investigated (e.g. genetic/metabolic testing).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: At which point in development does most cerebral palsy arise?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: About 80% of CP is antenatal in origin (cerebral malformations, congenital TORCH infection, vascular/genetic causes). Perinatal (HIE, prematurity/PVL, kernicterus) and postnatal (meningitis, head injury) causes account for ~10% each.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: A child born very prematurely has spastic diplegia with legs affected far more than arms and a scissoring gait. Which lesion is classically responsible?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: Prematurity predisposes to periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), the classic white-matter lesion behind spastic DIPLEGIA (legs >> arms, scissoring/tiptoe gait).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: Which is the commonest motor type of cerebral palsy, and where is the lesion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: Spastic CP is commonest (~70%) and reflects upper motor neuron damage (motor cortex/pyramidal tracts), producing increased (velocity-dependent) tone, hyperreflexia and clonus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: A child with a history of severe neonatal jaundice has athetoid (slow writhing) movements, dystonia and drooling. Which type of CP and lesion site is this?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: Athetosis/dystonia with oro-motor problems following kernicterus indicates DYSKINETIC CP from BASAL GANGLIA injury (bilirubin is toxic to the basal ganglia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: Which is a NICE motor red flag prompting assessment for cerebral palsy?
options: Hand preference established before 12 months of age
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.answer: Hand preference established before 12 months of age
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: Established hand preference BEFORE 12 months is a red flag (suggesting a hemiplegia). Other NICE red flags: not sitting by 8 months (corrected), not walking by 18 months, and persistent toe-walking. Walking at 13 months and sitting at 7 months are normal.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: Which two comorbidities are among the most commonly associated with cerebral palsy?
options: Congenital heart disease and cleft palate
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: CP is never 'just' a motor disorder: learning disability affects about half and epilepsy about a third, alongside visual/hearing impairment, speech/feeding difficulties and orthopaedic problems (hip dislocation, scoliosis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: What is the main role of MRI brain in cerebral palsy?
options: To make the diagnosis, which cannot be clinical
To accurately date a hypoxic-ischaemic injury
To investigate the underlying aetiology when the cause is unclear
To measure the degree of spasticity objectively
To screen for epilepsy before it becomes clinical
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.answer: To investigate the underlying aetiology when the cause is unclear
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: CP is largely a clinical diagnosis; MRI is used to investigate the underlying cause (PVL, malformation, HIE) when it is unclear. It does not accurately date a hypoxic-ischaemic injury, and subtle changes may not be visible until ~2 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: A child with spastic CP has focal spasticity of the calf causing toe-walking, despite physiotherapy. Which targeted treatment is appropriate?
options: Botulinum toxin type A injection to the affected muscle
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.answer: Botulinum toxin type A injection to the affected muscle
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: For FOCAL spasticity, botulinum toxin type A injection to the affected muscle is appropriate (alongside physiotherapy). Oral diazepam and baclofen are non-targeted; intrathecal baclofen is reserved for severe generalised spasticity, and selective dorsal rhizotomy for selected ambulant children with spastic diplegia at GMFCS II–III.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: Which single feature would argue AGAINST a diagnosis of cerebral palsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: CP is non-progressive, so REGRESSION (loss of acquired skills) argues against it and points to a progressive disorder. Delayed milestones, increased tone, persistent primitive reflexes and early hand preference are all consistent with CP.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: What is the overarching goal of cerebral palsy management?
options: Surgery aimed at curing the underlying brain lesion
Prolonged bed rest to prevent deformity developing
Care delivered by a single specialist working alone
An MDT approach maximising function and quality of life — there is no cure
Orthopaedic surgery for every child at diagnosis
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.answer: An MDT approach maximising function and quality of life — there is no cure
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: There is no cure for CP; management is a multidisciplinary effort to maximise function, participation and quality of life and to manage the many comorbidities (feeding, epilepsy, orthopaedic, sensory).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: A child with cerebral palsy and quadriplegia has an unsafe swallow with recurrent aspiration and faltering growth. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: SALT assessment and consideration of gastrostomy feeding
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.answer: SALT assessment and consideration of gastrostomy feeding
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: An unsafe swallow with aspiration and faltering growth warrants SALT assessment and often gastrostomy feeding to provide safe nutrition. Continuing/increasing oral feeds would risk further aspiration.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.question: Which type of CP localises to the cerebellum and presents with incoordination, intention tremor and an ataxic gait?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Cerebral Palsy.explanation: Ataxic CP reflects a cerebellar lesion, producing cerebellar signs - incoordination, intention tremor, ataxic gait and hypotonia. Spastic = UMN, dyskinetic = basal ganglia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Which pair of childhood exanthems below are BOTH statutory notifiable diseases?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Measles and scarlet fever
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Measles, rubella and scarlet fever are all notifiable, and chickenpox is now notifiable in England and Northern Ireland (not Scotland or Wales) — notify the Health Protection Team on clinical suspicion. Of the pairs offered, only measles and scarlet fever contains two notifiable diseases across the whole UK; roseola, hand-foot-and-mouth and parvovirus B19 are not notifiable anywhere.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A rash described as a bright red 'slapped cheek' followed by a lacy body rash is caused by which organism?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Parvovirus B19
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: The 'slapped cheek' appearance (erythema infectiosum, fifth disease) is caused by parvovirus B19, which is dangerous in chronic haemolytic anaemia (aplastic crisis) and pregnancy (hydrops fetalis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A miserable, feverish child has cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, then white spots on the buccal mucosa, followed by a blotchy rash spreading down from behind the ears. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Measles
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: High fever with the 3 C's (Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis), Koplik spots (pathognomonic buccal spots), and a maculopapular rash spreading downward from behind the ears in an unwell child is classic measles.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: What is the most appropriate FIRST action on clinically suspecting measles?
options: Wait for laboratory confirmation before taking any action
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent complications
Give the MMR vaccine to the patient to shorten the illness
Discharge with antipyretics and no planned follow-up
Notify the Health Protection Team the same day and isolate
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Notify the Health Protection Team the same day and isolate
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Measles is notifiable - notify the Health Protection Team the same day on clinical suspicion (do not wait for labs) and isolate immediately, as it is extremely contagious. Confirmation is by oral fluid IgM/PCR.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A non-immune pregnant woman is exposed to measles. What is the appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Human normal immunoglobulin (HNIG) within 6 days
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: MMR is a live vaccine, contraindicated in pregnancy. A susceptible pregnant contact should receive human normal immunoglobulin (HNIG) within 6 days of exposure. Immunocompetent, non-pregnant contacts can have MMR within 72 hours.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Which is the commonest cause of death in measles?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Pneumonia
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Pneumonia is the commonest cause of death in measles. Otitis media is the commonest complication overall; encephalitis (~1/1000) and SSPE (rare, fatal, years later) are serious neurological complications.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A supportive measure that reduces morbidity and mortality in measles, particularly in young/admitted children, is:
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Vitamin A
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Vitamin A is the only listed measure with evidence of reducing measles morbidity and mortality, but in the UK it is not routine — it is reserved for selected admitted children (under 2 years, malnourished, or with diarrhoea) after paediatric infectious diseases advice, and is not prescribed in the community. Antibiotics are used only for secondary bacterial infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A child has a mild fever, a faint pink maculopapular rash spreading from the face, and tender lymph nodes behind the ears and at the occiput. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Rubella
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: A mild illness with tender POSTAURICULAR/suboccipital/posterior cervical lymphadenopathy preceding a faint pink maculopapular rash ('three-day measles') is rubella. The prominent tender posterior nodes are the classic discriminator.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Why is rubella clinically important?
options: It commonly causes encephalitis in children, with lasting neurological damage
It causes an aplastic crisis in children with sickle cell disease or thalassaemia
It is usually fatal in children unless treated with antivirals within 48 hours
It causes a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue needing penicillin for 10 days
Infection in early pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome in the baby
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Infection in early pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome in the baby
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Rubella is usually trivial in a child; its importance is congenital rubella syndrome (deafness, cataracts, PDA) if a non-immune woman is infected in early pregnancy - risk is highest before 12 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A pregnant woman at 10 weeks is exposed to rubella. Which statement is correct?
options: The MMR vaccine should be given immediately to prevent fetal infection
Nothing prevents CRS once infected; MMR is contraindicated until postpartum
Immunoglobulin given within 72 hours reliably prevents congenital rubella syndrome
Rubella poses no risk in pregnancy once the first trimester is under way
Aciclovir started within 24 hours of exposure prevents fetal infection
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Nothing prevents CRS once infected; MMR is contraindicated until postpartum
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: No treatment reliably prevents CRS once maternal infection occurs; management is serology and counselling about fetal risk. MMR is a LIVE vaccine, contraindicated in pregnancy - susceptible women are vaccinated postpartum (avoiding pregnancy for ~1 month).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A 2-year-old has a mild fever, painful mouth ulcers, and small greyish vesicles on the palms, soles and buttocks. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Hand, foot and mouth disease
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Painful oral ulcers plus vesicles on the hands, feet (and buttocks) in a young child is hand, foot and mouth disease (usually Coxsackievirus A16). Chickenpox is widespread/truncal with crops of different stages; herpangina affects the mouth only.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: What is the most important supportive priority in a toddler with hand, foot and mouth disease?
options: Preventing dehydration by encouraging fluid intake
A course of oral antibiotics to clear the infection
Oral aciclovir started within 24 hours of the rash
Strict school exclusion until the lesions have healed
Topical corticosteroids applied to the hands and feet
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Preventing dehydration by encouraging fluid intake
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: The commonest practical problem is dehydration from the painful oral ulcers, so encouraging fluids (with analgesia) is the priority. It is a self-limiting viral illness needing no antivirals/antibiotics, and UK guidance does not require school exclusion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Which enterovirus is associated with more severe, neurological hand-foot-mouth disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Enterovirus 71
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Enterovirus 71 (EV71) is associated with more severe disease and neurological complications (encephalitis, meningitis). Coxsackievirus A16 is the commonest, usually mild, cause; A6 causes a more extensive rash with later nail shedding.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A child with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe anaemia with a very low reticulocyte count after a viral illness. Which infection is most likely responsible?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Parvovirus B19
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Parvovirus B19 destroys erythroid precursors, causing a transient APLASTIC CRISIS (severe anaemia with reticulocytopenia) in people with chronic haemolytic anaemia such as sickle cell disease - often requiring transfusion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A non-immune pregnant woman is infected with parvovirus B19. What is the main fetal risk and its management?
options: Congenital cataracts and deafness; give the mother MMR to limit fetal damage
Hydrops fetalis from fetal anaemia — fetal medicine referral and MCA Doppler
A sandpaper rash in the newborn; treat the mother with penicillin for 10 days
No fetal risk at all, so no monitoring or referral is needed at any gestation
Limb reduction defects, for which termination of pregnancy is mandatory
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Hydrops fetalis from fetal anaemia — fetal medicine referral and MCA Doppler
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy can cause fetal anaemia leading to hydrops fetalis and loss (especially <20 weeks). Management is fetal surveillance (serial ultrasound + middle cerebral artery Doppler) and intrauterine blood transfusion if severe anaemia/hydrops develops.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A well child is diagnosed with slapped cheek syndrome now that the facial rash has appeared. What should you advise about school?
options: Exclude from school until the facial rash has completely faded
Exclude from school for 4 days after the appearance of the rash
Exclude from school for 3 weeks, the full period of viral shedding
None needed — they are no longer infectious once the rash has appeared
Exclude from school until repeat serology confirms they are negative
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: None needed — they are no longer infectious once the rash has appeared
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Parvovirus B19 is infectious BEFORE the rash; once the slapped-cheek rash appears the child is no longer infectious, so no school exclusion is required. (The exception is a patient in aplastic crisis, who is still viraemic and infectious.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A 7-year-old has fever, sore throat, a fine 'sandpaper' rash sparing the area around the mouth, and a red, swollen tongue with prominent papillae. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
options: Scarlet fever; oral penicillin V for 10 days
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Scarlet fever; oral penicillin V for 10 days
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Fever and sore throat with a sandpaper rash, circumoral pallor and strawberry tongue is scarlet fever (Group A Strep). First-line treatment is oral phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) four times daily for 10 days, at 62.5/125/250/500 mg by age band (clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Which feature favours scarlet fever (bacterial) over a viral exanthem?
options: A prominent barking cough with marked coryza and conjunctivitis
A rash appearing after the fever resolves
A sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue and no cough or coryza
Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa before the rash appears
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: A sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue and no cough or coryza
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Scarlet fever features a sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue and exudative pharyngitis, with cough/coryza typically ABSENT (favouring bacterial). Cough/coryza, fever-then-rash, post-auricular nodes and Koplik spots point to viral causes/measles.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Why is it important to treat scarlet fever with antibiotics?
options: To stop the streptococcal infection from converting into a viral illness
Because scarlet fever is always life-threatening without immediate treatment
To prevent Koplik spots developing on the buccal mucosa later in the illness
Antibiotics are not actually needed, as scarlet fever always self-resolves
To shorten illness, cut transmission, and prevent rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: To shorten illness, cut transmission, and prevent rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Antibiotics shorten the illness, reduce transmission, and reduce both suppurative complications and non-suppurative immune complications - especially acute rheumatic fever (and, less preventably, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: For how long should a child with scarlet fever be excluded from school after starting antibiotics?
options: No exclusion is needed at any point in the illness
Until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics
For 5 days from the onset of the rash
Until the rash has fully desquamated
For a fixed 10 days from diagnosis
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: A child with scarlet fever should be excluded from school until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics (and until they feel well).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A child has an intensely itchy rash with macules, papules, vesicles and crusts all present at the same time, spreading from the trunk. What is the diagnosis and the key distinguishing feature?
options: Hand, foot and mouth; a peripheral distribution
Measles; a confluent rash spreading from the face
Scarlet fever; a fine sandpaper-textured rash
Chickenpox; lesions of different stages present at once
Roseola; a rash appearing as the fever settles
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Chickenpox; lesions of different stages present at once
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Chickenpox (primary VZV) produces an itchy vesicular rash appearing in successive crops, so lesions of DIFFERENT stages (macule, papule, vesicle, crust) are present at the same time - the key distinguishing feature.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Which analgesics/antipyretics should be AVOIDED in chickenpox, and why?
options: NSAIDs (severe soft-tissue infection) and aspirin in under-16s (Reye's)
Paracetamol, because it is the drug that causes Reye’s syndrome in children
All analgesia is contraindicated in chickenpox until the lesions have crusted
Only topical agents should be avoided, as they trap heat in the lesions
Antihistamines, because they are linked to varicella encephalitis in children
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: NSAIDs (severe soft-tissue infection) and aspirin in under-16s (Reye's)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: In chickenpox, NSAIDs/ibuprofen are avoided (linked to severe skin/soft-tissue infection, e.g. invasive GAS/necrotising fasciitis), and aspirin is avoided in under-16s due to Reye's syndrome. Paracetamol is the antipyretic of choice.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A healthy 5-year-old with uncomplicated chickenpox is seen on day 2 of the rash. What is the appropriate management?
options: Supportive care only (do not routinely give aciclovir)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Supportive care only (do not routinely give aciclovir)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: In a healthy child over 1 month, chickenpox is mild and self-limiting - management is supportive only (do NOT routinely give aciclovir). Antivirals are reserved for adolescents/adults (oral, within 24h) and immunocompromised/neonates/severe disease (IV).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Until when should a child with chickenpox be excluded from school?
options: Until 24 hours after the rash first appears on the trunk
For a fixed 10 days from rash onset, regardless of the lesions
Until the fever has settled and the child feels well again
No exclusion is needed, as chickenpox is only mildly infectious
At least 5 days from the onset of the rash AND until all lesions have crusted over
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: At least 5 days from the onset of the rash AND until all lesions have crusted over
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: A child with chickenpox is infectious from ~2 days before the rash until all lesions have crusted. UKHSA gives both criteria for exclusion: at least 5 days from the onset of the rash and until all lesions have crusted over.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A 10-month-old has 3 days of high fever but looks relatively well; the fever then abruptly resolves and a rose-pink, non-itchy rash appears on the trunk. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Roseola infantum
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: High fever for ~3 days in a relatively well infant, followed by a rose-pink truncal rash appearing AFTER the fever breaks, is roseola infantum (HHV-6). The rash marking recovery (after the fever) is the classic discriminator from measles.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: What is the commonest complication of roseola infantum?
options: An aplastic crisis with severe anaemia
Febrile convulsions during the fever phase
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Febrile convulsions during the fever phase
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Febrile convulsions are the commonest complication of roseola, triggered by the high fever in the susceptible 6-month-to-2-year age group; they are usually benign and self-limiting.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: During the febrile phase of roseola (before the rash appears), what is the key clinical priority?
options: Assess the high-fever infant for serious bacterial infection
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Assess the high-fever infant for serious bacterial infection
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Before the diagnostic rash appears, a high-fever infant must be assessed for serious bacterial infection; once the characteristic rash emerges after the fever resolves, it is reassuring and confirms the benign diagnosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Which rare, fatal, late complication of measles occurs years after infection, with higher risk if infected under 2 years old?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: SSPE is a rare, fatal, late complication (~7-10 years later) from persistent measles virus in the CNS, causing progressive behavioural/intellectual decline, myoclonus, seizures and death; risk is higher if infected under 2 years of age.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: How does the measles rash differ from that of secondary syphilis in distribution?
options: Measles involves the palms and soles
Both spare the palms and soles
Measles SPARES the palms and soles (unlike secondary syphilis)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Measles SPARES the palms and soles (unlike secondary syphilis)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: The measles rash is maculopapular, spreads downward from behind the ears becoming confluent, and SPARES the palms and soles - unlike secondary syphilis, which characteristically involves the palms and soles.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: For how long after the rash onset should a child with measles be excluded from school?
options: At least 4 days after the onset of the rash
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: At least 4 days after the onset of the rash
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: A child with measles should be excluded from school/nursery until at least 4 days after the onset of the rash (measles is infectious from ~4 days before to 4 days after the rash), and kept away from susceptible people.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: An immunocompetent, non-pregnant child is a susceptible contact of a confirmed measles case, seen 2 days after exposure. What is the appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis?
options: No prophylaxis is available after exposure
The MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: The MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: For an immunocompetent, non-pregnant susceptible contact, MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure is appropriate PEP. HNIG (within 6 days) is reserved for those in whom the live vaccine is contraindicated - pregnant women, the immunocompromised, and infants.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: What is the classic triad of congenital rubella syndrome?
options: Deafness, cataracts and congenital heart disease (PDA)
Short stature, webbed neck and coarctation
Hypotonia, single palmar crease and AVSD
Rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia and clenched fists
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Deafness, cataracts and congenital heart disease (PDA)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Congenital rubella syndrome classically causes sensorineural deafness, cataracts and congenital heart disease (particularly patent ductus arteriosus), with the greatest risk from infection before 12 weeks' gestation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Approximately what proportion of rubella infections are asymptomatic, and why does this matter?
options: ~25-50% are subclinical, yet can still infect a pregnant contact
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: ~25-50% are subclinical, yet can still infect a pregnant contact
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: About 25-50% of rubella is asymptomatic/subclinical, which matters because silent infection can still transmit the virus to a non-immune pregnant contact, risking congenital rubella syndrome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Which finding, seen in ~20% of rubella cases, is supportive but not diagnostic?
options: Forchheimer spots (petechiae on the soft palate)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Forchheimer spots (petechiae on the soft palate)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Forchheimer spots (petechiae on the soft palate, ~20%) are supportive but not diagnostic of rubella. Koplik spots are measles; strawberry tongue/Pastia's lines are scarlet fever; Nagayama spots are roseola.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Why was routine antenatal rubella screening stopped in the UK in 2016?
options: Because high MMR-driven herd immunity made individual screening low-value
Because rubella is no longer notifiable
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Because high MMR-driven herd immunity made individual screening low-value
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Antenatal rubella screening was stopped in the UK in April 2016 because MMR-driven herd immunity had made individual antenatal screening low-value; the programme goal is herd immunity to protect pregnant women.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: A child recovering from hand, foot and mouth disease sheds several nails weeks later. What is this, and is it concerning?
options: Onychomadesis - a benign, self-resolving sequela (especially Coxsackie A6)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Onychomadesis - a benign, self-resolving sequela (especially Coxsackie A6)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Onychomadesis (nail shedding) can occur weeks after hand, foot and mouth disease, especially with Coxsackievirus A6. It is benign and self-resolving and needs no specific treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: How is hand, foot and mouth disease distinguished from herpangina?
options: Herpangina is mouth-only, whereas HFMD also has vesicles on the hands and feet
Herpangina affects the hands and feet
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Herpangina is mouth-only, whereas HFMD also has vesicles on the hands and feet
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Herpangina (same enterovirus family) causes mouth-only vesicles/ulcers, whereas hand, foot and mouth disease additionally has vesicles on the hands, feet (and often buttocks). Chickenpox is more widespread/truncal with crops of different stages.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Why is school exclusion not required for hand, foot and mouth disease in the UK?
options: Because hand, foot and mouth disease is not contagious between children
Because it is a notifiable disease and is handled centrally by UKHSA instead
Exclusion does not reduce spread — stool shedding continues for weeks
Because a short course of antibiotics clears the infection within a few days
Because it affects only adults, so school contacts are never at risk
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Exclusion does not reduce spread — stool shedding continues for weeks
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: UK guidance does not require school exclusion for HFMD - exclusion does not reduce spread because the virus is shed in the stool for weeks regardless, so children can attend once they feel well enough.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: By what mechanism does parvovirus B19 cause its dangerous complications?
options: It suppresses platelet production in the bone marrow
It damages hepatocytes, causing a transient hepatitis
It triggers autoimmune destruction of circulating neutrophils
It causes progressive fibrosis of the bone marrow space
It destroys erythroid progenitors by binding the P antigen
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: It destroys erythroid progenitors by binding the P antigen
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Parvovirus B19 targets and destroys erythroid progenitor cells (binding the P antigen on red-cell precursors), halting red-cell production - harmless briefly in health, but catastrophic in chronic haemolytic anaemia (aplastic crisis) or a fetus (severe anaemia/hydrops).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: Which is a recognised feature of parvovirus B19 infection in adults, particularly women?
options: A fine sandpaper rash on the trunk
A strawberry tongue with prominent papillae
Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Symmetrical small-joint arthralgia or arthritis
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.explanation: Parvovirus B19 commonly causes a symmetrical small-joint arthralgia/arthritis in adults, especially women (sometimes the only feature); a 'gloves and socks' papular-purpuric eruption is also seen mainly in adults.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.question: An immunocompromised patient develops chronic anaemia (persistent red-cell aplasia) from parvovirus B19. What treatment may help?
options: Repeated blood transfusion alone, without any other specific treatment
A prolonged course of oral aciclovir to suppress viral replication
Erythropoietin alone to stimulate the marrow to make red cells
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, which contains anti-B19 antibodies)
Bone marrow transplantation to replace the failing erythroid line
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Childhood Exant.answer: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, which contains anti-B19 antibodies)
